name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska Supreme Court affirms state’s election ballot measure language, with one change
description: The Alaska Supreme Court issued a fast-tracked ruling on Thursday, affirming a lower court’s decision that the Alaska Division of Elections’ language for an elections overhaul ballot measure is “true and impartial,” but ordered the division to make one additional change.  The Court issued the ruling days after hearing oral arguments from two groups of […]
text:
A voter joins a line of voters waiting to cast their ballots on Aug. 15, 2022, at the state Division of Elections office in Anchorage. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)The Alaska Supreme Court issued a fast-tracked ruling on Thursday, affirming a lower court’s decision that the Alaska Division of Elections’ language for an elections overhaul ballot measure is “true and impartial,” but ordered the division to make one additional change. 
The Court issued the ruling days after hearing oral arguments from two groups of plaintiffs on opposing sides of the current ranked-choice voting system. The groups appealed a lower court’s ruling issued in June, challenging the language of Ballot Measure 2 as unclear, politically partisan and containing omissions they sought to change.
Ballot Measure 2, which will appear on the ballot as 24ESEG, would repeal the state’s current ranked choice voting and open primary systems, as well as repeal campaign disclosure rules enacted by voters in 2020.
The Supreme Court ruling Thursday affirmed a Superior Court’s finding that the Alaska Division of Elections’ fulfilled its legal duty in preparing the ballot measure title and summary in a “true and impartial” manner. 
But the justices identified one omission: the division must add language that explains if the measure is approved, and nonpartisan, open primaries are eliminated, candidates for Governor and Lieutenant Governor would run for election separately.
Currently, candidates for Governor and Lieutenant Governor run together on a combined ticket in the primary election. The top-four vote getters in the open primary advance to the ranked choice general election. 
A spokesperson for the Alaska Department of Law, which defended the division and its ballot measure language in court, said by email Friday they welcomed the ruling and would make the change.  
“We are pleased that the Alaska Supreme Court rejected nearly all the challenges to the lieutenant governor’s true and impartial ballot summary,” said Sam Curtis, an information officer. He called the court’s directive a small change. 
“The State had considered this a minor detail that did not need to be in a ballot summary, but the Court disagreed,” he said. “The Office of the Lieutenant Governor will issue a revised summary soon.”
The revised language is expected to be published by the division before a ballot printing deadline of Sep. 2. 
Both groups of plaintiffs that filed appeals in court expressed mixed reactions, saying they were “disappointed” but “appreciated” the court’s decision. 
One group of plaintiffs that also sponsored the ballot measure, called the “Repeal Now” campaign, filed a lawsuit challenging the language in court. Among a series of language changes requested, they had argued for language to explain the governor and lieutenant governor would run separately. Their attorney Julie Pack said by email Thursday they maintained concerns. 
“We’re disappointed that the summary will continue to incorrectly state that open primaries would end with Ballot Measure 2,” Pack wrote. “Primaries would remain defaulted at open following Ballot Measure 2’s passage, just like they previously were.”
The group argued, in part, that if approved Alaskans would still vote in “open primaries.” 
But the ballot measure language states “the act would get rid of open party primaries.” That’s because if voters approve the measure, the elections system would revert to a “closed,” partisan primary system where voters would only be able to vote for a candidate in the party they’re registered with. 
Voters would no longer be able to vote for candidates of any party running for statewide and federal offices, as they currently do.
The issue is of particular concern to another group of plaintiffs that filed suit in court, represented by attorney Scott Kendall, who was one of the primary sponsors of the 2020 ballot implementing the current ranked-choice voting system. 
He argued the current language on the ballot measure related to how the primaries would change is incomplete. 
“Our specific request was that it be made more clear that each political party will have the power to not only close their primaries, but to close them and make it unlawful for undeclareds and nonpartisans to vote,” Kendall said in an interview Friday. “There’s some language in the ballot measure that gestures at that, but I don’t think it really makes it clear.”
Overall Kendall said the group is grateful to the court and division for rejecting language proposed by Repeal Now he called “radical changes.” 
“We’re very, very grateful that the court correctly rejected those baseless edits,” he said. 
Kendall said the Supreme Court’s added change is “a good one.”
“It wasn’t so much about what’s good policy, bad policy. It was when a voter steps into the booth and picks up the pen, are they equipped with full knowledge of what their yes or no vote means?”



Ballot Measure 2 as currently proposed by the Alaska Division of Elections:
An Act Restoring Political Party Primaries, Ending Ranked Choice-General Elections, and Repealing Recent Campaign Finance Laws
This Act would get rid of open primary elections, where all candidates appear on one ballot. It would also get rid of ranked-choice general elections. It would bring back political party primaries and single-choice general elections. It would also repeal certain campaign finance rules that were added by a 2020 ballot measure.
Elections would occur as they did before open primaries and ranked choice elections. In the primary election, voters would choose a party’s ballot, unless prohibited by the party’s bylaws. They would only vote for candidates on that ballot. The winning candidates from each primary would be the party’s nominee. In the general election, voters would vote for only one candidate in each race. Party petitions, special runoff elections, and other processes would return.
This act would repeal campaign finance rules that were passed in 2020. It would remove the limits on donations to joint campaigns for governor and lieutenant governor. It would remove limits and disclosure rules under current law, including for digital ads, out-of-state donations, undisclosed donations and the true source of donations. It would change the meaning of a campaign expenditure and remove some fines.
Should this initiative become law?

title: ISU gets federal funding to support Watershed Innovation Farm in Ames
description: Iowa State University, in collaboration with Iowa Learning Farms, is working to build out water quality practices on and around its dairy farm in Ames as part of the Watershed Innovation Farm, which will include trails and signage for Iowans to learn about the practices. The project was recently awarded nearly $1 million from the […]
text:
Wetlands are an edge-of-field strategy used to try to improve water quality near farmland. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Iowa State University, in collaboration with Iowa Learning Farms, is working to build out water quality practices on and around its dairy farm in Ames as part of the Watershed Innovation Farm, which will include trails and signage for Iowans to learn about the practices.
The project was recently awarded nearly $1 million from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency as part of a funding package for “innovative” solutions that improve water quality in the Gulf of Mexico watershed. The Watershed Innovation Farm also has funding from the Iowa Department of Natural Resources and Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Jacqueline Comito, the director of Iowa Learning Farms, said the project will have bioreactors, saturated buffers, wetlands, grassed waterways and signage throughout that explains the practices and their benefits. 
Comito said water quality solutions involve a “suite” of different practices, and the innovation farm will “help explain” that to farmers, professionals, lawmakers, students and everyday Iowans who visit the “walking, scientific laboratory.”
“Water quality is important, and hopefully, people can see what some of the solutions are,” Comito said. 
Many of the projects, like several saturated buffers, a water quality improvement wetland and bioreactors that are already deployed at the farm were installed with cost-share funding from IDALS, according to Comito. 
While these practices have been installed at various farms across Iowa, Comito said the Watershed Innovation Farm will serve as a central area for folks to visit. The project will also showcase how the practices interact with one another and with an urban environment as the site sits alongside the city of Ames.
“Most of these practices were either initiated at Iowa State or developed here, so we’ve been cutting-edge with so much,” Comito said. “Now, one of our research farms is going to be like the ideal location to go out and really learn how these all connect and how they relate.” 
In addition to more common water quality improvement practices, Comito said the innovation farm will also explore woodland management practices in part of the existing wooded areas of the property.
Comito said ISU Extension Forestry Specialist Billy Beck will work on managing the wooded areas to show how the right interventions can make for a healthy woodland area. She said the EPA funding will help support drones that will help monitor woodland canopy and water quality in the area. 
“We know how each individual practice is effective,” Comito said. “This farm gives the opportunity to be able to look at it from the bigger picture.”
Many of these practices “don’t look like anything” from the surface. A bioreactor, for example, is a trench of wood chips buried along a drainage tile outlet to help filter out nutrients from the water. A saturated buffer, to the untrained eye, looks like an area of native or tall grasses. 
Comito, who is an anthropologist, said that’s why she is focused on making sure the signs throughout the farm “make sense” to visitors who walk or eventually bike on paths through the area. The signs will have illustrations explaining the agricultural, water quality and habitat benefits of the deployed practices and QR codes linking to additional information.
“The idea of this is that you should be able to go out there and understand what’s going on without somebody telling you,” Comito said.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Warnock calls for Georgia data center moratorium
description: This coverage is made possible through a partnership between WABE and Grist, a nonprofit environmental media organization. U.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock is calling for a statewide moratorium on data centers after visiting the site where OpenAI is planning a massive data center in coastal Georgia.  The OpenAI data center in Effingham County has drawn widespread [[...]
text:
Effingham County resident John Smith speaks after meeting with U.S. Senator Raphael Warnock about concerns over a proposed OpenAI data center. (Emily Jones/WABE)This coverage is made possible through a partnership between WABE and Grist, a nonprofit environmental media organization.
U.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock is calling for a statewide moratorium on data centers after visiting the site where OpenAI is planning a massive data center in coastal Georgia. 
The OpenAI data center in Effingham County has drawn widespread opposition from locals since it was announced last month. Many were surprised, and have called for more information about the project and a greater say in how it proceeds. After meeting with concerned residents on Friday, Warnock echoed their concerns at a press conference. 
“I’m demanding that those who come here to build, to create jobs and bring new opportunities, also take the time to build relationships with the people who already call this home,” he said.
OpenAI has said it will provide $80 million for a community fund and translate local concerns into specific commitments and accountability measures.
Warnock applauded the community for coming together to oppose the data center.
“In a nation and in a county or in a state where people say folks are divided, the residents of Effingham County are united in their concern about what’s about to happen to their community, and they’re demanding that their voices be heard,” he said.
Local resident John Smith echoed that sentiment. He stressed that concerns about the project cut across political lines, and thanked the Democratic senator for visiting a county that often votes Republican.
“As a community, we expect and demand our elected representatives to look out for all of our best interests, even if we didn’t necessarily vote for them,” Smith said.
Another local resident, conservationist Isaiah Scott, said it’s rare for people to come together the way they have around opposing the OpenAI project. 
“This has been the most united I’ve seen the Effingham community,” Scott said. “It’s unfortunate that it has to be around being against this data center. But it makes me feel proud to see people voicing their opinions.”
A contract for Georgia Power to provide the OpenAI data center with electricity was just approved by state regulators. It calls for 3,200 megawatts of electricity -– the most since the utility started reporting its large customers’ contracts. The utility also agreed to additional measures aimed at protecting Georgia residents and small businesses from data center-related energy costs. 
Other coastal communities have come out against data centers since the project in Effingham was announced. Savannah recently approved a 155-day moratorium. City officials in Richmond Hill say their local development ordinance already prohibits data centers.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Judge denies new trial for Alabama inmate who cited defense attorney’s ties to KKK
description: A Morgan County judge Friday denied a new trial for a former Alabama death row inmate who cited evidence that his attorney at his first trial had ties to the Ku Klux Klan. Morgan County Circuit Court Judge Charles Elliott denied the motion from Robin “Rocky” Myers, who is currently serving a life sentence for […]
text:
A Morgan County Circuit Judge Friday denied former death row inmate Robin "Rocky" Myers a new trial over his conviction for the 1991 murder of Ludie Mae Tucker in Decatur. Myers, who maintains his innocence, cited evidence that his defense attorney at his first trial had ties to the Ku Klux Klan. (Alabama Department of Corrections)A Morgan County judge Friday denied a new trial for a former Alabama death row inmate who cited evidence that his attorney at his first trial had ties to the Ku Klux Klan.
Morgan County Circuit Court Judge Charles Elliott denied the motion from Robin “Rocky” Myers, who is currently serving a life sentence for his alleged role in the death of Ludie Mae Tucker in Decatur in 1991. Myers, who maintains his innocence, was originally sentenced to death, but Gov. Kay Ivey commuted it to life in prison last year.
Elliott wrote that the Rule 32 appeals process, which allows people convicted of a crime the opportunity to present arguments for a new trial, “establishes a bright line rule on when a claim for ineffective assistance of counsel claim can be made.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
‘“In no event can relief be granted on a claim of ineffective assistance of trial or appellate counsel raised in a successive petition,’” Elliott wrote. “The only exception to this bright line rule is when a petition is filed to be able to obtain an out-of-time appeal.”
Messages seeking comment were sent Friday to John Mays, the attorney who represented Myers at his first trial, and the Morgan County District Attorney’s Office.
“No court has ever heard evidence or ruled on the central claim in this petition: that the lawyer appointed to defend Rocky Myers, a Black man on trial for his life, had spent the previous decade as the corporate counsel, public spokesman, and ideological champion for the United Klans of America,” said J. Mitchell McGuire, counsel for Myers. “That question has never been ‘tested.’ It has been avoided.”
Myers, who lived across the street from Tucker, was accused of entering her home in October 1991 to use the phone, getting into an argument with her cousin and husband, and stabbing Tucker, who died in the hospital a few hours later.
No murder weapon was ever found, and Myers maintains he never entered her home. No physical evidence connected Myers to the scene, and witnesses gave different descriptions of the potential assailant. A jury recommended sentencing Myers to life in prison, but the trial judge imposed the death penalty.
Gov. Kay Ivey granted Myers’ clemency petition last year, saying she harbored doubts about his involvement in Tucker’s murder.
“I am not convinced that Mr. Myers is innocent, but I am not so convinced of his guilt as to approve of his execution,” Ivey said in the news release when she announced that his clemency petition had been granted. “I therefore must respect both the jury’s decision to convict him and its recommendation that he be sentenced to life without parole.”
Myers filed his most recent request in September for a hearing to receive a new trial after members of his legal team learned that his attorney, John Mays, spoke at nine KKK rallies between 1977 and 1981 and defended Robert Shelton, an imperial wizard of the KKK, in a lawsuit filed against the FBI in 1977.
According to a newspaper account, Mays used a racial epithet when he spoke at a 1977 KKK rally in Suffolk, Virginia before 200 people.
The court filing from Myers also states that Mays spoke at KKK rallies in Alabama, Florida, Virginia, Kentucky, Mississippi and Tennessee. At one rally in Tennessee in 1981, Mays “exhorted caucasians to band together in the face of an oncoming race war,” according to a newspaper article published in 1981.
The DA’s Office for Morgan County opposed Myers’ request for a hearing because the accounts of Mays’ presence at rallies were already available and could have been presented at trial.
Myers plans to appeal.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: How much ice hides in Timpanogos Rock Glacier? Researchers compared its volume to an ancient wonder
description: With a novel 3D technique, a University of Utah team has brought to light the unaccounted masses of ice hidden at the Timpanogos rock glacier, finding both a good measurement of how much ice it contains, and also how the rock glacier located near Salt Lake City and Provo formed. The Timpanogos Rock Glacier stores […]
text:
Mt. Timpanogos rock glacier. (Photo by Bronson Cvijanovich)With a novel 3D technique, a University of Utah team has brought to light the unaccounted masses of ice hidden at the Timpanogos rock glacier, finding both a good measurement of how much ice it contains, and also how the rock glacier located near Salt Lake City and Provo formed.
The Timpanogos Rock Glacier stores 1.5 million cubic meters of ice, a University of Utah news release says. That’s enough frozen water to fill 600 Olympic-sized swimming pools. The number is also similar to the volume of the largest pyramid in Giza, Egypt, said Bronson Cvijanovich, a former graduate student in the Department of Geology & Geophysics.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Timpanogos Rock Glacier is surprisingly ice rich. It is 83% ice and 17% loose rock,” said Cvijanovich, lead author of a study measuring the internal ice content of the rock glacier.
Rock glaciers are common in the Wasatch and Uinta ranges. Timpanogos is one of 836 in the state. While their footprints can be outlined with satellite imagery, “the 3D shape, depth and ice they obscure is harder to reveal,” the university said in the release. 
“There’s a lot of ice that’s hidden in Utah’s mountains,” said Leif Anderson, a glaciology professor who oversaw the study. “When we are high in the mountains and walking across loose rocks or rubble, you don’t realize there could be 120 feet of ice buried beneath your feet.”
To estimate the ice content, a team hiked about five miles in an elevation gain of 3,500 feet to get to the rock glacier on different occasions in 2024, hauling sensitive instruments, like a gravimeter, and took gravity readings at 232 spots separated by about 80 feet in a grid atop the rock glacier. 
Geology graduate student Bronson Cvijanovich operates a gravimeter while taking measurements of the Mount Timpanogos rock glacier in 2024. (Photo courtesy of Bronson Cvijanovich)
The gravimeter measures density differences between rock and ice, the university said in the release, which allowed the researchers to calculate the 3D shape of the buried ice body. After those measurements were collected, the team had to correct them to take into account differences in gravity due to factors like the position of the sun and the moon, the location’s terrain, latitude and elevation.
But, how does ice get into the rock glacier in the first place? Another study from University of Utah researchers showed with a new mathematical model that rock glaciers gain mass because “rockfalls bury persistent snow in the upper parts of rock glaciers,” the release says.
“In the Wasatch, the mountains themselves are eroding and burying the snow, and that’s why the rock glaciers exist,” Anderson said.
And, despite climate change the Timpanogos Rock Glacier apparently keeps on adding ice, the researchers said. 
“Rock glaciers flow downhill just like a glacier or river, but the important distinction here is that the thick carapace of loose rock actually protects and hides the ice, making these climate-resilient water storage sites that may still be adding frozen water. From a water resource standpoint, it is really important, especially in a warm and arid state like Utah,” Cvijanovich said.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa nurses cited for theft, indecent exposure or patient care issues
description: The Iowa Board of Nursing has sanctioned several Iowa nurses accused of a range of violations, from inadequate patient care and theft of patient medications to indecent exposure. One of the accused nurses, Danette Weiler of Remsen, recently settled disciplinary charges related to patient care as well as a wrongful-discharge lawsuit she filed against one […]
text:
(Photo courtesy of the Iowa Board of Nursing)The Iowa Board of Nursing has sanctioned several Iowa nurses accused of a range of violations, from inadequate patient care and theft of patient medications to indecent exposure.
One of the accused nurses, Danette Weiler of Remsen, recently settled disciplinary charges related to patient care as well as a wrongful-discharge lawsuit she filed against one of her former employers.
The Iowa Board of Nursing alleges that on Feb. 10, 2026, Weiler was working as a licensed practical nurse at the Siouxland Mental Health Crisis Center in Sioux City when she was “awoken by a loud noise.”
According to the board, Weiler found a patient-client in the hallway with his medications, which were supposed to have been stored in a locked medication room. Other drugs were reportedly found two hours later in the client’s room.
According to the board, Weiler failed to initiate a medical assessment of the client after the incident, failed to immediately inventory the medications and failed to initiate a timely emergency response.
The publicly available board records don’t indicate why Weiler had been sleeping at work or describe the patient’s outcome.
The board charged Weiler with committing an act that might adversely affect a patient’s welfare, failing to assess a patient and engaging in behavior that is contradictory to professional decorum.
To settle the matter without a hearing, the board recently agreed to issue Weiler a warning. As part of that settlement, Weiler agreed to complete 60 hours of educational training on assessments, documentation and professionalism.
Lawsuit included allegations of abuse
Court records indicate that prior to working for the Siouxland Mental Health Crisis Center, Weiler was employed by AffiniCare, a staffing agency owned by the Care Initiatives nursing home chain, and that she regularly worked at the company’s facilities in Kingsley, Correctionville and Cherokee.
Weiler is suing Care Initiatives for wrongful termination related to allegations that in early 2025, she failed to properly report allegations of resident abuse at Correctionville Care Center.
In her lawsuit, Weiler alleges Shana Moss, at one time the facility’s director of nursing, was the focus of at least some of the complaints of abuse.
“Moss has been working at Correctionville Care Center and in the position of director of nursing despite being charged with dependent adult abuse,” the lawsuit claims.
Court records indicate the criminal charges against Moss involved the alleged theft of a resident’s Ozempic weight-loss drug in September 2024 when Moss was working at Salem Lutheran Home.
A plea agreement resulted in charges of dependent adult abuse and unlawfully obtaining a prescription drug being dropped and Moss pleading guilty to one count of third-degree theft.
The Board of Nursing charged Moss with misappropriating patient medications, then settled the case by issuing Moss a warning, cautioning her that any future violations could result in licensing restrictions. As part of the settlement, Moss agreed to complete 30 hours of educational training in ethics.
Weiler’s wrongful-discharge lawsuit remains active and was scheduled to go to trial on Aug. 25, 2026, but recent court filings indicate the case has been settled out of court.
Weiler’s attorney declined to comment on the specifics of the settlement or on the recent Board of Nursing sanctions.
Other Iowa nurses facing sanctions from the Board of Nursing include:
Jeremy Barth of Bondurant — Recently, the board charged Barth with one count of engaging in behavior that is contradictory to professional decorum. The board disclosed no information as to the underlying conduct that gave rise to the charge except to say that at some point in time, Barth had been convicted of harassment in Polk County.
The disciplinary case has been resolved with Barth agreeing to surrender his license with the understanding that he can apply for reinstatement in one year.
Court records show Barth was arrested in Altoona on Sept. 16, 2025, and charged with indecent exposure. According to the police report, Barth was masturbating in his car in the parking lot of a Target store when he saw a female in the lot and exposed himself to her. Police allege that when questioned, Barth admitted masturbating while watching a video but denied intentionally exposing himself to the woman.
According to the police, video surveillance showed Barth was initially parked “nowhere near the victim,” then drove around the lot and parked two spaces away from her, then left that space and backed into another slot directly alongside the woman.
Barth later pleaded guilty to a reduced charge of second-degree harassment, resulting in a sentence of 20 days in jail, a $430 fine and one year of probation.
Travis Boeckenstedt of Luxemburg — The board alleges that while working at eastern Iowa’s Cornerstone Family Practice at some unspecified time in the past, Boeckenstedt “added a patient on Facebook” and subsequently sent her several Facebook messages of an undescribed nature. The board charged Boeckenstedt with engaging in behavior that is contradictory to professional decorum, and attempting to initiate a sexual, emotional, social or business relationship with a patient.
As part of a recent settlement agreement with the board, Boeckenstedt agreed to complete a two-day course on medical ethics and professionalism.
Michele Diane McCarty of Adel — The board alleges McCarty was employed last year by Total Nurse Network, working as a traveling registered nurse within the state of Iowa. The board alleges that on Nov. 21, 2024, she pleaded guilty to disorderly conduct, a charge that stemmed from allegations that she had approached a woman outside an elementary school and said, “I see you out by yourself next time, me and you better get to fighting because I have no problem going to jail right now.” On May 22, 2025, McCarty pleaded guilty to possession of methamphetamine after drugs were found in her car during a traffic stop.
On Dec. 12, 2025, McCarty reported both convictions to the board and was charged with habitual intoxication or addiction to the use of drugs and with failing to notify the board of a criminal conviction within 30 days.
To resolve the case without a hearing, the board and McCarty agreed to a settlement that will result in her license being placed on probation for two years, during which time she will be enrolled in a chemical screening program.
Kathleen Kemming of Waverly — Court records indicate Kemming was criminally charged last year with felony prohibited acts involving controlled substances and tampering with records. After pleading guilty to the charges, she was given a deferred judgment that will result in the court case being expunged after the successful completion of three years’ probation.
Prosecutors alleged that between May 2025 and September 2025, Kemming was working at the Waverly Health Center when she obtained morphine intended for three residents of the home and then kept the drug for her own use. She was also accused of keeping a resident’s Tramadol for herself, and with concealing the thefts by falsifying entries in patient records.
The Board of Nursing charged Kemming with misappropriating patient medication or supplies. failing to assess or accurately document the status of a patient and failing to properly document or perform the disposal of medications.
The board recently agreed to a settlement that allows Kemming to retain her nursing license while accepting a warning for her conduct. As part of that settlement, Kemming agreed to enroll in the Iowa Practitioner Health Program that assists healthcare workers with substance abuse issues.
Board records indicate that in 2009, Kemming’s license was temporarily suspended after she was charged with practicing nursing while under the influence of alcohol or illicit drugs. Those disciplinary charges stemmed from allegations that she had been fired from an Iowa hospital for being impaired while on duty.
Suzanne Jurgensen of Newton — The board alleges that while working as a nurse for Angels Care Home Health, Jurgensen documented having completed four home visits for two patients in February and March 2026. Both patients later denied those visits ever took place.
Jurgensen was charged by the board with falsifying records, committing an act that might adversely affect a patient’s welfare and failing to assess or report the status of a patient or client.
Jurgensen recently agreed to a settlement in the case that calls for her license to be placed on probation for one year and for her to complete 30 hours of educational training on ethics and medical documentation.
Amanda Stroh of Parkersburg — The board alleges that while Stroh was working at the Maple Manor care facility in Aplington in May 2025, several tablets of Oxycodone and Hydrocodone intended for four different residents were discovered to be missing and Stroh was unable to account for them.
On the same day, she allegedly administered medication to a resident that was contrary to what had been ordered and failed to administer other medications that had been ordered. Stroh was criminally charged with two felony counts of prohibited acts involving controlled substances and one count of tampering with records.
Prosecutors alleged video surveillance showed Stroh placing the missing medications into a single medication cup and then walking off with it. Court records indicate she was convicted of one count of prohibited acts involving controlled substances and one count of tampering with records, after which she was granted a deferred judgment.
The Board of Nursing then charged Stroh with misappropriating patient supplies or medication, failing to properly dispose of medications and being convicted of an offense directly related to the practice of nursing. To settle the disciplinary charges, the board agreed to place Stroh’s license on probationary status for three years. As part of the settlement, Stroh agreed to enroll in the Iowa Practitioner Health Program.
Jamie Dooley of Clinton — In November 2025, the board charged Dooley with unauthorized possession of controlled substances, being convicted of a crime related to the practice of nursing, failure to notify the board of a conviction within 30 days and failure to respond to the board’s inquiries.
According to the board, Dooley was convicted in 2024 of possession of marijuana and possession of methamphetamine and received a deferred judgment. In April 2025, the board reviewed the matter and opted to close the case with a confidential letter of warning and a referral to the Iowa Practitioner Health Program. After Dooley failed to enroll in the program, the board publicly filed its disciplinary charges in the case. Recently, the board issued an order revoking Dooley’s license.
Board records indicate that while still licensed, Dooley worked at Hope Creek Nursing and Rehabilitation Center in East Moline, Ill., and at Silvis Center Nursing and Rehabilitation in Silvis, Ill.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Civil rights groups make urgent plea for voting rights in DC, ahead of midterm elections
authors: Matt Brown, Associated Press and Matthew Junkroski, Associated Press
description: Activists rally at the Lincoln Memorial during the March on Washington, Friday, Aug. 28, 2026, in Washington.
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Voting rights, the work of the civil rights movement and racial justice took center stage on the National Mall Friday, with protesters gathering ahead of midterm elections and following a wave of changes to voting laws and redistricting that some have condemned as detrimental to Black Americans.
Hundreds of people gathered near the steps of the Lincoln Memorial for the 2026 “Defend the Vote” March on Washington, organized by the Rev. Al Sharpton and Martin Luther King III, echoing the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr.’s 1963 march. The event follows the U.S. Supreme Court’s landmark April decision in Louisiana v. Callais that reinterpreted key provisions of the Voting Rights Act of 1965, allowing Southern states to redraw their congressional maps in a way that erodes equal representation in Black communities.
“We’ve been doing these marches for years, but this is probably the most important because this is the first year we are marching that the voting rights bill has been nullified by the Supreme Court,” Sharpton, founder of the National Action Network, said in an interview with The Associated Press.
Some call it a ‘very dangerous moment in American history’
Friday’s event harkened back to King Jr.’s historic March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom in 1963, when more than 200,000 people gathered at the foot of the Lincoln Memorial. That march, an inflection point in the Civil Rights Movement, came at a fraught moment, when economic headwinds, civil unrest, political division and the Vietnam War bitterly divided Americans.
Sen. Bernie Sanders speaks during the March on Washington rally at the Lincoln Memorial on the National Mall, Friday, Aug. 28, 2026 in Washington. (AP Photo/Manuel Balce Ceneta) Credit: AP Photo/Manuel Balce Ceneta
Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., one of dozens of speakers at the event, said that now is a “very dangerous moment in American history” and that the “dream of a more just and equitable society has never been under greater threat than it is right now.”
He placed blame on Republican President Donald Trump and the Supreme Court’s conservative majority, listing attempts to purge voter rolls, obtain sensitive voter data, restrict mail-in and early voting, and redraw Congressional districts as part of threats to voting rights.
“Today, we have a president along with the Supreme Court members he appointed carrying out the most significant assault on voting rights since segregation, targeting virtually every aspect of the electoral system,” Sanders said.
Martin Luther King III told the AP the Civil Rights movement’s work “is further eroding” in the wake of the April ruling.
He said his father would be disappointed with the state of the country, but current civil rights advocates should be undaunted.
“Had he lived, we’d be on a totally different trajectory,” the younger King said. “These would not be issues; they would have been resolved. I don’t think he would be surprised because he understands our history and understands those who are trying to retain power. But the challenge is challenging our communities to engage even more.”
King’s Drum Major Institute, a progressive think tank and community action group, co-hosted the march with Sharpton’s group.
Ray Turner, a 65-year-old Maryland retiree, sat Friday on the steps in front of the Lincoln Memorial. He came independently, carrying a sign that read “(Puny) Hands off our elections.”
“The lies about the 2020 election being stolen continue to be sounded, even though they’ve been disproved,” Turner said, adding, “Now they’re trying to use this to prevent people who are legal citizens, legal voters, from voting.”
Rev. Al Sharpton speaks during the March on Washington rally at the Lincoln Memorial on the National Mall, Friday, Aug. 28, 2026 in Washington. (AP Photo/Manuel Balce Ceneta) Credit: AP Photo/Manuel Balce Ceneta
Sharpton said the Trump administration’s immigration policy for Haitians and white South Africans, as well as cuts to social programs, are unifying concerns for this year’s march attendees. But redistricting efforts by Republican-led states set to reduce the number of Black lawmakers in Congress loom large.
“This march is about people who refuse to be counted out. When the courts and the legislature broke apart District 6, they did not just redraw lines,” Rep. Cleo Fields, D-La., said in a texted statement. “They told hundreds of thousands of Black families from Baton Rouge up through the Delta that their voice could be taken away at any moment.”
Fields’ district was central in the Supreme Court decision that hollowed out the Voting Rights Act of 1965. The court ruled that his district, created just one term ago to permit a second majority-Black district in a state where Blacks make up 33% of the population, was unconstitutional because it relied too heavily on race.
The court has held that maps can be redrawn for partisan reasons.
Louisiana’s legislature rushed to redraw the district after the decision, reshaping it to cluster around predominantly white communities in the Baton Rouge area and southern Louisiana.
Fields has opted not to seek reelection to Congress and instead is pursuing a seat in the state Senate.
Embattled Black lawmakers see need for continued rights push
Rep. Shomari Figures, an Alabama Democrat whose majority-Black district was targeted by the state’s Republican-led redistricting effort, said the original voting rights fight required local movements, national figures, lots of coordination and strategy. He sees this year’s march as a continuation of that legacy.
“My district includes Montgomery, which was the birthplace of it all. It started with a bus boycott in 1955 and that, ultimately, morphed into a broader struggle for civil rights and led to a more broad Civil Rights Movement,” Figures told the AP.
Demonstrators shout to speakers during the March on Washington, near the Lincoln Memorial, Friday, Aug. 28, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Mariam Zuhaib) Credit: AP Photo/Mariam Zuhaib
Ahead of Friday, organizations participating in the march filed new claims in their federal lawsuit against President Donald Trump’s executive order restricting mail-in voting. The Supreme Court cleared a path Monday for possible implementation of the order, though it remains unclear how much can be put in place before the midterms.
Late Thursday, a federal judge in Boston who is hearing some of the lawsuits against that executive order put a temporary halt on the administration from moving forward with it. Time is running short to make any significant changes to voting in the midterms, with the first mail ballots scheduled to be sent out next week.
Associated Press writers Gary Fields in Washington and Kimberly Chandler in Montgomery, Alabama, contributed.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: State legislators, candidates get a briefing on childcare issues ahead of elections
description: With New Hampshire’s legislative session finished and election season on the horizon, current and potential state legislators attended a candidate briefing in Concord on Thursday to learn about the issues impacting the childcare sector.  The event, called “The Workforce Behind the Workforce: A Candidate Briefing on Childcare,” was hosted by Save the Children[...]
text:
Childcare providers, policy analysts, and advocates speak at an event that briefs current and potential state legislators on New Hampshire childcare. (Photo by Maya Mitchell/New Hampshire Bulletin)With New Hampshire’s legislative session finished and election season on the horizon, current and potential state legislators attended a candidate briefing in Concord on Thursday to learn about the issues impacting the childcare sector. 
The event, called “The Workforce Behind the Workforce: A Candidate Briefing on Childcare,” was hosted by Save the Children Action Network, a bipartisan political advocacy group that prioritizes children’s issues. Hosted at Arts Alley in downtown Concord, the event had bipartisan attendance, with the majority of attendees currently serving as Democratic state legislators. 
Over 50 attendees got a nonpartisan briefing from young parents, childcare program directors and teachers, advocacy groups, and policy analysts about a wide range of topics and issues impacting the state’s childcare community. Panels on the financial realities for parents, the childcare scholarship program, business participation, and previous legislative work were held throughout the event.
Michelle Sheppard, chief operating officer of the Granite YMCA, started the briefing by talking about her interactions with parents every day. She said she constantly gets calls from expecting parents complaining about the difficulties of looking for childcare and finding only waitlists. 
“I always joke and say, ‘Oh you didn’t know? You call childcare before you call your OB-GYN,’” she said. 
Advocates also previewed some of their policy and legislative priorities for next year’s legislative session: increased state funding participation for the scholarship program and a dedicated funding stream in the budget for childcare support. 
Other speakers focused on the systemic financial constraints childcare providers face to keep the doors of programs open and how state and federal streams fund the state’s scholarship program, Head Start, quality initiatives, and more. More than a dozen panelists spoke on behalf of organizations, such as the Child Care Advisory Committee, Early Learning New Hampshire, New Hampshire Fiscal Policy Institute, New Hampshire Businesses for Social Responsibility, and Moms Rising.  
During the final Q&A session, campaigning candidates inquired about what regulatory changes and type of government intervention could best help the state’s childcare. They expressed interest in setting the scholarship’s income eligibility by region instead of statewide, improving communication between the Department of Education and Department of Health and Human Services, and increasing capacity without risking child safety. 
“If childcare is a public good,” one attendee said on their way out of the event, “it shouldn’t be this hard to have.”

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma House set to hear evidence in staff allegation of lawmaker’s ‘improper behavior’
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahoma House Republican leaders have blocked off three days next month to look into allegations of misconduct against a member of their own party.  Rep. Mike Osburn, who chairs the House Rules Committee, said lawmakers will meet behind closed doors  Sept. 8 to discuss the allegations made by House staff against Republican […]
text:
Rep. Danny Williams, R-Seminole, listens to the State of the State Address on Feb. 2, 2026, at the state Capitol in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Kyle Phillips/For Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahoma House Republican leaders have blocked off three days next month to look into allegations of misconduct against a member of their own party. 
Rep. Mike Osburn, who chairs the House Rules Committee, said lawmakers will meet behind closed doors  Sept. 8 to discuss the allegations made by House staff against Republican Rep. Danny Williams, as well as the outcome of related investigations ordered by House staff.
Details of the allegations have not been made public. The committee’s actions could range from determining Williams was innocent of the accusations to recommending expulsion or sanctions.
Williams, R-Seminole, did not return a phone call seeking comment Friday as of publication. He previously told a KFOR reporter that he was told not to publicly discuss the allegations, and that he didn’t remember what all the claims were. Williams said they weren’t sexual in nature and denied any wrongdoing.
Osburn, whose committee has been tapped by House Speaker Kyle Hilbert to lead the legislative probe, said Thursday that he has not yet seen the reports from the investigations, and that he was not sure exactly what the hearings will look like. 
The public will be allowed to attend at some point, Osburn said, but the first day will not initially be open because the House does not want to jeopardize the privacy of anyone who made allegations against Williams. Osburn said the committee may also meet Sept. 9 and 10 if more time is needed. 
“This is uncharted territory, and we are going to build the plane as we’re flying it, I think,” said Osburn, R-Edmond. 
In an email to House lawmakers in July, Hilbert wrote that Williams was being investigated after being accused of “improper behavior” toward chamber staff and also “potential misuse of state resources.”  
Hilbert, R-Bristow, did not elaborate in that email on what those allegations are, but wrote that a private law firm, Fuller Tubb Bickford Warmington & Panach, PLLC, was hired to conduct an external investigation.
On Thursday, Hilbert’s office said they did not know what the external investigation into Williams has cost Oklahoma taxpayers. Rep. Trey Caldwell, R-Faxon, who chairs the chamber’s budget committee, said he would not comment on internal investigations and also did not provide a cost. 
In Hilbert’s July 23 email, which was provided to Oklahoma Voice, the chamber leader wrote that he became aware of a complaint against Williams earlier this summer. 
“Our House HR Division and the external firm focused their fact finding on alleged improper behavior towards House staff,” Hilbert wrote. “However, during the investigation additional concerns of potential misuse of state resources emerged. The matter of use of state resources is likewise being reviewed to determine if it should also be referred to the House Rules Committee and/or the Ethics Commission upon completion of the investigation.”
The law firm had completed their review of eight current or former House employees and other documentation, according to the email. Hilbert wrote that the findings and the House’s human resources investigation prompted him to refer the issue to the House Rules Committee, which Osburn chairs. Hilbert did not disclose the content of the HR investigation.
Hilbert wrote that referring the matter to the Rules Committee follows House precedent from 2017, a year with several, separate investigations into lawmakers. 
One involved accusations that Republican lawmaker Dan Kirby sexually harassed a legislative assistant. In another case, Democrat Will Fourkiller was accused of making inappropriate comments to a high school page. 
In his resignation letter, Kirby called the accusations “unfounded,” but said he would no longer be able to effectively represent his district because of the “unreasonable committee recommendations.” 
Fourkiller at the time said he did not recall what he said or did wrong, but apologized. 
Kirby resigned after a committee recommended expulsion, while Fourkiller accepted sanctions, including a recommendation that he be barred from involvement in the House page program.
Williams, whose district includes Pottawatomie and Seminole counties, faces Democrat Blake Cummings, of Prague, in November’s general election.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: To save SC’s historic Black schools, nonprofit launches statewide coalition
description: The South Carolina Historic Black Schools Preservation Network is meant to help pool resources and knowledge in saving Black schools.
text:
Wilfred Pace, who is helping lead an effort to save Bull Swamp Colored School and Community Center in Orangeburg, describes the school's history at Central Carolina Community Foundation's office in Columbia, S.C., on Thursday, Aug. 27, 2026. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — Helping save Lakeview School in West Columbia is Earnestine Holden’s retirement job.
Like many of the people trying to save historic Black schools, Holden, who graduated from the school in 1967, isn’t a professional historian or grant-writer. She’s a passionate alum who wants to see the school she graduated from preserved for future generations to see.
Recognizing the difficulty many alumni associations face in navigating complicated barriers to saving the state’s historic Black schools, the Central Carolina Community Foundation on Thursday officially launched the South Carolina Historic Black Schools Preservation Network.
Proposed national historic park would highlight history of SC’s Rosenwald schools for Black students

The network is meant to act as a way for alumni associations and nonprofits to pool their knowledge and resources about funding sources, historical designations and research, said Georgia Mjartan, the foundation’s president.
So far, the effort involves about a dozen long-closed K-12 schools. But the work is also open to historically Black colleges and universities, said Trimease Carter, the foundation’s director of community impact.
Each endeavor is starting from a different place, with different needs, which allows the nonprofits and alumni associations behind their preservation to help each other out, she said.
“No matter where your school is along this preservation network, we want to be here to be a help and support,” Carter said.
Starting a network
South Carolina once had thousands of Black schools. The exact number is unclear, said Virginia Harness, a researcher for the state Department of Archives and History.
Many closed as the school systems were required to desegregate. They were then left to deteriorate, often forgotten by surrounding communities.
But the schools played a vital role in the state’s history, alumni said. Children’s futures depended on the schools that provided their only opportunity for education, Holden said.
“There were so many kids who would never have gotten to college if it were not for the nurturing they received at these Black schools,” Holden said. “I can tell you story after story after story.”
Wanting to save the schools, alumni started calling the Central Carolina Community Foundation asking about opportunities for funding. After several similar requests, Carter asked one caller if the schools had some sort of collective that would make it easier to work together.
Photographs and artifacts from Booker T. Washington High School in Columbia, S.C., sit on display at Central Carolina Community Foundation’s office on Thursday, Aug. 27, 2026. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)
“Not that I know of,” replied Deloris Pringle, an alumna of Lincoln High School in Sumter. “Would you all be willing to host this?”
The foundation decided to act as a connector, giving alumni a space to meet and help in finding resources. Although the foundation typically serves the Midlands, the network is open to schools across the state, Carter said.
“I feel like so many were working in silos, and they were trying to do things by reinventing the wheel,” Carter said.
Historic designations
Many preservation efforts are led by established nonprofits, but saving Black schools typically falls to passionate alumni. Some might have a background in running a business or working in government, but most know little about what opportunities are out there or how to get them, Carter said.
For instance, getting a spot on the National Register of Historic Places can offer certain protections, said Virginia Harness, who oversees that process for the state Department of Archives and History. But the designation comes with a set of requirements, and most applications are written by professionals, she said.
“It’s serious business,” Harness said. “It’s sort of like a graduate-level research paper.”
At least 67 schools are listed on the national register, Harness said. That doesn’t include schools that are part of a larger historic district, such as the one encompassing downtown Charleston, since they aren’t listed separately, she said.
Most of the listed schools are general public schools built to educate Black students. About a fifth are Rosenwald schools, founded by Sears CEO Julius Rosenwald to give rural Black students in the South an education. Another fifth are equalization schools, which were built in the 1950s with the state’s inaugural 3% sales tax in a failed effort to thwart desegregation by proving public schools could be “separate but equal.”
Some rarer examples of schools include Faith Cabin Libraries. Around 100 of the libraries were built across South Carolina and Georgia to make sure students, including those who attended school elsewhere, had access to books at a time when most libraries remained segregated.
The state also has one Black mill school still standing, which is a rarity, Harness said. Marysville School in Spartanburg County was built to educate the children of Black families who worked in Pacolet’s textile mills between 1915 and 1954.
Historians have found 33 other schools that would likely qualify but haven’t applied. Other schools that were demolished, repurposed or rebuilt over the years are out there but don’t qualify for that designation, she said.
Interest in saving historic Black schools has grown in recent years, Harness said. In the last decade, the Department of Archives and History recommended adding 17 schools to this list. Less than six years into this decade, the agency has recommended 18.
Earnestine Holden, president of Lakeview High School’s alumni association, talks to historian Rachel Young at Central Carolina Community Foundation’s office in Columbia, S.C., on Thursday, Aug. 27, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Central Carolina Community Foundation)
“We’re definitely seeing a big increase in interest in listing these properties,” she said.
Recent statewide efforts to save Rosenwald schools are part of that. Pushes from alumni associations are another, she said.
Even professional historians sometimes need some help in filling out those types of applications. The register initially rejected a bid to list Booker T. Washington High School in Columbia because renovations to save the building “impacted the historical integrity of the original building,” said Bobby Donaldson, a history professor involved in the effort.
“I said, ‘You’ve got to be kidding,’” said Donaldson, who leads the Center for Civil Rights History and Research at the University of South Carolina, located in the former high school built in 1956 as part of the so-called equalization effort.
So, he called up Pringle and others working on Lincoln High School, which also underwent extensive renovations and got listed. They gave some advice on how to phrase the application, and, sure enough, Booker T. Washington got added to the list, Donaldson said.
Getting a spot on the national register can open up federal funding, but it’s far from the only resource associations might need help with, Carter said.
Many of the schools want to open museums for the public to see what learning was like for Black students during segregation. Some want to expand and become community hubs.
Bull Swamp Colored School in Orangeburg, for instance, is planning to add a commercial kitchen, food pantry, media lab and activity center to the 2 acres surrounding the historic three-room school house, said Wilfred Pace, who is helping lead the effort.
That sort of work is only fitting, since the schools once served as hubs for Black communities, Pringle said.
“Even though we were unequal in terms of our facilities, these schools just were the heart of these African American communities,” Pringle said.
Funding
The biggest barrier for most is fundraising, Carter said.
School groups typically cobble together money from various sources.
Bull Swamp has gotten money from various federal grants, as well as from donations and local partnerships, for its $1.2 million renovations, Pace said. Lakeview High School is in the process of getting nonprofit status to collect donations from alumni and apply for grants, said Holden.
SC had 500 Rosenwald schools for Black children. Nonprofits want to save the 44 that remain.

Long Point Schoolhouse in Mount Pleasant has gotten $150,000 from the state budget, with $250,000 more expected in a bill legislators sent to the governor this week. St. George Rosenwald School in Dorchester County received an agricultural grant for repairs, showing how schools can get creative, Harness said.
Getting funding often requires going through complex processes involving lots of paperwork and research on a school’s importance.
That’s not knowledge most people have, Carter said. But it is something the Central Carolina Community Foundation and other partners know about and can help with, she said.
The spirit of collaboration is built into the schools, Pace said. Without help from various places, including government funding, philanthropy and community support, most of the schools would never have existed, he said.
“It just shows you the resilience of working together and having a vision for the future and then living that dream,” Pace said.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Minnesota attorney general allows out-of-state acquisition of North Memorial Health
description: South Dakota-based Sanford Health may move forward in acquiring North Memorial Health next month after the hospital systems signed a 10-year oversight agreement with the Minnesota Attorney General’s Office. As part of the agreement, Sanford committed to maintaining hospital and emergency services at North Memorial’s Robbinsdale hospital, which is the health[...]
text:
Bill Gassen, CEO of Sanford Health, speaks at a press conference announcing a 10-year oversight agreement on the acquisition of North Memorial Health by Sanford, alongside North Memorial CEO Trevor Sawallish and Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison, Friday Aug. 28, 2026. (Photo by Alyssa Chen/Minnesota Reformer)South Dakota-based Sanford Health may move forward in acquiring North Memorial Health next month after the hospital systems signed a 10-year oversight agreement with the Minnesota Attorney General’s Office.
As part of the agreement, Sanford committed to maintaining hospital and emergency services at North Memorial’s Robbinsdale hospital, which is the health system’s flagship safety net hospital, for the next decade. The 10-year agreement is far longer than Sanford’s initial commitment to maintain core services at Robbinsdale for only two years. The agreement also stipulates that North Memorial maintain its extensive emergency transportation services across the state for 10 years.
“We’ve talked about the financial concerns of the hospital. We now have a path forward,” said North Memorial CEO Trevor Sawallish, who spoke at a press conference Friday announcing the agreement alongside Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison and Sanford CEO Bill Gassen.
The proposed acquisition had alarmed healthcare advocates and labor leaders, who worry further consolidation will hurt patient care, drive up costs and lead to the reduction of critical services at Robbinsdale and the possible closure of one of the state’s few Level 1 trauma centers. A coalition of union organizers and faith leaders advocated for a “community benefits agreement” with worker and patient protections throughout the merger review, including at public forums held by the Attorney General’s Office.
JaNaé Bates, the co-director of the progressive ecumenical group ISAIAH, said that much of what’s in the final agreement was included in the coalition’s original proposal.
“Robbinsdale Hospital remaining open for at least 10 years with its full services is incredible,” Bates said at the news conference alongside the hospital leaders.
Citing the hospital’s financial troubles, Sawallish previously said that North Memorial risks closing unless it’s acquired by Sanford. The Robbinsdale hospital has been losing money, in part because many patients are uninsured or on lower-paying government insurance. The Legislature approved a cash bailout of Hennepin County Medical Center, another struggling safety net hospital, but a proposal for additional cash assistance to North Memorial was dropped by the time the bailout was passed.
The agreement binds Sanford to maintaining Robbinsdale’s Level 1 trauma center, its emergency department, cardiac and cath lab services, labor and delivery, ICU, stroke care, reproductive health and gender affirming care, mental health services and oncology services for ten years.
The merger also includes protections for union contracts, $100 million of upgrades to the Robbinsdale hospital and $500 million in investments to North Memorial’s newer, income-generating hospital in the more affluent Maple Grove area.
The proposed acquisition of North Memorial by the $11.7 billion Sanford Health is part of a broader trend of healthcare consolidation — hospitals and clinics combining into sprawling health systems. Evidence has shown that consolidation has led to higher prices, though effects on quality of care are less clear, according to health policy research organization KFF.
The Minnesota Attorney General’s Office was bestowed with expanded regulatory powers over healthcare mergers by the Legislature in 2023. It’s now able to analyze and sue to block hospital mergers if they are against the public’s interest — for example, if they increase healthcare costs for patients.
Sanford has unsuccessfully tried to enter the Twin Cities before, with proposed acquisitions of Fairview Health in 2013 and again in 2022. The effort faced intense scrutiny from the Attorney General’s Office, especially after the 2023 law gave the attorney general sign-off power on any out-of-state or for-profit acquisition of University of Minnesota health facilities.
In signing the oversight agreement, the Minnesota Attorney General’s Office gave its blessing to the merger, though it still has the ability to intervene if Sanford doesn’t meet the terms.
The Attorney General’s Office has also been reviewing the proposed acquisition of the Upper Midwest’s health giant Allina Health by the even bigger California system, Sutter Health.
The community benefits agreement coalition published a statement lauding the North Memorial-Sanford oversight agreement and contrasting it with Allina and Sutter’s leadership’s failure to meet with the coalition.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Brown external review identifies security, leadership gaps in mass shooting response
description: Two campus police dispatchers were on duty at Brown University when reports of gunfire first emerged at 4:04 p.m. on Dec. 13, 2025. Within minutes, they were overwhelmed. The flood of incoming calls and radio chatter that stunned dispatchers is one of the communication breakdowns described in an independent review of the mass shooting at […]
text:
Crime scene tape surrounds Brown University's Engineering Research Center on Sunday, Dec. 14, 2025, a day after a gunman killed two students and wounded nine others in a classroom inside. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)Two campus police dispatchers were on duty at Brown University when reports of gunfire first emerged at 4:04 p.m. on Dec. 13, 2025. Within minutes, they were overwhelmed.
The flood of incoming calls and radio chatter that stunned dispatchers is one of the communication breakdowns described in an independent review of the mass shooting at the Ivy League university on Providence’s East Side, released Friday afternoon by the university.
It’s “highly unlikely” the mass shooting that left two students dead and injured nine others could have been prevented, the global consultancy Teneo Risk, which conducted the review at Brown’s request, concluded. 
“The events of Dec. 13 demonstrate that the university, a community of 16,000-plus students, employees and campus area residents and billions of dollars invested in complex and sensitive infrastructure, has need for more robust emergency management staffing and capability,” the executive summary states.
Brown hired Teneo Risk in January to analyze the school’s actions before, during, and after the shooting committed by suspected gunman Claudio Manuel Neves Valente inside the Barus & Holley building. Brown commissioned COSECURE, a Philadelphia-based security consulting firm, to do a separate physical assessment of campus facilities.
The university only released a summary of the outside reviews because they “contain sensitive information relating to injuries and fatalities, safety and security,” according to the university’s action plan containing Teneo’s executive summary.
“We hope it will help our community gain a deeper understanding of the incident, the ways Brown effectively responded to the tragedy, and how our response and level of preparation can be strengthened for the future,” Brown University President Paxson and Chancellor Brian T. Moynihan wrote in a message to the campus community Friday.
The university’s afternoon dossier complements a separate city-commissioned report released Friday morning, which praised Providence’s response to the shooting.
Independent review praises Providence response to Brown shooting but flags communication gaps

Teneo’s assessment found plenty of fault with campus police department’s top leaders, who “failed to provide vital assistance to the unified command at the crime scene” and did not adequately prepare officers for an active shooter incident. 
“Stronger leadership by the individuals in question might have improved the investigative process,” the summary states.
The report did not name any specific police officials.
Rodney Chatman, the campus police chief at the time of the shooting, was removed from his position and replaced in December by former Providence Police Chief Hugh T. Clements Jr. Clements assumed the job on a permanent basis in April.
Brown’s own action plan calls for a series of changes, including improvements to emergency communications and coordination with Providence police. Among them is integrating the university’s camera network with the city’s Real Time Crime Center, provided the university and the city can reach an agreement over how the data will be shared and stored.
The city-commissioned report also called for integrating campus surveillance cameras with the city’s system.
The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) of Rhode Island has urged Brown and other universities not to give police access to their cameras, a position the organization reiterated in a statement Friday afternoon. 
“Meaningful statewide laws must be in place before systems like these are implemented to ensure that the privacy rights of all Rhode Island residents and visitors are protected,” the ACLU wrote.
Teneo’s reviewers called for the university to tighten campus building security, noting Brown’s Department of Public Safety “was aware of non-threatening suspicious activity” in Barus & Holley before the incident. That included frequent trespassing by “John,” a homeless man who later ended up helping police identify the gunman via a Dec. 15 Reddit post.  
“Although the frequent trespasser was not the perpetrator and was not himself a threat, earlier trespassing incidents at the building complex showed areas in which security could have been strengthened,” the executive summary states.
Still, Teneo’s assessment reiterated it was “unlikely” that enhanced security measures would have made much of a difference. The report states even if Neves Valente hadn’t had access to Barus & Holley “he might have gone to another building on campus or targeted individuals outside.”
“Thus, nothing about these events changes our main conclusion that nothing in our review suggests that Brown could have prevented the shooting,” reviewers wrote.
Neves Valente, who shot and killed a Massachusetts Institute of Technology professor two days after the Brown shooting, was found dead in a storage locker in Salem, New Hampshire, on Dec. 18. 
Federal investigators in April concluded that Neves Valente, who briefly attended Brown in 2000, appeared to be fueled by personal grievances and resentments tied to his own personal failures. Teneo’s assessment found “nothing in Neves Valente’s academic history or records to suggest a propensity for violence or an animus toward the University. 
“Nor is there any evidence that he had any contact with Brown personnel prior to the attack,” reviewers wrote.
Reporter Alexander Castro contributed to this story.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Court: Former Washington Commanders player can get workers’ comp for training camp injury
description: A former Washington Commanders football player who ruptured his Achilles tendon during training camp in 2023 is entitled to workers’ compensation benefits for the injury, the Appellate Court of Maryland ruled this week.
text:
A look at Northwest Stadium on April 28, 2025, home of the Washington Commanders. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)A former Washington Commanders football player who ruptured his Achilles tendon during training camp in 2023 is entitled to workers’ compensation benefits for the injury, the Appellate Court of Maryland ruled this week.
The Wednesday ruling upheld an earlier Prince George’s County Circuit Court decision that said Curtis Brooks, who signed with the team Aug. 3, 2023, to play on the defensive line, was a “covered employee” when his injury happened three days later during an early training camp practice.
According to the 20-page ruling, Brooks never made it on the Commanders’ active roster and didn’t play a game.
But the terms of his contract at the time said it “covers 1 football season(s), and will begin on the date of execution, and end on the last day of the 2023 League Year, unless extended, terminated, or renewed as specified elsewhere in this contract.”
In terms of injury, another part of the contract states, “Unless this contract specifically provides otherwise, if Player is injured in the performance of his services under this contract and promptly reports such injury to the Club physician or trainer, then Player will receive such medical and hospital care during the term of this contract.”
Brooks, who hasn’t played in the National Football League since his injury, filed a worker’s compensation claim with the Maryland Workers’ Compensation Commission in March 2024. Two months later, the commission rejected his claim, saying Brooks did not qualify as a covered employee in the state and that the injury occurred at a practice at the team’s training facility in Ashburn, Virginia.
DC approves new stadium, clearing the way for Commanders to leave Maryland

Brooks appealed to the county circuit court, which held a hearing on May 6, 2025.
The circuit court reversed the commission decision, writing that all players’ primary employment and home games with the Commanders in the National Football League are at Northwest Stadium in Prince George’s County.
A three-judge panel with the Appellate Court – Judge Stuart R. Berger who wrote the opinion, and Judge Rosalyn Tang and Senior Judge James A. Kenney III – affirmed the county Circuit Court’s decision.
In an email Friday, a team official said the Commanders would not be commenting on the case. Representatives with the workers’ comp commission did not respond to requests for comment.
According to the court document, Rob Rogers, the Commanders senior vice president of football operations, testified in circuit court that Brooks likely would have played in two preseason games in Maryland, but he “likened the games to a tryout.”
But when asked directly by Brooks’ attorney, “At no time before Mr. Brooks signed his contract, did you tell him that you did not think he was going to make the team, did you?” Rogers replied, “No.”
The circuit court entered an verbal ruling for Brooks on May 13, 2025.
In part, the court said, “This is just a contract for a season. And at the time, on August 6 of 2023, he [Brooks] was an employee of this football team. And quite honestly, there was an argument about, well, you know, ‘consistent and predictable.’ But what this contract says is that he is employed by the Commanders for the 2023 NFL season.”
On appeal to the Appellate Court of Maryland, the Commanders focused on the fact that Brooks was injured in Virginia, and that his employment with the team “was not consistent and predictable” because he had only been with the team for three days prior to his injury “and was not likely to play games in Maryland on a consistent and predictable basis.”
But Berger wrote that the team “invites us to engage in speculation regarding how many games Mr. Brooks would have played in Maryland to determine whether Mr. Brooks would have been covered. We decline to engage in such speculation. Indeed, effectively establishing a certain number of games that would meet the threshold for ‘regular’ and ‘predictable’ employment is an inexact estimation.”
Brooks finished his collegiate career in 2021 at the University of Cincinnati as a defensive tackle and an All-American Athletic Conference First Team honoree. He was drafted in the sixth round in 2022 by the Indianapolis Colts.
He was transferred to the Colts’ practice squad and then released in December 2022 before signing with the Tennessee Titans practice squad in January 2023. But he was cut by the Titans in July, during preseason camp, and signed by the Commanders in August of that year.
