name: VTDigger
title: Sen. Peter Welch calls for making it easier for Vermont schools to buy more food directly from local farms
description:
Welch and others gathered at a school nutrition conference to find ways to strengthen the connection between Vermont’s local food system and school nutrition programs.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Sen. Peter Welch calls for making it easier for Vermont schools to buy more food directly from local farms.
text:
Elementary school students head back to class after lunch and recess at the Coventry Village School in September 2019. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

SHELBURNE — Vermont leads the U.S. in providing local food in schools.
In fact, 89% of Vermont schools purchase some local food, according to Vermont FEED, a collaborative farm to school project. U.S. Sen. Peter Welch, D-Vt., introduced the Farm to School Act in the Senate last year, which would support schools accessing local food and builds on former Vermont U.S. Sen. Patrick Leahy’s influential Farm to School Grant Program.
Vermont also runs a Local Foods Incentive Grant program, where schools are incentivized to meet local purchasing targets in their school meal programs. They get as much as 25 cents per meal if 25% of their food is sourced locally, which decreases as the portion of locally-sourced food decreases. Vermont made school breakfast and lunch free for every student starting in the 2022-2023 school year.
Still, about 10% to 12% of food in Vermont school meals comes from “brown box commodities,” or bulk foods made elsewhere in the U.S. that are delivered to places like schools and food banks. 
Welch, speaking at the School Nutrition Association of Vermont’s annual conference at Shelburne Farms last week, voiced his commitment to strengthening the connection between Vermont’s local food ecosystem and healthy meals for students.
Welch acknowledged it has historically been a challenge to create national policies that guarantee nutritious school meals.
“The idea that we have to make an argument that it’s important to feed kids, I mean, what kind of country is that?” he asked. He also fielded a question from an audience member, who pointed to a “cash in lieu” program in effect in Kansas and requested that Welch look into adopting the program in Vermont. This program provides schools with funds instead of physical commodities, which schools can use to purchase more local foods.
“We’ll look right into it,” he said. “But it’s very consistent with our commitment to the Farm to School Program, which is about supporting farmers as well as kids.”
Last November, Welch, along with other senators, reintroduced the Farm to School Act, which would get more local foods into schools nationwide. It would do that by increasing funding to the Farm to School Program.
Welch also praised SNA-VT, a leadership group for child nutrition professionals, for supporting a local food ecosystem in the state. He said he’s been in schools during lunchtime and appreciated the value of students gathering for a meal and learning how to get along with each other.
“The heart of agriculture, the heart of nutrition, is about community,” he said. “We need that sense of togetherness.”
Welch is on the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry, which is working on a new version of the Farm Bill. The Farm Bill, an omnibus bill that passes about every five years, includes nutrition programs like SNAP, a food benefits program for low-income families and individuals, and school nutrition, as well as commodity and crop insurance programs for farmers. Welch is working on a new Farm Bill, which is currently stalled in the Senate.
“We in Washington have to approach things the way you do,” he said, addressing the school nutrition professionals at the conference. “It’s like you don’t ask, ‘Who (did) the parents vote for?’ You ask, ‘What does your son, what does your daughter need for a good meal?’ And that’s something that brings us together.”
Rosie Krueger, state director of child nutrition programs, also spoke at the conference, giving an update on the federal Dietary Guidelines for Americans, which were published in December and prioritize protein and dairy at every meal and limits to added sugars. Although these guidelines are meant for every American, Krueger explained that they have specific impacts for school nutrition.
The federal government plans to release a rule later this fall that will guide these standards, and Krueger urged those in the room to respond to the rule during the public comment period following that release.
“We have an opportunity during a comment period to tell federal decision makers how we think we could do it better,” she said. 
Krueger expects the new rule will include increased requirements for protein and limits on added sugar, which could tighten budgets for school meals. She suggested that schools start planning how to use beans as a source of protein if the requirements go into effect.
She said it’s been nearly 15 years since nutrition standards changed, and it had a big impact on school nutrition the last time around. Krueger said schools are serving better and healthier foods as a result of those changes, but that the initial implementation could have been improved.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Healey moves to grow behavioral health workforce as access lags
authors: Alison Kuznitz | State House News Service
description: Massachusetts is "facing a behavioral health access crisis," says a May report from the Health Policy Commission's Behavioral Health Workforce Center.
text:
THE HEALEY ADMINISTRATION rolled out a statewide campaign Thursday to bolster career interest in the behavioral health care sector, where persistent workforce shortages have made it difficult for some Bay Staters to access care.
The campaign, called “Turn Your Compassion Into Your Career,” launched “this summer” and will continue into September with a mix of billboards, digital and social media, videos, and community partnerships, Gov. Maura Healey’s office said. The campaign’s website delves into different behavioral health care roles; education and job-training programs; scholarships, grants and state financial aid programs; and job search and MassHire resources.
“Many people are drawn to work that helps others, but they may not know how many career pathways exist within behavioral health or where to begin,” said Funmi Aguocha, assistant commissioner of the Office of Behavioral Health Promotion and Prevention. “This campaign gives people a clear starting point and connects them with information that can help them turn their compassion, skills, cultural knowledge, and lived experience into impactful work.”
Healey administration spokespeople did not immediately disclose the cost of the campaign. The fiscal 2026 budget called for a $500,000 mental health workforce pipeline program, aimed at encouraging a “culturally, ethnically and linguistically diverse behavioral health workforce through collaboration between colleges and behavioral health providers.”
The campaign’s website outlines the types of responsibilities and skills needed for behavioral health jobs, including peer-to-peer professionals, community health workers, mental health counselors, social workers, psychiatrists, and psychologists. Campaign materials are available in English, Spanish, Brazilian Portuguese, Vietnamese, Arabic, Haitian Creole and Simplified Chinese, the administration said.
“A diverse workforce helps ensure that behavioral health programs and services are responsive to the needs of the communities they serve and that individuals can access support from professionals who understand and reflect their experiences,” the website says. “As demand for behavioral health programs and services continues to grow, there is a need for people from all backgrounds to help build a stronger, more equitable behavioral health system.”
More than one in five residents reported having a behavioral health care visit in 2025, and more than one in six individuals paid entirely out of pocket for the appointment, according to an annual survey from the Center for Health Information and Analysis. One in 10 residents had an unmet behavioral health need, which 5.4 percent attributed to the cost of care. 
Massachusetts is “facing a behavioral health (BH) access crisis” that’s largely fueled by provider shortages “across all settings,” says a May report from the Health Policy Commission’s Behavioral Health Workforce Center. Multiple inpatient psychiatric facilities and intensive outpatient programs have shuttered since 2020, and more than 25 percent of independent psychotherapy providers accept only cash payment that’s partly due to low insurance reimbursement rates.
Providers with master’s degrees delivered the majority of non-medical psychotherapy and psychiatric evaluation services but “often received the lowest reimbursement for those services,” the HPC report found. Commercial insurers reimbursed those clinicians for psychotherapy at about 66 percent of the rate for physicians.
Health and Human Services Secretary Kiame Mahaniah on Thursday embarked on a statewide community mental health tour in Lawrence, where he visited a clinic run by Beth Israel Lahey Health Behavioral Services. Mahaniah plans to visit other centers and organizations focused on prevention, treatment, and recovery in the coming months.
“This tour will not only amplify the good work happening in our communities but will also help make sure residents know the resources available to them to preempt an emergency response,” Mahaniah said.

title: Dems push Trump administration for investigation into wildfire response near Boren’s Idaho ranch
description: Three Democratic U.S. senators are demanding the Trump Administration investigate reports that Undersecretary of Agriculture for Natural Resources and Environment Michael Boren allegedly pushed officials for additional resources to fight a small wildfire near his Idaho ranch this summer. U.S. Sens. Ron Wyden, D-Oregon; Amy Klobuchar, D-Minnesota; and Martin[...]
text:
U.S. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins (left) swears in Michael Boren as the under secretary for Natural Resources and Environment in her office on Jan. 20, 2026, at the USDA Headquarters in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Christophe Paul/U.S. Department of Agriculture)Three Democratic U.S. senators are demanding the Trump Administration investigate reports that Undersecretary of Agriculture for Natural Resources and Environment Michael Boren allegedly pushed officials for additional resources to fight a small wildfire near his Idaho ranch this summer.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
U.S. Sens. Ron Wyden, D-Oregon; Amy Klobuchar, D-Minnesota; and Martin Heinrich, D-New Mexico, requested a full investigation into Boren’s involvement and influence in the Cabin Creek Fire in a letter they sent to U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins.  
“Mr. Boren’s actions constitute potentially a misuse of taxpayer funds and put American families at further risk by diverting scarce resources from high-priority wildfires threatening communities elsewhere in the region and country,” the senators wrote. “We request a full investigation into the nature and extent of Boren’s involvement in response to the Cabin Creek Fire and a detailed accounting of the safeguards the agency has implemented or plans to implement to prevent political interference and conflicts of interest in wildfire response.”

CONTACT US



Earlier this month, the Washington Post reported that Boren pushed U.S. Forest Service officials to increase the number of aircraft responding to a small fire near a ranch Boren owns in the Sawtooth National Recreation Area.
“Western states are already facing a shortage of firefighting personnel and resources as a direct result of the Trump administration’s staffing and funding cuts,” the Democrats wrote in a press release issued Friday. “During this record setting fire season, fires of much larger size threatening American lives and homes have not received even a fraction of the same commitment of resources.”
Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a nonprofit legal watchdog group, has also called for an investigation into the allegations and filed a complaint with the Agriculture Department’s Office of Inspector General, according to an Aug. 17 press release.
“The Inspector General must investigate whether Undersecretary Boren risked public safety to protect his property,” said CREW President Donald K. Sherman in the release. “Not only are Boren’s priorities in doubt, but his actions raise questions about his ‘scant’ qualifications for his role. His reported actions could be the result of incompetence, deliberate malfeasance or both. Regardless, they are inexcusable.”
Boren is a founder of Clearwater Analytics, a Boise-based financial technology company. 
In 2025 President Donald Trump appointed Boren as undersecretary of natural resources and the environment at the U.S. Department of Agriculture.
Boren has clashed with the federal government before his appointment and been involved with multiple lawsuits related to a private airstrip he owns near Stanley.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Whitmer attorneys dispute Enbridge argument that Michigan lacks authority to revoke Line 5 easement
description: After a federal court ruling found Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer’s move to terminate the easement to operate the Line 5 pipeline in the Great Lakes unenforceable, the governor and the head of the Department of Natural Resource challenged the decision, filing further arguments with the 6th Circuit Court of Appeals on Friday.  In their initial […]
text:
(File photo by Laina G. Stebbins/Michigan Advance)After a federal court ruling found Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer’s move to terminate the easement to operate the Line 5 pipeline in the Great Lakes unenforceable, the governor and the head of the Department of Natural Resource challenged the decision, filing further arguments with the 6th Circuit Court of Appeals on Friday. 
In their initial brief filed in May, attorneys representing Whitmer and DNR Director Scott Bowen argued that Judge Robert Jonker of the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Michigan’s Southern Division had erred in siding with the pipeline’s operator, Enbridge, which argued that the Pipeline Safety Act of 1992 prevents states from imposing safety regulations on interstate pipelines. 
The Canadian company also pointed to a 1977 treaty between the United States and Canada, arguing Whitmer’s decision to revoke the pipeline’s easement would breach the nations’ agreement regarding the flow of oil and natural gas across borders.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
On appeal, attorneys for Whitmer and Bowen argued Jonker’s decision deprived the state of its rights over the Great Lakes bottomlands, asking the federal appeals court to determine whether the Pipeline Safety Act and the Foreign Affairs Doctrine bar the state from terminating Enbridge’s easement. 
“In the district court’s view, it does not matter whether Enbridge has any valid property rights: Congress forced states, having once granted permission to use state land, to forever surrender their rights in that land regardless of whether the occupier complied with the terms under which the state granted access—an endless, congressionally compelled occupation,” the state’s initial brief reads. “No law remotely supports that outcome.”
2026-08-28 (Dkt 58) State Officials Reply Brief
 
Enbridge filed its response at the end of July, noting that the lower court determined “the Governor sought to enforce ‘multiple state-imposed safety requirements to justify shutting down Line 5, ’” reasoning that these actions were taken to enforce a safety standard.
“On appeal, the Governor does not challenge the district court’s reasoning directly but tries to achieve the same preempted result via
slightly different paths,” Enbridge’s attorneys wrote in their response. 
“She urges the Court to look past the safety motivations driving her shutdown order and focus on the source of the state law she invokes — which she claims is property law,” the attorneys continued, arguing that the district court correctly rejected this argument.
In their response to Enbridge filed Friday, attorneys for Whitmer and Bowen hit back, stating that “Enbridge is wrong: neither the Pipeline Safety Act (PSA), the Foreign Affairs Doctrine, nor the 1977 Treaty entitles it to use Michigan’s land without consent or a valid easement.”
They noted another federal appeals court had recently underscored the importance for pipeline operators to obtain valid land rights in the Bad River Band of the Lake Superior Tribe of Chippewa Indians case against Enbridge. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 7th Circuit affirmed a lower court’s decision that Enbridge has been trespassing on the Bad River reservation since its easements to operate Line 5 on the band’s sovereign territory expired in 2013.
“The same is true here,” Whitmer’s attorneys wrote. “The State Officials allege that Enbridge does not have consent or a legal privilege to operate Line 5 in the Straits because its easement was terminated and revoked.  Nothing in the PSA authorizes Enbridge to operate an oil pipeline on the State’s land without its consent or a valid easement.”
They also argued that the 1977 Transit Pipelines Treaty does not preempt the state’s notice revoking Enbridge’s easement, noting that the Canadian Government acknowledges that the terms and conditions for operating a pipeline may include “obtaining easements,” and multiple Presidential Permits point to valid easements under state law as a condition for operating a transit pipeline. 
Tribal leaders, clean water advocates rally in Lansing as Line 5 fight intensifies

“The Great Lakes power Michigan’s economy, supply drinking water to millions, and define our way of life,” Whitmer said in a statement. “Protecting these natural treasures is a top priority. My brief continues my seven-year fight to stop Enbridge from pumping oil through the Great Lakes. Michigan must have a say in what runs through our waters. We must get Line 5 out of the water and work together to protect our precious Great Lakes for generations to come.”
In a statement to Michigan Advance, Enbridge spokesperson Ryan Duffy said the state had fought for more than five years to shut down the pipeline due to “unsupported claims about its safety.” 
“The Court affirmed that the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA) is the exclusive federal regulator of pipeline safety,” Duffy said. “PHMSA has taken no action against Line 5, underscoring its safe operation. Enbridge has always worked closely with PHMSA and will continue to do so.” 
Duffy argued that any further dispute around the pipeline’s operations must be handled through the 1977 Transit Treaty’s dispute resolution process, noting that Canada has already invoked this process. 
“The Court’s ruling makes clear that efforts by Michigan officials to permanently shut down Line 5 would interfere with U.S. foreign affairs – authority vested exclusively in the federal government,” he said.
While pipeline opponents back state’s legal arguments, bad blood with Whitmer remains
During her 2018 campaign for governor, Whitmer promised she’d take action to get Line 5 out of the Great Lakes. However, in recent months, the support Whitmer once enjoyed among opponents of the pipeline has soured, as her administration approved permits for the controversial Line 5 tunnel project, which would replace the dual pipelines resting on the bottom of the Straits of Mackinac with a single segment housed in a tunnel beneath the lakebed.
Tribal leaders and environmental advocates gathered in Lansing earlier this week to lay out the future of their fight against Line 5, with Liz Kirkwood, the executive director of Flow Water Advocates, urging attendees to push Whitmer to “finish the job” she started when she revoked Enbridge’s easement in 2020.
David Holtz, coordinator of the Oil and Water Don’t Mix Coalition, remained skeptical, calling Whitmer’s Friday statement about protecting the Great Lakes “message management.”
“We’d welcome a governor who actually opposes Line 5, full stop, with the Straits, tunnel, and the 645 miles in between,” Holtz said in a statement. “Today’s filing isn’t evidence of that.”

U.S. Senate candidate Brian Bengs speaks to supporters on Nov. 7, 2022, at the Washington Pavilion in Sioux Falls. (Photo by John Hult/South Dakota Searchlight) 


Searchlight Report is a podcast from South Dakota Searchlight. Reporter and host Meghan O’Brien works with other Searchlight journalists to take listeners inside politics and policy in The Mount Rushmore State.			




Brian Bengs is an independent running in the Nov. 3 election against incumbent Republican Mike Rounds for a seat representing South Dakota in the U.S. Senate (there is no Democrat in the race after that party’s nominee withdrew). Bengs, a veteran of the Air Force and Navy who has a law degree and formerly taught at Northern State University in Aberdeen, previously ran in 2022 as a Democrat against Republican Sen. John Thune, who’s now the majority leader.
Bengs joined Searchlight Report host Meghan O’Brien to share what motivated him to join another Senate race, and what it could mean to have an independent representing South Dakota.

title: Firefighters make progress on state’s largest fire, scenic byway closed
description: Several large fires are burning in southwestern Montana, though cooler temperatures and precipitation have helped crews make progress on the blazes. Southwestern portions of the state have dealt with significant wildfire activity during the past month and several large fires are burning in Ravalli, Beaverhead and Granite counties. The approximately 33,000 ac[...]
text:
A Lolo Hotshots sawyer creates fire line on the Sand Creek Fire on 8/19/26. (Photo via Sand Creek Fire Inciweb page)Several large fires are burning in southwestern Montana, though cooler temperatures and precipitation have helped crews make progress on the blazes.
Southwestern portions of the state have dealt with significant wildfire activity during the past month and several large fires are burning in Ravalli, Beaverhead and Granite counties.
The approximately 33,000 acre Sand Creek fire is the state’s largest, burning about 7.5 miles southeast of Wisdom. The Pioneer Mountains Scenic Byway is currently closed and firefighters are planning to make use of it as a shaded fire break, which a press release from fire managers said involves cutting some trees and leaving others.
The shaded fire break will also serve as a control line between the Sand Creek Fire and the Bobcat Fire, an approximately 10,000-acre wildfire burning just miles away. The Northern Rockies Complex Incident Management Team 1 is managing both blazes jointly.
“The western fire edge is irregular, with areas of heat and pockets of thick, dead and downed timber that limit safe access. Indirect line construction continues from Clemow Cow Camp east to the Old Tim Creek area,” a fire press release said. “Crews attempted a strategic burnout north of this line yesterday, but gusty winds paused the operation; ignition work in this large, unburned area will resume today as weather allows. Bringing the fire edge out to these established lines and securing them will help protect private property to the south and west of the fire area.”
There were 660 personnel listed on those fires, which a press release said has access to aerial firefighting resources.The two blazes have cost about $30 million combined to fight, according to the National Interagency Fire Center. Four structures have been lost in the Sand Creek fire.
Map of the Sand Creek and Bobcat fires. (Graphic via Inciweb)
The Sand Creek fire was listed at 11% containment on Friday, with the Bobcat fire at 40%.
Firefighters are working to protect private property threatened by the Sand Creek fire, a release said. The weather has also been favorable.
“Fire activity will be moderated by cloud cover and humidity levels, but gusty winds may push the fire in exposed areas,” a Sand Creek fire press release said.
The Moose Fire, burning 24 miles northwest of Philipsburg in the Beaverhead-Deerlodge National Forest, was listed at slightly less than 6,000 acres on Friday.
Weather was a far greater concern on that wildfire.
“Warming and drying conditions will bring elevated fire weather concerns today,” a release from the Moose fire said, adding that, “Fire activity has started to slowly pick up.”
There were 107 personnel listed as working on that fire, which started in late July and is about 10% contained.
National Weather Service maps show increased chances for some parts of Montana to see rain headed into the weekend.
Another larger fire, the Camp Creek Fire, has burned approximately 8,000 acres deep within the Bob Marshall Wilderness and is currently about 40 miles west of Augusta. About a dozen personnel are on that fire, which is expected to head into even more remote sections of the Bob Marshall Wilderness.

name: VTDigger
title: Killington seeks financial help after cash crunch, TIF compliance issues
description:
The town needed to take out a loan as it works on public infrastructure for the multibillion-dollar Killington Village project.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Killington seeks financial help after cash crunch, TIF compliance issues.
text:
Killington’s welcome sign in June 2022. File photo by Natalie Williams/VTDigger

This story by Katy Savage was first published by the Mountain Times on Aug. 26, 2026. 
Monday, Aug. 24 was Celia Clancy’s first time sitting with the Killington Selectboard since she defeated Roger Rivera for the seat on Aug. 11. She was largely quiet during the meeting.
Killington officials are trying to stabilize the town’s finances after a cash crunch left it without enough money to cover all of its financial obligations earlier this month. Staffing shortages have contributed to confusion and reporting problems with public financing supporting infrastructure for the multibillion-dollar Killington Village development.
About $6.3 million was due recently, but the town had only about $5 million in the bank, forcing officials to seek a 30-day extension. The town has since paid about $6.3 million in obligations, including $1.3 million in maturing debt, according to interim Town Manager Rob Kovalesky.
But the town still needed cash to cover upcoming expenses. Working with Community Bank, Killington secured a $3.4 million tax anticipation note, expected Sept. 2. 
Tax anticipation notes are short-term loans used to cover expenses while waiting for tax revenue to come in.
“That was a really rough telephone call, but we got it done,” Selectboard chair Jim Haff said at the Aug. 24 selectboard meeting, referring to the call with the bank. “So we will have $3.477538 (million) put into our general fund to start funding some other payments.”
Another $2.4 million in expenses will come due by Nov. 15, which Kovalesky said will be covered by incoming tax revenue.
Killington’s cash-flow problems follow months without an approved municipal budget. The first budget failed on Town Meeting Day, and voters did not approve a new budget until Aug. 11. The approved budget allows the town to send tax bills and collect needed money.
“We’ve got to run this like a business,” Haff said.

READ MORE

The town has also used tax money collected for education to cover municipal expenses, Haff acknowledged during Monday’s meeting. Haff had previously been adamant that the town could not use education funds for municipal expenses. But he said the town’s auditor has since reviewed the relevant statutes and approved temporary use.
“We’ve had a conversation with our auditor, Ron Smith, and he’s looked into the statutes,” Haff said. “Yes, we probably used some of the education fund money that has come in to pay that $1.3 million. But per statute, you have 30 days to turn it over to education.”
Town brings in financial help
Killington has been operating without a finance director since Kirsten Hathaway-Olson resigned in June.
The town is now looking both for outside financial help and potential permanent hires.
Shasta Mattino, director of finance and interim executive director for the Chamber & Economic Development of the Rutland Region, was expected to provide the town with a contract proposal.
“She is extremely financially oriented,” Kovalesky said. “She knows systems backwards and forwards, and she is providing us, hopefully, by tomorrow, a proposal to work with us to be able to help us better organize and streamline our processes to be able to capture the right types of grants, the reimbursements for TIF.” 
Sarah Macy, a finance director for the city of St. Albans, is also expected to provide Killington with 3-4 hours of help every few weeks, with a particular focus on the town’s tax increment financing district.
“She is the TIF person,” Haff said. “If you ever want to see somebody get excited about Excel and NEMRC, I mean, just have a conversation with her. She’s amazing.”
Her work will be reimbursed through the town’s TIF district.
Town officials are also expected to meet with the Vermont Economic Progress Council in Montpelier on Aug. 31 to explain the town’s financial situation and its failure to provide the council with required documentation. Stephanie Clarke, the vice president of White + Burke Real Estate Advisors, who is advising the town on its TIF projects, submitted a response and corrective action plan after VEPC notified Killington that it had found compliance issues, which centered on widespread financial discrepancies.
The board also discussed how the town ended up without a retained municipal auditor. R.H. Smith had served as the town’s auditor for about 15 years. Kovalesky said he learned the firm reached out twice in March and April seeking to meet with the selectboard. On April 3, Kovalesky said, the town’s finance director told R.H. Smith that Killington was holding off on signing a contract for fiscal year 2026 because of increased costs and was considering seeking bids from other firms.
Selectboard members claim they were unaware of this decision, but town employees had told VEPC.
VEPC Executive Director Jessica Hartleben called the period without an auditor a “serious control matter” in an email that Kovalesky read during the meeting, while emphasizing that it did not change Killington’s responsibilities to properly administer and document its TIF district.
The town has since reestablished its relationship with R.H. Smith.
The board also directed Kovalesky to begin advertising several of the town’s vacant leadership positions.
Among those, the fire chief position has been vacant since Billy Austin resigned in May. 
“Now that we know we got money coming in, and there’s a budget for a fire chief at $85,000, let’s get that together,” Haff said.
The town will also seek to fill a finance director and public works director positions, while it works toward a hybrid model.

title: 2 candidates file for Arkansas House vacancy created by lawmaker’s resignation
description: Two candidates are seeking to fill the vacancy left by Republican Rep. Austin McCollum’s resignation following domestic violence charges this month.  Republican Kara Armas of Pea Ridge and Democrat Parker Stohlton of Bella Vista filed by the noon deadline Friday to run for the House District 8 seat in a special election that will coincide […]
text:
Voters cast their ballots during the primary election at Saint Mark Baptist Church in Little Rock, Arkansas on March 3, 2026. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)Two candidates are seeking to fill the vacancy left by Republican Rep. Austin McCollum’s resignation following domestic violence charges this month. 
Republican Kara Armas of Pea Ridge and Democrat Parker Stohlton of Bella Vista filed by the noon deadline Friday to run for the House District 8 seat in a special election that will coincide with the Nov. 3 general election. 
The winner will serve the remainder of McCollum’s term, which ends in January. His resignation left Republicans with a 79-20 majority in the House.
Arkansas state Rep. Austin McCollum resigns after domestic violence arrest

Kara Armas is the wife of Brian Armas, a Republican seeking a two-year term representing House District 8, which includes a portion of northern Benton County, in November’s general election. Brian Armas, who serves on the Benton County Quorum Court, is running unopposed. 
Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders called the special election last week to fill the vacancy left by McCollum’s resignation. The Bentonville Republican stepped down earlier this month, just days after being arrested on charges of aggravated assault against his wife. Sanders and other top Republicans urged him to resign after the arrest. 
McCollum, who served in the House since 2017, was not running for reelection and won the Republican nomination for Benton County judge in March. McCollum, who has not dropped out of the race, is unopposed in November’s election.
McCollum’s vacancy is the fifth that will be filled in 2026. Republican Sen. Brad Simon and Democratic Rep. Alex Holladay won special elections in March to represent Senate District 26 and House District 70, respectively. 
Republican Bill Teeter won the House District 44 special election in August to replace the late Republican Rep. Stan Berry.  
In the Arkansas Senate, Republican Harrell Wilson will face Tomeka Butler, the Democratic mayor of Eudora, for the Senate District 1 seat in a special election that also coincides with the November general election.
The seat became vacant when Republican Sen. Ben Gilmore resigned in June to work for Attorney General Tim Griffin. Republicans hold a 28-6 majority in the Senate with the vacancy.

name: WyoFile
title: What cost the Wyoming Freedom Caucus its power?
description:
Politicos of different stripes agree: Opposition to the caucus was better organized, and funded, than it was in 2024, when the group won control of the House. 
The post What cost the Wyoming Freedom Caucus its power? appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Ahead of Wyoming’s primary election, Freedom Caucus member Rep. Jeremy Haroldson said he had a bad feeling. 
The Wheatland lawmaker ran unopposed this year while most of his fellow caucus members and allies faced Republican opponents in the primary. Haroldson’s hunch, he told WyoFile this week, had to do with “the amount of mailers going out in all these races” that spun “a whole lot of misinformation, or skewed information.” 
“Hence, in a way,” Haroldson said, “I had a sinking feeling it may go poorly” for his bloc.
And it did. Voters across the state supported candidates who campaigned on traditional, middle-of-the-road conservative issues like business, education and healthcare. The result was a near complete ousting of the hardline group of Republicans who won control of the state House just two years ago.
Without an opponent, Haroldson is set to begin his fourth term in 2027. But his return to the House will be without most of his Freedom Caucus allies. Thirteen of the group’s aligned incumbents lost their reelection bids. Four more representatives lost their attempts to join the Senate. And over a dozen other candidates aligned with the caucus, including some political newcomers and some former lawmakers seeking rematches from 2024, were also defeated. As for legislators associated with the caucus who sought higher office in the executive branch, they, too, lost. 
The results fell well short of the caucus’s goal to win control of the Senate and grow its House presence to a supermajority. Instead, the caucus will likely have 10 reliable votes in the House and five in the Senate come January. 
(Tennessee Watson/WyoFile)
The Freedom Caucus entered campaign season on the defensive in some ways. Most of its top priorities failed during the recent legislative session, including proposed budget cuts that faced significant public backlash. Plus, several caucus members and allies were embroiled in a controversy, known as Checkgate, involving the delivery of campaign donations on the House floor, which is currently under criminal investigation. After a legislative committee determined the checks did not constitute bribery, the House unanimously voted to approve a report that said: “the conduct that occurred on the House floor was undesirable and must never occur again.” 
Few, however, believe that Checkgate, and a raft of narrow legislative defeats, solely account for the caucus’ dramatic reversal of electoral fate and loss of power. What explains the rest of the story depends on who you ask. Caucus opponents say the bloc’s priorities were simply, fundamentally unpopular with most of the state. Supporters say the media represented the Freedom Caucus’ agenda as more extreme than it actually was. Both sides agree, however, that opposition to the caucus was better organized, and funded, than it was two years ago when the hardline faction ousted several longtime Republican incumbents and won control of the House. 
In the last year, several political action committees formed to directly oppose the caucus, including Common Sense Republicans for Wyoming, which reported spending more than $95,000. Other newly formed PACs championed specific issues, like public lands. The Protect Wyoming PAC was catalyzed by legislation from Sen. Bob Ide, a Freedom Caucus ally in the upper chamber, that called on Congress to turn over 30 million acres of federal public land to Wyoming. 
Meanwhile, established groups, like Better Wyoming, worked strategically on voter education and community engagement. Americans for Prosperity, a veteran conservative group, reported spending nearly $286,000 opposing several Freedom Caucus candidates. 
“Those that were trying to defend the Freedom Caucus were very few,” Haroldson said. “And those that were trying to defeat the Freedom Caucus were many.” 
Sen. Cale Case, a Lander Republican, sees things in a different light. 
“The good guys just got better organized,” Case told WyoFile. 
Case triumphed over his primary challenger, Lisa Wilson, despite more than $17,000 in attack ads against him paid for by Make Liberty Win. The Virginia-based political action committee spent more than $549,000 largely backing Freedom Caucus candidates. Still, most of those candidates lost. 
“People were very ready for the change,” Case said. “And it seems like they just got tired of those policies when they figured out the implication of them.” 
Several Freedom Caucus leaders did not return WyoFile’s multiple requests for comment, including Rep. John Bear, R-Gillette, Rep. Rachel Rodriguez-Williams, R-Cody, and Jessie Rubino, the Wyoming state director for the State Freedom Caucus Network. 
The media and negative campaigning
Bear previously chaired the caucus and has remained one of its most prominent leaders, including as chairman of the House Appropriations Committee. He lost his reelection bid in Gillette’s House District 31 to Douglas Moore, a longtime energy industry manager and political newcomer.
Several days after the election, he made an appearance on Cowboy State Daily’s Morning Show, where he said “I don’t think it’s too far-fetched to consider” the outcome of the election “to be an anti-Freedom Caucus vote.” 
“The question is how did we get there?” Bear said, before pointing to several things, including anti-Freedom Caucus campaigning and the media’s coverage, which he said “leans left.” 
Rep. John Bear, R-Gillette, gathers with members of the Wyoming Freedom Caucus to pray early Monday, Feb. 9, 2026, outside the Wyoming Supreme Court in Cheyenne. (Mike Vanata/WyoFile)
During the session, when Rebecca Bextel, the woman at the center of Checkgate, handed over text messages to the House Investigative Committee, they included correspondence with Bear. 
“I’m not planning on announcing until after the session,” Bear told Bextel sometime in January. “Too much media on my cuts to the budget.”
In his interview with WyoFile, Haroldson also pointed to what he sees as unfair media scrutiny. 
“I’m going to be 100% honest with you. The media was against the Freedom Caucus. There was a lot of slanted media coverage through the session,” Haroldson said. “There was a lot that came out of that, and in all reality, things like Checkgate didn’t help anyone. Was that legal? 100%. Was that blown out of proportion? Absolutely.”
Haroldson also pointed to specific coverage. 
“I think more than anything, what hurt the caucus is how the media portrayed the entire conversation around the budget when they say things like ‘University of Wyoming budget slashed.’”
The Freedom Caucus pushed to reduce the university’s block grant by 11%, or $40 million, which Haroldson said is “a long ways from being a slashed budget.”
Haroldson said the caucus’s work on the budget was about “asking questions and challenging the status quo.”
“Why would we not kick the tires on this?” he said. 
Bear told the Morning Show that while negative campaigning gets a lot of complaints, it works, including against the caucus.
“The voters responded in a positive way to that negative campaigning, and they did in 2024 as well,” Bear said. “We held no punches back when we were illustrating the things that Republican legislators were doing that were antithetical to what the people of Wyoming desired.” 
Two Republican lawmakers sued the caucus’s political action committee  for defamation in 2024 after it sent text messages and mailers claiming they had voted to remove former President Donald Trump from the presidential ballot. No such vote occurred in the Wyoming Legislature, but the case was dismissed in May when a district court judge determined there was insufficient evidence to indicate the PAC had made statements with actual malice.
During this election cycle, Make Liberty Win spent more than $14,000 in digital ads, door hangers and text messages to voters supporting Bear, but it was “too little, too late,” he told the Morning Show.
“The negative stuff on me started right at the end of the session,” Bear said. “And by the time these campaigns were being started on our end — and this is an indictment of how conservatives campaigned — we were too little, too late in defeating those negative messages, and so we’ll have to learn from that.”
Different groups
Bear also named Rep. Liz Storer, a Jackson Democrat, and accused her of 
“funding candidates that were on the Republican side, as well as PACs that were attacking Freedom Caucus members.”
State campaign finance records show that Storer personally donated a total of  $5,500 to candidates across Wyoming, including Bear’s opponent and Robert Short for secretary of state as well as the Democratic Caucus of the Wyoming Legislature. 
Rep. Liz Storer, D-Jackson, during the 2026 Wyoming Legislature’s budget session in Cheyenne. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)
Storer is also president and CEO of the George B. Storer Foundation, which has funded an array of causes and organizations over the last 70 years. 
(Editor’s note: The George B. Storer Foundation is a financial supporter of WyoFile. The foundation has no role in WyoFile’s editorial content.) 
“I think there are a lot of groups that did a lot of things in the election,” to oppose the caucus, Storer said, “I probably don’t even know all of them.” 
As for the Storer Foundation, she said, it “has worked for a long time to engage voters, with the idea that to get good policy done, sometimes you need to change who’s sitting in the seat,” Storer told WyoFile. 
The foundation, for example, is a key funder of Better Wyoming, a progressive nonprofit that has focused much of its community organizing on voter turnout. 
As to the Freedom Caucus loss this year, Storer pointed to voter turnout, which saw about 27,600 more residents cast ballots than they did in 2024, when the caucus was largely successful. “Primaries tend to get people that are out on the fringes, on both sides,” Storer said. “So if more people vote, it just means more people who aren’t quite so far out there are going to vote, and that will shift the outcome.” 
Nate Martin, executive director of Better Wyoming, pointed to what he called the “Achilles’ heel” of the Freedom Caucus.
“They don’t support policies that are actually popular in Wyoming,” Martin said. 
Martin, who’s married to Rep. Karlee Provenza, a Laramie Democrat, said the caucus proved its efficacy as the opposition party “by picking holes in the policy agenda of the people who were in charge.”
But it was given a different task in 2024 when it won control of the House, Martin said. 
“When it actually came time to govern, and they said they were going to defund the University of Wyoming and abolish the business council and take local control away from public school districts and not give state employees raises, people in Wyoming were like, ‘What the hell are you talking about?’” he said.
As such, Martin said, it became important for Better Wyoming and its associated organization, Better Wyoming Action + Research, to “articulate the harm that the Freedom Caucus as a group does.” 
Those efforts included mobilizing more than 200 volunteers across six of the state’s communities “to write handwritten postcards talking about the Freedom Caucus and how they vote,” Martin said. 
The group also launched a website that used voting records, formal membership and endorsements to identify Freedom Caucus-aligned lawmakers and candidates. 
“If you put up a big billboard that just says, ‘Vote out the Freedom Caucus,’ not everybody knows who the Freedom Caucus is,” Martin said. “The billboard isn’t necessarily targeting people who are going to vote, and the words Freedom Caucus don’t appear anywhere on a primary ballot.” 
The page got nearly 20,000 unique viewers in recent months, according to an Aug. 20 press release from Better Wyoming A+R.
As for Haroldson, he rejected Martin’s characterization of the caucus as being out of step with Wyomingites.
“I haven’t met a single grandmother who’s upset that their little girl, their granddaughter, is not going to have to worry about a man walking into the locker room. I haven’t met a single one yet,” Haroldson said. “I haven’t met a single parent who’s like, ‘You know, what I really want is less parental rights when it comes to education. I haven’t met a single person yet that’s sitting there saying, ‘You know what, I think it’s okay to have men competing in women’s sports in the state of Wyoming.’” 
After the election, the Freedom Caucus posted a statement on its Facebook page titled, “The WYFC Is Not Going Anywhere.” 
“Last night’s results will not undo the policy wins we’ve delivered on behalf of the people,” the statement says, pointing to tax cuts, school choice, voting restrictions and anti-trans legislation that the caucus helped usher into law. 
Rep. Jeremy Haroldson, R-Wheatland, during the 2026 Wyoming Legislature’s budget session in Cheyenne. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)
As the sole remaining caucus member with House leadership experience, Haroldson is effectively left to carry the torch in the Legislature. He currently serves as speaker pro tempore, the second-most powerful position in the House, which presides over the lower chamber in the absence of the speaker. 
Asked about what’s next, he said, “right now there’s a lot of introspection” and asking questions.
“What are we supposed to do? What does it look like moving forward? What did we do well? What did we do poorly?” Haroldson said. “What do the people of Wyoming want?”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: School district cuts student access to Central Arkansas Library System’s online materials
description: A central Arkansas school district cut students’ access to the local public library’s online educational materials in response to a federal court ruling that a 2023 law restricting library content can take effect, a district spokesperson said Thursday. The Pulaski County Special School District, which covers most of the rest of the county outside Little […]
text:
(Leonardo Fernandez Viloria/Getty Images)A central Arkansas school district cut students’ access to the local public library’s online educational materials in response to a federal court ruling that a 2023 law restricting library content can take effect, a district spokesperson said Thursday.
The Pulaski County Special School District, which covers most of the rest of the county outside Little Rock and North Little Rock, started participating in the Central Arkansas Library System’s “tech card” program in 2018. The online portal provides “recommended resources divided by grade level for research, homework help, and more,” according to the CALS website.
District communications director Fredricka Sharkey on Friday declined to comment further on administrators’ decision.
Central Arkansas school district will reinstate access to library’s digital learning tools

The district previously stopped using the program at the start of the 2023-24 school year due to administrators’ concerns about Act 372 of 2023.
At the time, two sections of the law had been temporarily blocked by a federal judge, including the section that would criminalize “furnishing a harmful item to a minor.” One unchallenged portion of the law gives school boards the final say over the placement and availability of library materials.
District officials said in 2023 that the lack of a “filter” on CALS’ online learning materials led an attorney to suggest that the district stop using the program. The district reinstated the program in January 2024.
In July of this year, a federal appeals court removed the injunction on Act 372. The court has yet to issue its order for the law to go into effect, and the 18 plaintiffs filed a motion Thursday asking the court for a rehearing and clarification on compliance.
The Pulaski County district, which has about 11,000 students, is not the first to limit students’ digital access to books in response to state policies and concern over what might be considered inappropriate content for minors.
Last year, the North Little Rock School District made dozens of LGBTQ+ books unavailable on its digital reading platform.
North Little Rock School District orders 50 LGBTQ+ books hidden on students’ digital platform

Additionally, Act 372 was one of two laws that Benton School District cited last year when it removed a book from elementary and middle school libraries in response to a parent’s complaint about its LGBTQ+ content.
PCSSD administrators have not mentioned LGBTQ+ content as a reason for dropping CALS’ online educational resources.
CALS and its executive director, Nate Coulter, are among the plaintiffs challenging Act 372. Coulter said Friday that he is “sympathetic to the district’s concerns about the possible implications” of the law but found it frustrating that thousands of Pulaski County students no longer have access to CALS’ online learning resources.
“This is yet another negative consequence of an ill-advised law that supposedly solves a nonexistent problem,” Coulter said.

title: Tennessee governor backs plan to name Nashville airport for Dolly Parton
description: Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee and Nashville International Airport officials announced plans Friday to rename the airport in Dolly Parton’s honor. Lee discussed the idea this week with Parton’s team after the legendary singer, songwriter and philanthropist died at age 80, and they said they were touched by the idea and open to the form of […]
text:
Online petition group 
@change.org
 flew a plane over the Tennessee Capitol pulling a banner promoting the renaming of the Nashville International Airport for the late, beloved Dolly Parton. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee and Nashville International Airport officials announced plans Friday to rename the airport in Dolly Parton’s honor.
Lee discussed the idea this week with Parton’s team after the legendary singer, songwriter and philanthropist died at age 80, and they said they were touched by the idea and open to the form of recognition, according to a release from the governor’s office.
“Dolly Parton’s extraordinary life is forever woven into the fabric of our state,” Lee said. “From her rural mountain home in East Tennessee to global stages, Dolly carried the Volunteer spirit with her.”
Lee said he believes naming the airport in her honor would be a fitting way to welcome travelers to Nashville where her music has a strong legacy. Besides selling millions of albums and winning multiple awards, Parton established the Dollywood Foundation and Imagination Library to provide scholarships, provide books worldwide to young children and provide aid during tragedies such as the Gatlinburg fire and Hurricane Helene that ravaged East Tennessee areas.
Doug Kruelen, president and CEO of the airport, said in the statement he supports the proposal, calling the airport the “front door to Music City.”“Dolly’s remarkable legacy reminds us that what makes Nashville special is our ability to welcome people from every walk of life. She understood that dignity, kindness and opportunity should never be defined by where you come from or your socioeconomic status,” Kruelen said in the release.
The Metro Nashville Airport Authority, which is tied up in litigation over the appointment of a state-controlled board versus a Metro-appointed board, will consider the renaming at a Sept. 17 meeting.
In addition to the support from Lee and Kruelen, Republican state Rep. Todd Warner of Chapel Hill started pushing the recognition of Parton at the airport shortly after her death, as did Metro Councilmember Russ Bradford, who began circulating a petition for the change.
An airplane flew over the Capitol Friday and downtown Nashville carrying a banner urging people to sign the petition.

title: Collins warns Canadian tariffs will hit $170M in Maine goods, urges return to negotiations
description: Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins said Friday that roughly $170 million in local goods will be impacted by the proposed Canadian tariffs, with more than half of that coming from the forest product sector.  Collins wrote to U.S. Department of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and urged them to resume […]
text:
Maine's forest product industry report that tariffs imposed in October have particularly hurt the state's forest products industry. (Photo by Lauren McCauley/ Maine Morning Star)Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins said Friday that roughly $170 million in local goods will be impacted by the proposed Canadian tariffs, with more than half of that coming from the forest product sector. 
Collins wrote to U.S. Department of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and urged them to resume trade negotiations with Canada. 
“Maine’s economy is uniquely intertwined with Canada, and the consequences of an escalating trade dispute will be felt by American families, businesses, workers and communities across the state,” Collins wrote. “Thousands of American jobs and businesses across a variety of sectors are at risk.”
Canada excludes seafood from tariffs, sparing Maine’s lobster industry

Collins said two Maine paper mills, which she said were the largest employers in their towns, reached out to her office and said the tariffs will cause “crushing increased costs” and could potentially impact the mills’ staffing levels. 
Nearly 90% of Maine is forested, and the forestry sector supports roughly 30,000 jobs and contributes more than $8 billion to the state economy, the senator noted. 
Collins said she appreciated that Canada revised the tariffs to exclude seafood and fish products, but the remaining import taxes will still have a significant impact on Maine communities. 
“For example, Maine municipalities rely on road salt from Canada to keep roads safe from snow and ice in the winter,” Collins said. “Frenchville, a very small town on the Canadian border, will have to pay $10,000 more for road salt as a result of the new tariffs.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Opioid settlement advisory council to open portal for fund applicants Monday
description: Katie Storr, from left, Jon Hubanks and Doug Miracle lead the Mississippi Opioid Settlement Fund Advisory Council in its meeting on Tuesday, July 21, 2026, in Jackson.
text:
With reformed policies and outside help, the Mississippi Opioid Settlement Fund Advisory Council will open its second annual grant application Monday for tens of millions of lawsuit dollars intended to address the state’s overdose crisis. 
The council, along with the state Legislature, oversees most of the $430 million of Mississippi funds paid by corporations accused of catalyzing hundreds of thousands of overdose deaths. Now, the council instructs organizations to apply for grants through an online portal. 
Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch also serves as council chair and is campaigning to be the Republican candidate for state governor. In an email, her office’s spokesperson, MaryAsa Lee, said the application portal is designed to “reduce the burden on applicants.” The office has also created an email for organizations to send questions they may have about the application process.
“If a question and its answer would be useful to other applicants, it will be added to the published FAQ on the website,” Lee said. 
The new website was designed and administered by The Steadman Group, a Colorado-based behavioral health consulting group the council contracted this year. The Mississippi Legislature passed a bill in the 2026 legislative session that instructed Fitch’s office to partner with a third-party group, one that could address opioid settlement application problems lawmakers and councilmembers identified in the previous cycle. 
One of those issues was opportunities for council members to influence the reviews of applications that could benefit their own organizations. The portal website echoes language in the law, telling applicants that people who review their proposals have confirmed they have no conflicts of interest. 
The application will be live for six weeks, during which Steadman plans to host two webinars for groups interested in applying for Mississippi opioid money. Lee said those who cannot attend can email the new applicant support address with questions. 
At the opioid committee’s August meeting, Deputy Attorney General Doug Miracle said Steadman will do the initial review of applications before council members finalize their recommendations to the Legislature. State lawmakers will then consider those suggestions in the 2027 regular legislative session.
Steadman told Mississippi Today in June that one of its main focuses this fall will be ensuring each application is held to a consistent standard.
Like other states, Mississippi began receiving its first national opioids settlement payments in 2022. Unlike other states, Mississippi didn’t use any of the over $130 million it accumulated over its first few years until July — except for lawyers fees and dollars local governments could use for any public purpose.

name: VTDigger
title: Out of sight isn’t a policy
description:
Public drug use isn't rising because more people are using. It's rising because they have nowhere left to go.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Out of sight isn’t a policy.
text:
This commentary is by Beach Conger, a physician who works at the Johnson Health Center in Burlington, a clinic that provides medical care to homeless people and those with substance use disorders.
“Human kind cannot bear very much reality.” So wrote T.S. Eliot in “Burnt Norton,” the first of his “Four Quartets.”
I have been reminded of this line by several opinion pieces and letters to the editor in recent weeks about the public visibility of opioid use. The common theme among these pieces is that those who use drugs in public should be held accountable for their actions. It is not the drug use itself that is disquieting, but the fact that the writers can see it. What form this accountability should take includes increased police presence, increased incarceration for public drug use and involuntary treatment. Although the term “rehabilitation” is used, it’s not specified what this means.
It raises the question: Is the individual sick? Or is it society?
If it is the individual, then the increase in public drug use would be due to an increase in the number of opioid users. Although it is hard to find precise data on this question, two observations suggest it’s not the case. The first is that the annual survey of drug use conducted by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration reports that in the past three years, opioid misuse in Vermont has declined from an estimated 18,000 people to 13,000. In addition, overdose numbers have declined even more, from a high of 269 in 2022 to a projected 130 this year, extrapolating from the first four months of data from the Vermont Department of Health.
This suggests that the more likely explanation for the increase in public outdoor drug use is not that there are more drug users, but that they have nowhere to go. Support for this hypothesis is that the homeless population in Chittenden County has more than tripled from 260 in 2020 to an estimated 834 this year.

READ MORE

I work in a facility in downtown Burlington that provides medical services to this population. Most of the people I see were successfully in recovery until Covid-19 disrupted their lives. Like the children who were socially isolated during Covid, they have struggled to regain their footing. Many have given up. They have been in and out of jail and in and out of rehabilitation facilities, after which they are released back to the streets. We do our best to provide treatment, but our efforts, like those of law enforcement, have only a transitory effect. A permanent solution will require both a bigger commitment to long-term treatment in supportive facilities and permanent housing upon release. It is not a commitment our society is willing to make at this time.
I don’t know how to solve this problem. But I do know this: None of the people using drugs on Church Street or in the garages or in City Hall Park or on the waterfront are there because they want to be.
Whenever possible, I eat my lunch in City Hall Park. There are people stumbling around in a daze. There are people transacting drug business. There are people zonked out on the benches. There are people screaming and gesticulating. Some are wild. A few look frightening. It is not a pretty sight, and it is disturbing to watch. I understand how distressing it is for people to witness, especially if they have children with them. But when I sit there, I am not outraged. I am not angry. 
I am sad.

name: Nevada Current
title: Lombardo asks Trump for Hawk Fire emergency declaration
description: Governor Joe Lombardo signed a formal request on Friday asking the White House to issue a presidential emergency declaration for Nevada following the Hawk Fire impacting northwest Reno.  The Hawk Fire is now 95% contained as crews focus on areas with heavy fuel and remove remaining burning materials near control lines to prevent rekindling. As […]
text:
Local residents look over a fence at the Hawk Fire burning on August 23, 2026 in Reno, Nevada. (Photo by Trevor Bexon/Getty Images)Governor Joe Lombardo signed a formal request on Friday asking the White House to issue a presidential emergency declaration for Nevada following the Hawk Fire impacting northwest Reno. 
The Hawk Fire is now 95% contained as crews focus on areas with heavy fuel and remove remaining burning materials near control lines to prevent rekindling.
As of Friday morning, the fire has burned through 15,085 acres, with 550 personnel assigned to ongoing response and recovery efforts.
Officials said at least seven people, including three first responders, have been injured. The fire has destroyed 47 homes and one commercial structure. Eight other commercial structures have also been damaged.
The emergency declaration seeks immediate federal assistance to protect public health and safety, as well as to maintain essential services and support communities still recovering from the Hawk Fire. 
Lombardo, in close coordination with the Nevada Office of Emergency Management (OEM), concluded federal assistance is necessary to protect Nevadans, their property, public assets, and assist in recovery. 
“The actions from our first responders, state agencies, and local and federal partners have been nothing short of heroic while battling the Hawk Fire,” said Lombardo in a statement. “Now, as we begin the road to recovery, Nevada is requesting the full support of our federal partners to protect our communities, restore critical infrastructure, and help those impacted by this devastating fire recover and rebuild.” 
A Presidential emergency declaration would authorize FEMA to identify, mobilize, and provide the equipment and resources necessary to alleviate the impacts of the Hawk Fire. Those emergency protective measures would be funded at the discretion of President Donald Trump.
On Monday, the FEMA Region 9 Regional Administrator authorized the use of federal funds to assist the state of Nevada in combating the Hawk Fire burning in Washoe County.
“We are incredibly grateful for the nationwide and international response to the Hawk Fire,” said Nevada OEM Chief Brett Compston. “A Presidential emergency declaration is crucial, as Nevada’s long-term recovery efforts are just as important as response. We want to restore community lifelines and resources as quickly as possible to those impacted.” 
Preliminary damage assessments from local and state agencies are ongoing, and the state may request additional federal assistance in the coming days.
The latest fire information and recovery resources can be found at oem.nv.gov/wildfire-info-2026

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana high court orders Jeffrey Weisheit executed Nov. 5
description: The Indiana Supreme Court on Friday ordered the state to execute Jeffrey Weisheit before sunrise Nov. 5, clearing the way for Indiana’s fourth execution since it resumed carrying out death sentences less than two years ago. All five justices concurred in the Aug. 28 order. Weisheit is scheduled to be executed by lethal injection at […]
text:
Indiana is preparing for its fourth execution since ending a 15-year pause in December 2024. The state is scheduled to execute Jeffrey Weisheit before sunrise Nov. 5 at the Indiana State Prison in Michigan City. (Photo by Joe Raedle/Newsmakers)The Indiana Supreme Court on Friday ordered the state to execute Jeffrey Weisheit before sunrise Nov. 5, clearing the way for Indiana’s fourth execution since it resumed carrying out death sentences less than two years ago.
All five justices concurred in the Aug. 28 order. Weisheit is scheduled to be executed by lethal injection at Indiana State Prison in Michigan City.
Weisheit was sentenced to death for the 2010 murders of 8-year-old Alyssa Lynch and her 5-year-old brother, Caleb Lynch, who died in a fire at their Evansville home.
“The State of Indiana intends to execute Mr. Weisheit despite the repeated refusal of state and federal courts even to consider the effects of his complex and severe brain damage and mental illness,” attorney Joseph Perkovich of Phillips Black said in a statement to the Indiana Capital Chronicle on Friday. “In this extreme tragedy, killing Jeff will achieve nothing but the infliction of harm upon new victims who will lose their son, brother, or friend.”
Death row inmate Jeffrey Weisheit, currently housed at the Indiana State Prison in Michigan City. (Photo courtesy the Indiana Department of Correction)
The court’s decision came a little more than two months after Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita asked the justices to schedule Weisheit’s execution.
State attorneys argued Weisheit had exhausted his state and federal appeals, had no active stay of execution and could lawfully be put to death. The inmate’s attorneys opposed setting a date, saying they needed more time to pursue available legal proceedings and possible executive clemency.
The defense additionally pointed to public records that it said showed the Indiana Department of Correction lacked the drugs needed to conduct an execution and had no lawful source from which to obtain them.
But the justices said those issues were not properly before them as part of the state’s request to set an execution date.
“A petitioner can raise constitutional claims through a successive petition for post-conviction relief under Post-Conviction Rule 1(12), raise challenges to an execution protocol through a civil lawsuit, or petition the Governor for clemency,” the court said. “But we agree with the State that a ‘Motion to Set Execution Date’ does not implicate any of those proceedings, and the only thing properly before us is the State’s motion.”
The court said it was required to complete the “administrative task” of setting a date.
The order does not prevent Weisheit from pursuing additional legal challenges or seeking clemency from Gov. Mike Braun.
Weisheit’s attorneys said they plan to file a clemency petition and “intend to pursue (other) available legal challenges in the courts,” as well.
Braun denied clemency requests from Benjamin Ritchie and Roy Lee Ward before their executions in 2025.
More than a decade of appeals
Weisheit was caring for Alyssa and Caleb while their mother, Lisa Lynch, worked on the night of April 9, 2010, according to court records.
Firefighters arrived at the family’s Evansville home early the next morning and found it engulfed in flames. Alyssa was found in a closet. Caleb was found on a mattress, bound with duct tape and with a washcloth secured in his mouth. Investigators found one railroad flare in his underwear and another beneath his body.
Both children died from smoke and soot inhalation.
Weisheit fled Indiana and was apprehended in Kentucky after a high-speed chase. A jury convicted him in 2013 of two counts of murder and Class A felony arson resulting in serious bodily injury. Jurors found that the state had proven two death-penalty aggravators — multiple murders and the murders of two children younger than 12 — and recommended that Weisheit be put to death.
Story continues below.
JAW-2026.08.28-order.setting 2026.11.05 execution
 
The trial court imposed the death sentence, which the Indiana Supreme Court unanimously affirmed on direct appeal in 2015.
Weisheit later sought post-conviction relief, arguing in part that his trial and appellate attorneys had been ineffective. A trial court denied that request, and a majority of the Indiana Supreme Court affirmed the decision in 2018.
Chief Justice Loretta Rush dissented from the portion of that ruling upholding the death sentence. Rush concluded that Weisheit had been denied effective assistance during the penalty phase of his trial and would have ordered a new sentencing proceeding.
“An execution tainted by constitutional error corrodes the integrity of the justice system and of the state that imposed it,” Rush wrote.
Weisheit subsequently sought relief in federal court. The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Indiana denied his habeas corpus petition, and the 7th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals upheld that decision in August 2025.
The federal appeals court concluded that most of Weisheit’s claims were procedurally defaulted and that the remaining claims did not warrant relief. The U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear his case June 8.
Ongoing questions about execution drugs
Indiana law currently requires executions to be carried out by lethal injection.
DOC records obtained by the Capital Chronicle earlier this year showed the state had no pentobarbital or other execution drugs remaining in its inventory as of October 2025, after Ward’s execution.
Indiana has spent at least $1.275 million obtaining pentobarbital since 2024. State officials have repeatedly declined to identify the drug supplier, citing an Indiana law that makes the identities of execution-drug suppliers confidential.
Indiana’s new prison already equipped for firing squads as death penalty debate continues

Braun said in June that he was confident Indiana could obtain more pentobarbital once the Supreme Court set another execution date, although he acknowledged that acquiring the drug remained difficult and expensive.
Indiana resumed executions in December 2024, when it put Joseph Corcoran to death after a 15-year pause attributed largely to the state’s inability to obtain lethal-injection drugs. Ritchie was executed in May 2025, followed by Ward in October.
Lawmakers considered, but did not pass, legislation during the 2026 session that would have authorized firing squads as an alternative execution method. The DOC has since confirmed that its new prison in Westville was designed to accommodate both lethal injections and firing squads, although firing squads remain unauthorized under Indiana law.
Weisheit’s execution is scheduled to occur at Indiana State Prison in Michigan City, where the state carried out its three most recent executions.
News organizations, including States Newsroom, which operates the Capital Chronicle, are separately challenging Indiana’s prohibition on media witnesses inside the execution chamber. A divided federal appeals court in June upheld the denial of a preliminary injunction, but the underlying litigation is still ongoing in federal court.
