name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Proposed Lincoln city charter amendments too late for Nov. 3 ballot, city attorney decides
description: LINCOLN — Lincoln City Attorney Yohance Christie announced Thursday that the deadline has passed for any proposed Lincoln City Charter amendments to go to voters this November. The decision sets up an imminent court battle over the fate of three proposed city charter amendments from the petitioning group Good Government Lincoln. A spokesperson for the Nebras[...]
text:
Lincoln City Attorney Yohance Christie during a hearing where the Nebraska Attorney General's Office is challenging a Lincoln city ordinance enacted in response to a new state minimum wage law at the Lancaster County Courthouse on Thursday, July 2, 2026, in Lincoln. (Pool photo by Kenneth Ferriera/Lincoln Journal Star)LINCOLN — Lincoln City Attorney Yohance Christie announced Thursday that the deadline has passed for any proposed Lincoln City Charter amendments to go to voters this November.
The decision sets up an imminent court battle over the fate of three proposed city charter amendments from the petitioning group Good Government Lincoln. A spokesperson for the Nebraska Attorney General’s Office confirmed the office filed a lawsuit against city officials seeking to certify the measures for November. The office declined to comment further.
In a news release just after 6 p.m. Thursday, Christie said two of the three petitions from Good Government Lincoln have qualified for the ballot. However, because the Lincoln City Council must provide proper public notice, host a public hearing and then vote on including the measures on the ballot, Christie said, it’s too late for them to get on the Nov. 3 ballot.
The seven-member Lincoln City Council. Top row, from left, Sändra Washington, Justin P. Carlson, Tom Beckius and James Michael Bowers. Bottom row, from left, Tom Duden (vice chair), Brodey Weber (chair) and Bennie Shobe. (Photo courtesy of City of Lincoln)
State law requires Lincoln officials to place any measures on the November ballot by Tuesday.
“The City Council is under no obligation to bypass their processes for placing petitions on the ballot because of a missed deadline,” Christie wrote. “The City Council will place the Charter amendments on the next general election ballot (May 2027) pursuant to state law.”
The three petitions seek to limit Lincoln City Council members to two consecutive four-year terms, move the dates of city elections from odd to even years and let certain residents within a 3-mile buffer around Lincoln city limits vote in municipal elections, excluding bond votes.
The Lancaster County Election Commission is still verifying signatures for the petition to expand Lincoln municipal election boundaries, but the other two measures have enough valid signatures.
Christie said resolutions must be drafted and reviewed by the City Law Department. He said the Charter Review Commission is a bipartisan body that will independently review both the petition language and alternatives drafted by city law and make recommendations to the council.
The Good Government Lincoln campaign declined to comment Thursday.
Nebraska AG stepped up pressure
For three days, Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers had amped up pressure on city officials and threatened to sue if this very decision occurred.
Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers hosts a news conference in his office in the Nebraska State Capitol in Lincoln on Aug. 26, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
He released an opinion Monday saying the city had to place any qualifying charter amendments on the November ballot so long as county election officials found they had enough signatures. On Tuesday, Hilgers ordered the city to tell him whether they would comply, or risk legal action, by 5 p.m. Thursday. And at a news conference Wednesday, Hilgers accused city officials of plotting to violate the Nebraska Constitution.
“The city has a non-negotiable, non-discretionary requirement,” Hilgers said Wednesday.
The attorney general said he saw “no reason” why the Tuesday deadline could not be met. He cited the Nebraska Constitution that any city charter amendments could be certified as late as early October.
Christie, however, cited state and local laws giving Sept. 1 as the ultimate deadline for 2026.
‘Constitutional right to vote’
Hilgers is a former state senator for Legislative District 21 in northwest Lancaster County. He lives in the 3-mile “extraterritorial zoning jurisdiction” around Lincoln and confirmed Wednesday he is “absolutely” a supporter of the Good Government Lincoln campaign.
He said he had spread the word and encouraged voter support. Hilgers said if Lincoln officials try to block the measures from the ballot, he might become a financial contributor, too. 
‘Sad period in Nebraska history’: AG Hilgers speaks on ongoing petition fraud investigations

In a two-page letter Tuesday, Hilgers cited reporting from the Lincoln Journal Star that city officials had not yet decided what to do.
“If the City Council and City Clerk do not agree to obey their constitutional duty, we will be forced to consider immediate legal action to ensure that Nebraskans residing in Lincoln can exercise their constitutional right to vote on proposed amendments to the Lincoln City Charter this November,” Hilgers wrote.
The Good Government Lincoln campaign submitted signatures in mid-July to qualify its measures, but on Aug. 5, the Lancaster County Election Commission said no measure had enough valid signatures.
More than 65% of the group’s 30,000-plus signatures were rejected. A supermajority of those were flagged as possibly fraudulent.
The campaign regrouped and submitted a new set of signatures Aug. 17.
‘Worst kind of political theater’
Lincoln City Council Chair Brodey Weber, in a statement Thursday morning, said Hilgers was “inappropriately intervening” in the city charter amendment process.
Lincoln City Councilman Brodey Weber durring a press conference in Lincoln on Aug. 13, 2026 (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)
“The City of Lincoln was not responsible for Good Government Lincoln’s failure to appropriately ensure that the signatures being collected were legitimate,” Weber said. “As a result of those failures, we as a city now have an obligation to do our due diligence and ensure we are following the correct process to uphold the law.”
Hilgers gave over “operational control” of his office’s assistance in the Lancaster County-led investigation but said he does not see a conflict of interest in what he considers upholding the constitution.
Weber, a Democrat who unsuccessfully challenged Hilgers for the Legislature in 2020, said Hilgers is seeking to intimidate Lincoln officials and “engaging in the worst kind of political theater, potentially at the expense of the integrity of his office.”
The general election is Nov. 3.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Melissa Hoffer, nation’s first state-level climate chief, to step down
description: Hoffer was chosen for the new position after holding several high-powered roles in climate policy, serving under then-AG Healey before working at the Biden administration’s Environmental Protection Agency and then moving back to the Bay State to link up with Healey again under this newly crafted role.
text:
MELISSA HOFFER, who was tapped by Gov. Maura Healey as the nation’s first state-level climate chief, is leaving her role. 
Hoffer, whose cabinet-level position was announced by Healey on her first day as governor, is leaving to take over as president of Vermont Law and Graduate School effective December 1.  
“It has been the honor of a lifetime to serve as Massachusetts’s — and the nation’s — first cabinet-level climate chief, and to make our whole-of-government approach a successful model for other states and local governments,” she said in a statement. 
Hoffer’s climate chief role was created amid a wave of momentum toward fighting climate change and adapting to a warming world. The position touched on a dizzying array of issues on Beacon Hill, from state procurements to insurance costs to biodiversity goals, in order to infuse ambitious emissions reduction targets across state government. 
She’s credited, among other initiatives, with helping launch the state’s climate bank, establish a disaster response and resilience fund in the wake of devastating 2023 floods, and launched the state’s first youth climate council. 
The state is confronting rising power demand, soaring energy costs, and climate commitments that are teetering, a confluence that’s rattling state officials around the country. What’s more, President Trump has moved to stifle an offshore wind industry that Massachusetts officials had been bullish on. 
The contentious nature of the current energy affordability landscape in the Bay State has also collided with Healey’s bid for a second term as state residents rank energy costs as a top household concern. Massachusetts electricity prices are double the national average as the governor pursues an “all of the above” approach to energy, which underscores the importance of natural gas in the energy mix in addition to a push for clean power sources. 
Those dynamics – marked by the pivot away from a single-minded focus on clean energy — have further strained Hoffer’s job, and left some in state government, advocates, and energy insiders to wonder what exactly her role is in the administration and what kind of influence she holds on policy issues. 
In a wide-ranging interview with CommonWealth Beacon earlier this summer, Hoffer seemed to recognize the challenges in a job that’s basically something of an experiment. 
“We are asking people to do things differently, and that can be quite threatening sometimes,” she said of her role to push others in state government on climate issues. “You’re asking somebody who’s been quite successful at doing something one way for a long time to think about something else when they’re already very busy, they’ve got an overflowing plate. Because it’s state government, most of them could go out into the private sector and get paid three times what they’re getting paid here. And then here’s the climate chief knocking on your door and asking you to do something else.” 
Hoffer was chosen for the new position after holding several high-powered roles in climate policy, serving under then-AG Healey as head of the office’s energy and environment bureau before working at the Biden administration’s Environmental Protection Agency as principal deputy general counsel and then moving back to the Bay State to link up with Healey again under this newly crafted role.  
The relationship between Hoffer and Healey dates back to their time at law school together at Northeastern University in the 1990s. 
Hoffer’s departure comes at a natural pivot point toward the end of a governor’s four-year term. But it’s also another data point in the exodus from Healey’s Cabinet, which has seen more than half of her top lieutenants leave the administration in about a year.  
In this case, questions have swirled around Hoffer’s level of authority and place in the decision-making pecking order alongside a number of other top energy and environmental officials in the administration — and whether Healey feels as tied to the necessity of the climate chief role itself as the state’s climate commitments face attack both from the federal level and from within Beacon Hill’s Democratic supermajority.  
Healey previously told CommonWealth Beacon that Hoffer’s job is a “national model,” and her administration said on Thursday that it would name a successor to Hoffer prior to her departure.  
“Melissa Hoffer has been an extraordinary partner and climate leader for Massachusetts,” Healey said in a statement. “When I created the nation’s first cabinet-level climate chief position, I knew we needed someone with the expertise, determination and vision to make climate action a whole-of-government priority — and Melissa delivered on that mission.” 
Vermont Law and Graduate School is regarded as one of the leading schools in the country for environmental law. 
“I cannot wait to get to work with the VLGS community and help build on its remarkable legacy of educating leaders who are ready to make a difference,” Hoffer said.

title: Veterans incarcerated in Idaho support local food bank through new vegetable garden
description: A group of veterans who are incarcerated at the Idaho State Correctional Institution is providing fresh vegetables to local families from a new garden the inmates started this year.   The Idaho State Correctional Institution Veterans Group partnered with the Kuna Food Bank to distribute the food to families in the community, officials with the Idaho […]
text:
The Idaho State Correctional Institution Veterans Group started a new vegetable garden and partnered with Kuna Food Bank to provide fresh, healthy food for local families. (Photo courtesy of Idaho Department of Correction)A group of veterans who are incarcerated at the Idaho State Correctional Institution is providing fresh vegetables to local families from a new garden the inmates started this year.  
The Idaho State Correctional Institution Veterans Group started a new vegetable garden and partnered with Kuna Food Bank to provide fresh, healthy food for local families. (Photo courtesy of Idaho Department of Correction)
The Idaho State Correctional Institution Veterans Group partnered with the Kuna Food Bank to distribute the food to families in the community, officials with the Idaho Department of Correction announced Thursday.
Members of the veterans group spent the year learning about crops, planting vegetables and caring for the garden, Case Manager Steve Mitchley said. 
In the first year of the garden’s existence, the veterans group harvested potatoes, onions, bell peppers, squash and beets.
American Legion Post 113, A New Path Idaho and Lowe’s provided about $800 worth of donated materials to support the garden, officials said. 
Correction officials said that while the garden is small, it has grown into something much bigger  by providing a sense of community service and hope.
“This first season has been a valuable learning experience,” Mitchley said in a written statement. “The group hopes to expand the number of garden boxes next year.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Attorney argues to force government to release more surveillance records in ‘Minnesota 15’ case
description: A defense attorney in the conspiracy case against 15 Minnesotans asked a federal judge Thursday to order the government to release more documents related to the Department of Homeland Security’s wide-ranging surveillance campaign of anti-ICE activists, labor unions and nonprofits in Minnesota.  Attorney Kevin Riach, who represents defendant Isaac Sant, asked[...]
text:
Alec Stewart, one of the 15 people federally indicted for conspiracy to impede or injure federal officers, speaks during a press conference condemning federal surveillance Tuesday, Aug. 18, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)A defense attorney in the conspiracy case against 15 Minnesotans asked a federal judge Thursday to order the government to release more documents related to the Department of Homeland Security’s wide-ranging surveillance campaign of anti-ICE activists, labor unions and nonprofits in Minnesota. 
Attorney Kevin Riach, who represents defendant Isaac Sant, asked U.S. District Judge David Schultz to order the federal government to turn over information including downloads of undercover agents’ phones and laptops; all reports related to surveillance of Minnesota unions, non-profit organizations and activists; and communications between local prosecutors and their bosses in Washington D.C., among other records.
In the top floor of the federal courthouse in Minnesota — the largest courtroom in the state, according to Riach — nearly every member of the “Minnesota 15” and their attorneys crowded into the space behind the counsel tables, and supporters filled the courtroom. All 15 have pleaded not guilty to conspiracy to assault or impede federal agents.
Riach argued that the additional discovery is necessary in order to determine whether the federal government has selectively, or vindictively, prosecuted anti-ICE activists, and to craft defenses for his client and the other 14 defendants. 
If granted, the discovery would also make public additional details of the federal government’s surveillance campaigns — potentially on a national scale. 
“The purpose of this prosecution is to chill the conduct of the defendants and others and to squash dissent in this district,” Riach said. 
Assistant U.S. Attorney Sommer Lindsay Honeycutt argued that the government has already provided more than enough discovery materials, including terabytes of Signal chats and dozens of reports from undercover agents, and maintained that the prosecutions are based solely on criminal conduct by the defendants. 
Honeycutt said the defense hadn’t cleared the high threshold required to obtain additional discovery materials on suspicion of targeted prosecution by the government. 
That threshold, Riach argued, is based on the “presumption of regularity” — the assumption that agents of the government have acted in good faith.
Riach listed off a number of examples of U.S. attorneys voluntarily tossing out their own cases for lack of evidence; being called in front of the court for contempt hearings; and voluntarily dismissing cases after a judge ordered them to produce internal communications, Riach said, seemingly to avoid discovery — just in Minnesota.
“We are in times these days where that presumption — it’s evaporated,” Riach said.
Schultz said he would issue an order as soon as possible but did not provide a timeline. 
Outside the courthouse, supporters and family members of the Minnesota 15 chanted “f*ck ICE.”
The 15 charged in this case were among tens of thousands of people who vehemently pushed back against President Donald Trump’s winter immigration crackdown, Operation Metro Surge. Two Americans were killed during the operation, and citizens and legal residents were arrested or injured. 
Previously released DHS documents in the case describe undercover agents noting license plate numbers of cars in the parking lots of meetings of anti-ICE groups, including at churches.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT sues Kalshi over unlicensed sports betting
description: State Attorney General William Tong said what the app does constitutes gambling — making it subject to Connecticut consumer protection laws.
text:
Connecticut is suing the online prediction market Kalshi.
Kalshi allows users to trade on the outcome of nearly anything: typical events, like the Super Bowl, and niche things, like the Connecticut governor’s race. Users buy contracts priced between one cent and 99 cents, with the price being higher if the event is more likely to occur.
If a user buys a contract and it becomes true, the payout is $1.
State Attorney General William Tong said that’s gambling — making it subject to Connecticut consumer protection laws.
Only three entities are licensed to operate sports betting in the state: the Mashantucket Pequot Tribal Nation, the Mohegan Tribe, and the Connecticut Lottery Corporation. They partner with sites like FanDuel and DraftKings, which is why those sites are allowed in Connecticut.
Tong accused Kalshi of operating an unlicensed sports betting operation in Connecticut, and is seeking a court injunction to force them to stop.
“Sports event contracts are no different than sports betting and are not magically shielded by federal law from Connecticut’s commonsense consumer protection laws,” Tong said. “These laws exist for a reason — to protect minors, to prevent problem gambling, to ensure your money is safe and your personal information is protected. None of that is happening now on Kalshi, and we’re suing to put a stop to it.”
Kalshi is currently regulated by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. Connecticut sent the company a cease-and-desist in December of 2025. In response, Kalshi sued; it was denied, and they have since appealed.
“These markets have been waging a coordinated campaign to convince people they are offering investments that are somehow safe when the reality is they are indistinguishable from sports wagering,” Connecticut Department of Consumer Protection Commissioner Bryan T. Cafferelli said. “They target minors and individuals who have purposefully opted out, don’t adhere to any of our technical standards designed to protect consumers’ money and personal information, and violate all of Connecticut’s gaming laws.”
The company’s head of litigation, Jovy Dedaj, called Wednesday’s lawsuit arbitrary and accused the state of being inconsistent in how they enforce consumer protection laws.
“Connecticut just filed this lawsuit to shut down Kalshi immediately, but they’re okay with other prediction markets operating there in the meantime,” Dedaj said on X. “This is the latest in a line of arbitrary and inconsistent enforcement by the states, which shows this has nothing to do with consumer protection.”
This story was first published Aug. 27, 2026 by WSHU.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Maryland, 22 other states sue Trump administration over family planning restrictions
description: Maryland is co-leading a lawsuit with 22 other states against new Trump administration funding requirements that threaten family planning grants unless states comply with what Attorney General Anthony Brown calls “unlawful and discriminatory conditions.”
text:
Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown (D) at a 2024 news conference. Brown lead a coalition of 23 states that sued the Trump administration over new restrictions on funding for family planning programs. (Photo by Elijah Pittman/Maryland Matters)Maryland is co-leading a lawsuit with 22 other states challenging new Trump administration funding requirements that threaten family planning grants unless states comply with what Attorney General Anthony Brown calls “unlawful and discriminatory conditions.”
In the suit filed Thursday in U.S. District Court for Maryland, Brown, along with New York Attorney General Letitia James and officials from 21 other states, says the new conditions on the Title X program in the upcoming fiscal 2027 funding period will penalize states that “refuse to abandon nondiscrimination protections.”
Those new conditions require states to demonstrate that their programs align with federal priorities that Brown said would discourage the use of contraception, exclude transgender people from healthcare and eliminate diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives, among other changes.
“For decades, federal family planning funding has enabled Maryland to provide tens of thousands of families with care they could not otherwise afford,” Brown said in a written statement. “Cutting off that funding does not merely eliminate a budget line. It means fewer cancer screenings and more preventable diseases going undetected. My office will not stand by while the federal government puts politics ahead of patients’ health.”
Officials with the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, the target of the lawsuit, did not immediately respond to request for comment on the legal challenge.
The Title X program was created by Congress over 50 years ago to promote comprehensive family planning programs and related reproductive health services, particularly for low-income communities.
Maryland, nine other states sue White House to protect interest payments to homeowners

Through Title X, the Health and Human Services provides grant funding for states to establish family planning programs covering a wide range of services, such as preventing unintended pregnancies, detecting cervical and breast cancer and treating sexually transmitted infections, among other services.
In 2026, Congress earmarked $286 million for Title X, according to the court filing.
But a notice of funding opportunity, or NOFO, issued in July for the next five-year funding cycle tacked on new conditions for states to receive those funds. The lawsuit claims the new terms are unlawful, and the states are asking the federal court to vacate the new requirements and prohibit federal officials from imposing those restrictions.
Brown and the other states’ officials allege that the Trump administration overstepped its own authority to cram in “agency priorities” that force states to demonstrate “alignment” with certain political goals or risk losing that funding.
Those goals include ending “support for gender ideology,” likely referring to policies that support transgender individuals, though one of the complaints in the lawsuit is that the terms are vague and will be challenging to adhere to.
The lawsuit notes that the state of Maryland has “never been denied a Title X grant.” For fiscal 2026, Maryland received $3.7 million in federal dollars and added $6.3 million in state funding to support the program.
In fiscal 2025, there were 31,657 individuals who “received services at no cost” under Maryland’s Title X program, called the Maryland Family Planning Program. About 27% of those individuals lived in rural counties.
“A reduction in family planning funds would disproportionately limit access to essential screenings and care for rural Marylanders,” the lawsuit said. It adds that without the federal funding, “MFPP expects to provide 1,447 fewer Pap smears each year, resulting in an anticipated 25 high-grade cervical pre-cancers going undetected annually.”
Another challenge raised in the lawsuit are conditions that have states demonstrate that their programs “end ‘overmedicalization,’ a category that the NOFO indicates includes hormonal contraception;” along with safeguarding “‘life-affirming’ program delivery” and adopting “directive counseling that pushes patients towards parenthood and marriage.”
Maryland law prohibits state health officials from accepting federal funds that “exclude comprehensive family planning providers or mandate abortion-related censorship,” the lawsuit says.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE“To apply under the 2027 NOFO, MDH [the Maryland Department of Health] must choose between substantially restructuring its existing application and usual programming to conform to the NOFO’s new priorities — which appear to be inconsistent with the existing Title X statute and regulations — or risk being denied federal funding for MDH’s longstanding approach and programming,” the lawsuit says.
“If … MDH cannot pursue or does not receive Title X funding, the loss of funding would represent a 38.5 percent reduction in MFPP’s total operating revenue,” according to the lawsuit. “MDH’s standard allocation of State-only family planning funding could sustain only a limited portion of the program’s existing activities.”
Attorneys general from the other states raise similar concerns. New York says that its version of the family planning program helped almost 254,000 clients in 2025, with 70% of them coming from households below the federal poverty level.
Massachusetts argues that the funding helps support screening and early-stage medical interventions.
“Absent those critical screening, contraceptive, and early-stage interventions,” the lawsuit said of Massachusetts, “public sector healthcare costs for necessary downstream procedures such as maternity and birth related services to 60 months, miscarriage and ectopic pregnancy management, and downstream STI [sexually transmitted infection] testing would have totaled $155,220,000.”
California officials question how states can comply with the new conditions while upholding intended goals of the program, including requirements that have little to do with family planning.
“For example, it is unclear how to appropriately deemphasize hormonal birth control while continuing to ensure access to hormonal contraception consistent with Title X program requirements, or how the priority of reducing crime should be operationalized within a family planning program,” the lawsuit says of the impact the federal policy will have on California programs.
Other states joining Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Kentucky, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Washington and Wisconsin.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Regulators investigate Black Hills Energy’s high number of pipeline safety violations
description: The Iowa Utilities Commission is evaluating potential penalties and corrective action for Black Hills Energy following a hearing Thursday on an investigation into the gas company’s safety and management practices in Iowa. Routine inspections from IUC revealed Black Hills Energy had disproportionally more instances of probable violations than the other top ga[...]
text:
The Iowa Utilities Commission is investigating a high volume of safety violations from Black Hills Energy. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) The Iowa Utilities Commission is evaluating potential penalties and corrective action for Black Hills Energy following a hearing Thursday on an investigation into the gas company’s safety and management practices in Iowa.
Routine inspections from IUC revealed Black Hills Energy had disproportionally more instances of probable violations than the other top gas providers in Iowa over the past several years. The IUC also flagged that Black Hills has significantly longer correction times for probable violations than the other major gas providers. 
Black Hills representatives acknowledged that the number of probable violation instances was high in a recent audit and said the company has a “structured continuous improvement approach” to address the commission’s concerns and improve compliance.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Pete Hamell, the general manager for Black Hills Energy Iowa Gas, said that while the number of probable violations is notable, the “nature of the observations really isn’t alarming.”
Hamell said many of the probable violations observed by IUC were related to environmental, homeowner or business factors. That means things like oxidation of pipes over time, damage from homeowners doing landscaping projects or regulatory changes. 
“We have alignment with the commission that the safe, reliable, and affordable delivery of gas service to our customers in all of our communities is a shared responsibility and priority for us,” Hamell said, speaking as a witness during the hearing. “We take the commission’s, not only their observations, but the commission’s partnership to heart.”
Volume of violations 
In June 2025, IUC submitted a routine inspection report on Black Hills’ Spencer Unit in northwest Iowa that had more than 100 safety issues in 16 violation categories. IUC said that while the violations didn’t pose and immediate threat to the public, the high volume was cause for an investigation.
As IUC reviewed additional data with other Black Hills operations in the state, it “became increasingly concerned” about potential “company-wide safety issues” across Black Hills’ operations in the state, according to a news release from IUC. 
While IUC can levy civil penalties to utilities that commit violations, the commission decided to defer its final decision on civil penalties for Black Hills until it could evaluate compliance standards through the rest of the utility’s systems in Iowa. 
According to IUC, Black Hills is the smallest of the three major natural gas utilities in Iowa, behind Interstate Power and Light Company and MidAmerican Energy Company. According to data presented by IUC Thursday, Black Hills has just under 3,000 miles of main pipe in Iowa, compared to more than 4,500 miles operated by IPL and more than 11,000 miles operated by MidAmerican. 
While smaller than the two other major operators, an IUC chart showed Black Hills’ instances of probable violations between 2023 and 2025 were nearly the same as MidAmerican’s. When scaled to the number of violations in the time frame per 1,000 service lines, Black Hills’ violations were nearly three times that of MidAmerican or IPL. 
Adam Buhrman, corporate counsel for Black Hills Energy, said the utility was not given this data prior to the hearing to verify its accuracy. 
In Black Hills’ July 29 filed response, it said certain inspection reports contained “a significant number of findings” but that “none of those findings involved active leaks or other immediate threats to public safety.” 
The findings from the recent reports pertained to issues like compliance, documentation, maintenance, corrosion prevention or facility maintenance, according to Black Hills’ filing. In its response to IUC’s notice, Black Hills contended that civil penalties were “not warranted” as part of the commission’s review.
The Iowa Utilities Commission held a hearing Aug. 27, 2026 as part of its investigation into a high volume of safety violations from Black Hills Energy. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
“The Company believes that continued implementation of its corrective action plan, together with ongoing reporting, collaboration, and evaluation of compliance performance, will provide a more effective means of addressing the Commission’s concerns and promoting continued improvement than the assessment of civil penalties,” Black Hills’ filing said.
Hamell said many of the instances flagged in the Spencer report that initiated the IUC’s investigation were related to what Black Hills would call “oxidation” which he said “is not necessarily bad for pipelines.” 
Further discussion around oxidation and corrosion in the hearing led commissioner Joshua Byrnes to say that it seems IUC inspectors are seeing instances of corrosion while Black Hills technicians see oxidation. 
“How do we get to a point where we’re all seeing the same thing?” Byrnes asked. 
Matt Mangin, a senior specialist with Black Hills overseeing corrosion control, among other things, said the training would need to be equal between the agencies to properly identify the difference between oxidation and corrosion. Corrosion, he said, is an electrochemical reaction and has to present all four elements of corrosion. 
Speediness
IUC also presented information comparing Black Hills’ correction times compared to other utilities from 2023 through 2025. While MidAmerican and IPL had an average time to correct issues of about 30 days, Black Hills’ average was 132 days. 
Hamell said certain projects take longer to complete than others, due to things like engineering and permitting. But generally, Hamell said to his knowledge, Black Hills’ response times have not “exceeded” the standards set by the U.S. Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration, or PHMSA. 
Many of the questions from commissioners centered on staffing concerns at Black Hills, but Hamell assured commissioners that staffing was not currently a concern for the company. 
In its June 29 order giving notice of possible civil penalties, IUC noted that Black Hills closed violations from the 2025 Spencer audit “faster than those found throughout the remainder of Black Hills’ gas system.” IUC said faster response time must be examined to understand why it has not been replicated in the utility’s other Iowa systems.  
Black Hills, in its filed response, said past closure times “needed improvement” and that its “current trend demonstrates meaningful progress in that regard.” 
Kevin Jarosz, the vice president of Black Hills’ Iowa & Nebraska gas operations, said safety is the “highest priority” at the company. 
“We firmly commit safety to our employees, our customers, and communities that we serve, and we also commit to a strong compliance program, investment in our infrastructure, and continuously improving where we need to,” Jarosz said during the hearing. “We also commit to continue to work collaboratively with the commission to ensure that safe operations continue, and we will continue to provide safe, reliable service to our customers, like we have for decades and into the future.”
The Iowa Utilities Commission will review the testimony and the written responses to determine applicable civil penalties and corrective actions in the matter.

title: Cook Political Report shifts FL gubernatorial race from ‘solid’ to ‘likely’ Republican
description: One of the top political prediction websites in the country says Byron Donalds remains the favorite for Florida governor but sees some shift toward Democrat David Jolly. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report on Thursday moved the race from “Solid Republican” to “Likely Republican.” “While Jolly trails Trump-backed Rep. Byron Donalds by more than a 10:1 […]
text:
Florida Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly speaking in Ybor City in Tampa on Aug. 17, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)One of the top political prediction websites in the country says Byron Donalds remains the favorite for Florida governor but sees some shift toward Democrat David Jolly.
The nonpartisan Cook Political Report on Thursday moved the race from “Solid Republican” to “Likely Republican.”
“While Jolly trails Trump-backed Rep. Byron Donalds by more than a 10:1 margin in fundraising, his ability to potentially reach out to independents and disaffected Republicans makes this a unique contest that could possibly become competitive,” writes Jessica Taylor with the Cook Report.
“Jolly would still need a significant financial boost to mount a statewide television campaign and have a real shot,” she adds.
Jolly acknowledged to reporters last week on the eve of the primary that he does need “resources to reach the mark.”
“But this is a cycle where you can get outspent 10:1 and still win,” he said. “Now, I will tell you I think that you’re going to see money come in.”
That remains to be seen.
Last Tuesday, the Jolly campaign released a survey from the Democratic Governors Association conducted by Hart Research showing a statistical tie in the race, with Jolly at 46% and Donalds at 45%. Other polls have shown Donalds up by at least five percentage points.
“David and Gwen [Graham] have the momentum in this race, attracting independents and Republicans in profound numbers. National observers are seeing that shift and understanding that — in this change election — Florida is ready to elect a Democrat,” said Jolly senior adviser Mark Riddle in a written statement.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Data centers must report water, energy use under new law signed by Gov. Sherrill
description: Gov. Mikie Sherrill said the law she signed Thursday would prevent data center developers from operating “in the shadows.”
text:
Gov. Mikie Sherrill said the law she signed Thursday would prevent data center developers from operating “in the shadows.” (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Gov. Mikie Sherrill signed legislation Thursday requiring data centers to report their water and energy use to state energy regulators every six months, touting it as a highlight of her plan to “hold data centers accountable.”
Sherrill, a Democrat who pledged months ago to seek limits on data center construction, said during a bill signing ceremony in South Brunswick that she will not “let these developers operate in the shadows.”
“New Jerseyans deserve to know how much water and electricity the data centers coming into their community will use. Data center companies often treat their usage statistics like a trade secret,” she said.
Data center fight moves to NJ courts, with developers blaming local bans on ‘public hysteria’

Data center critics have said their mammoth power needs are behind rising electric rates. Sherrill pledged during her campaign for governor last year to freeze those rates for New Jerseyans.
The law requires operators to disclose total energy consumption, energy used for cooling and IT equipment, peak daily water use, water sources, and backup power supplies to the state Board of Public Utilities twice a year. Bill sponsor Sen. Teresa Ruiz said the reporting requirement should be “the start of an ongoing public record” rather than a one-time disclosure.
That data would be summarized for public release, but a provision of the law limits how much of that information could be released to the public under the state Open Public Records Act.
Advocates say that carve-out undercuts the law’s transparency goal. Ben Dziobek, executive director of Climate Revolution Action Network, griped that state officials are claiming to offer “guardrails” for data center construction while declining to actually cap what data centers can build or consume. Companies will be able to report without any independent verification or audit, he noted.
He and other environmental activists said the legislation Sherrill signed does not go far enough. They have called for Sherrill to issue a statewide moratorium on all data center construction.
“Data center reporting for energy and water use after the damage is done is the antithesis of guardrails,” said Jaclyn Rhoads, executive director of the Pinelands Alliance. “New Jersey is paving the way for data centers to contaminate our air and waterways while leaving the public to suffer. We demand more of our government officials. Pass a moratorium now.”
Sherrill pushed back on the idea that a statewide moratorium would be the right approach, saying that data centers who want to build in New Jersey will “play by our rules.”
“We don’t have to choose between innovation and accountability, and we won’t,” she said.
More than three dozen New Jersey towns have voted to block new data centers, largely after public pressure from residents.
Sherrill also announced new state guidance aimed at helping municipalities negotiate community benefits agreements with data center developers. She said the agreements are meant to get towns and developers “on the same page” on issues like noise and lighting before construction starts, secure local infrastructure investments, and lock in prevailing wage and project labor agreement standards on the biggest projects.
“We know these companies drive a hard bargain, so I’m not going to leave communities on their own to negotiate,” she said.
She also signed legislation Thursday that would end a $500 million tax credit program that encouraged the development of new data centers, a program created under Sherrill’s predecessor in an attempt to lure AI companies to the Garden State.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota postpones ban on using food assistance for soda, candy
description: A ban on purchasing candy, soda and other sweetened drinks with federal food assistance was postponed for North Dakotans days before it was set to take effect. The restrictions on the Supplemental Nutritional Assistance Program were expected to take effect Sept. 1, followed by a three-month grace period to give retailers more time to update […]
text:
Candy sits on the shelves at a retail store in Bismarck on Aug. 27, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)A ban on purchasing candy, soda and other sweetened drinks with federal food assistance was postponed for North Dakotans days before it was set to take effect.
The restrictions on the Supplemental Nutritional Assistance Program were expected to take effect Sept. 1, followed by a three-month grace period to give retailers more time to update their systems. 
But the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services announced Thursday morning that the start date for the waiver is postponed to Nov. 1.
That decision followed an Aug. 25 letter from the U.S. Department of Agriculture to North Dakota officials, which referenced a recent federal court case that struck down similar SNAP restrictions in five states. A court opinion criticized the USDA for not following requirements to publish notice of the SNAP restrictions and accept public comment.
North Dakota grocers prepare for new SNAP restrictions amid uncertainty

Shiela Corley, acting administrator of the federal Food and Nutrition Administration, asked North Dakota officials to postpone the SNAP restrictions to Nov. 1. Corley wrote that the agency planned to publish a public notice in the Federal Register related to North Dakota’s SNAP changes and assess public comment before it goes into effect. 
The USDA approved North Dakota’s request to ban candy and soda from SNAP purchases in December 2025. The state pursued the change in part to secure more federal money from the Rural Health Transformation Program.
The Department of Health and Human Services has said it plans to spend $3.5 million to $4 million on implementation and enforcement of the changes. It is unclear if the delay will impact that estimate. 
In a news release Thursday, Rebecca Askins, economic assistance director for the department, highlighted the benefits of delaying the start date. 
“This pause provides an opportunity for our federal partners and retailers to continue to prepare and for SNAP households to become more familiar with the changes to items that can be purchased with an EBT card,” Askins said in the statement. “The new timeframe also allows HHS to expand support for this initiative.”
Just under 54,400 North Dakotans were enrolled in SNAP in April, and around 600 stores statewide are able to accept their benefits as payment. 
John Dyste, president of the North Dakota Grocers Association, has been working as a liaison between the department and grocers across the state. He said he wasn’t notified about the postponement and learned about it through the department’s public announcement. 
Dyste said the delay will relieve some pressure for retailers, particularly small, independent grocers, who he said are struggling to get their systems updated. 
“Whoever thought this was going to be a fairly simple process didn’t have a clue,” he said.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Neronha urges state regulators to reject proposed health insurance premium hikes
description: Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha is urging state regulators to reject two insurers’ proposed increases to premiums for individual health plans in 2027. After a July administrative hearing by the state’s Office of the Health Insurance Commissioner (OHIC), Neronha’s office formally submitted a brief objecting to Neighborhood Health Plan of Rhode Isl[...]
text:
The Blue Cross & Blue Shield of Rhode Island headquarters in Providence. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha is urging state regulators to reject two insurers’ proposed increases to premiums for individual health plans in 2027.
After a July administrative hearing by the state’s Office of the Health Insurance Commissioner (OHIC), Neronha’s office formally submitted a brief objecting to Neighborhood Health Plan of Rhode Island’s (NHP) request for a rate increase of 22.4%.
Premium increase requests are submitted annually by insurers, and this year they were submitted to the commissioner’s office on May 18. The agency then reviews the submissions and can accept, modify or reject them, with the final approved rates expected to arrive in September. Rate hike requests trigger a formal, public, administrative hearing if they exceed 10%.
So the health insurance commissioner’s office held a hearing for Neighborhood Health Plan but not for Blue Cross Blue Shield of Rhode Island, which requested a 9.8% increase. The AG instead submitted public comments encouraging the office to reject Blue Cross Blue Shield’s proposed rates.
Collectively, the two insurers cover more than 50,000 Rhode Islanders who purchase their individual plans through the state’s health insurance marketplace.
Health Insurance Commissioner Cory King heard two days of testimony on Neighborhood’s rate hike request in July. Comments came from Neighborhood, witnesses for the commissioner’s office, and an expert retained by Neronha’s office. 
The proposed increases are not final and need approval from King’s office, which will review insurers’ submissions along with pricing assumptions, administrative charges and other information before taking action on the rates. Final numbers are expected sometime next month.
“The rate review process does not occur in a vacuum; health insurance rates are a major factor contributing to Rhode Islanders’ struggles to stay afloat financially,” Neronha said in a news release Tuesday. “While insurers continue to report multimillion dollar financial surpluses, residents of our state have not been so lucky.” 
All good in the neighborhood?
Neighborhood initially sought a higher increase of 24.9% for its 34,555 individual market planholders. The insurer revised that request to 22.4% after state lawmakers created the Rhode Island Marketplace Affordability Program (RIMAP), which will take effect in 2027. 
The program’s approximately $22 million in enhanced insurance subsidies is meant to partially replace enhanced federal premium subsidies that expired at the end of 2025. About $19 million of the Marketplace Affordability Program funding can be applied as direct subsidies for customers who purchase insurance on the state marketplace and earn less than 200% of the federal poverty level. 
An analysis conducted by Brown University health economist Christopher Whaley, whom Neronha retained to scrutinize the rate filings and testify before the health insurance commissioner’s office showed that more than 90% of Rhode Islanders eligible for these subsidies would likely be within Neighborhood’s customer population, which he noted has “disproportionately lower-income enrollment…among the Rhode Island insurance market.”
One year after steepest premium increase in a decade, RI health insurers seek double-digit hikes

So Neighborhood subsequently tweaked its request to accommodate the anticipated uptick in enrollment — about 3,825 people, in Whaley’s estimate — and roughly $17.1 million in Marketplace Affordability Program subsidies expected to flow to its customers. 
But Whaley’s analysis argued that Neighborhood’s new influx of subsidies could possibly support a premium increase of about 19%. 
“In my opinion, these increases are harmful to Rhode Island consumers and threatens the stability of the Rhode Island insurance market, and NHPRI’s future viability,” Whaley wrote in an addendum to his analysis. “Consistent with my initial report, this increase far exceeds medical inflation and places many Rhode Island consumers in financial harm.”
Whaley suggested in his analysis that “Neighborhood’s recent premium increases are increasingly disconnected from the underlying costs of medical care.” 
Neronha also argued that the insurer could do more. His written arguments sent to the health commissioner contend that Neighborhood has failed to fund primary care spending as outlined by the office’s affordability standards — a case of déjà vu for Neronha, who claimed the shortfall is then passed onto consumers via premium increases. 
“NHPRI’s submission provides no credible plan to limit consumer cost growth,” Neronha wrote. “This deficit is glaring given this is the second year NHPRI has requested to increase rates over 20%.” 
If approved, the rate would push the annual cost of a benchmark Neighborhood plan above $7,000, according to Whaley’s analysis — a cost Neronha thought untenable.
“It is hard to imagine how low- or even middle-income Rhode Islanders will be able to bear that increase,” the AG wrote. “Rather than shoulder the burden of another year of seeing their premium skyrocket another 20%, consumers will likely choose to forego coverage.”
Gail Leach Carvelli, a spokesperson for Neighborhood, wrote in an email Thursday that the rates “reflect a number of trends such as rising medical and pharmacy costs, including required hospital rate increases tied to inflation, and the growing cost of prescription drugs — particularly high-cost specialty medications entering the market.” 
“Even with the requested 2027 rates, Neighborhood continues to offer the lowest-cost plans on HealthSource RI and is focused on delivering value to its members,” she wrote.
A smaller increase for Blue Cross amid larger costs
Blue Cross, meanwhile, wants a 9.8% increase for 2027, which would apply to its 16,138 individual-market customers. It’s a much smaller ask than last year, when the commissioner’s office approved a 22% increase for the insurer.
Still, Neronha objected to the payor’s request partly because of Blue Cross’ recent financial performance. Whaley’s analysis cited an increase of about $54 million in the company’s individual market premium revenue when compared to the same period last year, even with an enrollment drop of roughly 2,000 people.
Blue Cross’ first-quarter results, Whaley projected, could generate a more than $50 million positive difference between premium revenue and claims expenses in the individual market for 2026. 
“Where BCBSRI has ample reserves to protect itself prudentially, asking consumers to pay up further is antithetical to the public interest,” Neronha wrote in his comments. 
He argued that the company has not demonstrated any consideration of alternative pricing that might make its pricing more affordable for consumers.
Still, the payor’s request is much slimmer than last year’s initial request of 28.9% for individual plans, and its 9.8% request for 2027 was also the lowest among Rhode Island insurers offering individual plans. Blue Cross’ proposed increases for small- and large-group plans were likewise smaller than their competitors this year. 
When asked for a response to Neronha’s objections on Thursday, Blue Cross spokesperson Rich Salit described via email the “affordability crisis” Rhode Islanders face, “with the cost of food, housing, energy, and healthcare all extremely high, with little relief on the horizon.”
“While our requested 2027 rate increases are substantially lower compared to last year, we understand the cost of coverage is still difficult for many individuals, families, and employers to absorb,” Salit wrote. “Unfortunately, even as we work to better manage medical and prescription drug costs and reduce our operating expenses, overall healthcare costs continue at unprecedented levels.”
Salit added that Blue Cross is working to reduce its operating expenses and more deftly manage its expenses amidst higher medical and prescription drug costs, but maintained that premiums still need to adequately cover the underlying costs of care.
“Adequate rates to cover the cost of care are critical to protecting coverage for all our members,” Salit wrote, adding that the payor is also seeking to “better support complex members [and deliver] more proactive care in Rhode Island, which improves their experience and reduces their total cost of care.”
In March, the insurer reported a $78 million normalized operating loss for 2025 — better than the $115 million loss the year before — with the vast majority of its premium revenue, 90.4%, going toward medical, prescription drug and dental claims.

name: VTDigger
title: Class action lawsuit filed in federal court over local PFOA contamination
description:
The suit was filed Thursday against 3M, Dupont and others.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Class action lawsuit filed in federal court over local PFOA contamination.
text:
The former ChemFab plant in Bennington seen in Feb. 2022. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

This story by Mark Rondeau was first published in the Valley News on Aug. 26, 2026.
A team of attorneys has filed a class-action suit in federal court on behalf of Shaftsbury and Bennington residents suffering from well contamination from PFOA.
The suit was filed Tuesday in U.S. District Court, District of Vermont, against Saint-Gobain Performance Plastics Corporation, 3M Company, E.I. Dupont De Nemours Company and others.
It lists eight local individuals as class representatives, who live in either Bennington or Shaftsbury. The suit, just under 70 pages long, includes a demand for a jury trial.
The suit says the plaintiffs and the class they represent have suffered, and are suffering, damages “arising out of Defendants’ manufacture, distribution, sale, use, handling, release, discharge and disposal of perfluorooctanoic acid (‘PFOA’) and products releasing PFOA, a known toxic, perfluorinated chemical,” at two local manufacturing plants.
PFAS, of which PFOA is part, are man-made compounds that have been used in a wide range of industries since the 1950s, are persistent in the environment, and are harmful to human health. Two former ChemFab facilities, owned by Saint-Gobain Performance Plastics, were located on Northside Drive and Water Street and operated in Bennington from 1969 to 2002.
Their operations resulted in “the severe contamination of the local groundwater aquifer, soils, and private drinking water supply wells with PFOA in and around Shaftsbury and Bennington,” according to the suit.
Bringing the suit are David F. Silver and Alexander M. Dean, of Barr, Sternberg, Moss, Silver & Munson, P.C., of Bennington, along with attorneys from two firms which specialize in such cases, Faraci Lange, LLP, Rochester, New York and Davis, Johnston & Ringger, PC, Asheville, North Carolina.
In April, representatives of the three firms spoke with local residents with contaminated wells at a meeting at Bennington College.
‘The science is very clear’
This is the second class-action suit filed due to contamination alleged to come from these plants. Sullivan v. Saint-Gobain Performance Plastics, brought in 2016 and settled in 2022, was a successful federal class action on behalf of Bennington residents.
“The reason we’re doing a second suit is because over time it’s become clear that outside the original area of contamination that was the subject of the 2016 lawsuit, there was further contamination that increased over time,” Silver said in an interview on Wednesday. “And the science is very clear that Saint-Gobain’s use of the PFOA in their process, and then burning it off in their smokestacks, and then letting that out into the atmosphere is what caused the PFOA to settle into the ground and eventually get its way into the groundwater and the soil.”
Testing of wells in the last few years has discovered more well contamination. This includes in southeastern Shaftsbury in the East Road area near the border with Bennington. In Bennington, more contamination has been found on Rocky Lane, Middle Pownal Road, South Stream Road, Coleville Road, Niles Road, and Fuller Road.
“Since 2023, approximately 25 wells in Shaftsbury and 100 wells in southern Bennington have tested positive for PFOA. Testing coordinated by the State of Vermont remains ongoing,” according to the suit.
The class action is brought on behalf of the following classes: Those suffering from property devaluation due to groundwater contamination, those suffering from property devaluation due to soil contamination, those suffering from nuisance due to having a contaminated well, and a medical monitoring class.
As detailed in the suit, the medical monitoring class includes, in part, individuals “who resided and ingested tap water for at least six months at a property located in the Town of Shaftsbury and/or Town of Bennington that was supplied with drinking water from a private well contaminated with PFOA, and who have suffered an accumulation of PFOA in their bodies as demonstrated by blood serum tests disclosing a PFOA level in their blood at or above 2.00 ug/L.” (micrograms per liter)
Under relief, the suit seeks a declaration that the defendants “acted with negligence, gross negligence, and/or willful, wanton, and careless disregard for the health, safety, and property” of the member classes and an award of an amount more than $5 million to compensate the injured parties.
In addition, relief sought in the suit includes an injunction requiring the defendant to connect each impacted water supply within the zone of contamination onto municipal water; establishment and implementation of remedial measures sufficient to prevent further PFOA contamination; establishing a long-term medical testing protocol for plaintiffs and class members “to monitor their health and diagnose at an early stage any ailments associated with exposure, inhalation or ingestion of PFOA.”
The suit also seeks an award of the cost to fund a court-supervised, long-term medical monitoring program and the awarding of punitive damages and attorney fees.
‘Get things rolling’
“We brought this suit now because we want to get things rolling for the people that are dealing with the contamination,” Silver said.
Some of the affected residents have point-of-entry water treatments systems (POETS) and others are drinking bottled water.
“And not only that, them and their families have been drinking this contaminated water for years, and it’s a known carcinogen as well as associated with other diseases,” he said.
“I’m a member of this community, and I know many people who are affected, and they’ve actually contacted me over the last few years,” Silver said. “Large groups of people in Shaftsbury and in parts of Bennington, and they’re worried not only about their health, but about how this contamination is affecting their property values, which of course it will.”
The suit also includes the manufacturers of the chemicals, 3M and Dupont.
“It’s quite clear when you read the complaint, which sets it out pretty clearly, that for decades and decades these corporations knew that PFOA was a toxic chemical that would be harmful to humans, and that they did not take the precautions, or that they didn’t tell anybody about it, and they just made billions and billions of dollars selling a product that they knew was going to hurt people and hurt  the environment,” Silver said. “And we believe that Saint-Gobain knew as well. So, we think the science is really clear. The evidence is really strong.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah clerks don’t expect lawsuits over Trump’s mail-in voting rule to impact elections this year
description: Though recent federal rulings have cast uncertainty over voting by mail with Utah’s November general elections around the corner, clerks — at least for now — are preparing for business as usual.  “Any dramatic change at this point really is extremely impractical,  and it’s very risky to introduce any changes this late into the election […]
text:
Ballots await processing at the Salt Lake County Government Center in Salt Lake City on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 5, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Though recent federal rulings have cast uncertainty over voting by mail with Utah’s November general elections around the corner, clerks — at least for now — are preparing for business as usual. 
“Any dramatic change at this point really is extremely impractical,  and it’s very risky to introduce any changes this late into the election (season),” Weber County Clerk/Auditor Ricky Hatch told Utah News Dispatch on Thursday. 
A national legal fight continues over President Donald Trump’s moves to create new regulations to restrict voting by mail, though a couple of rulings this week handed procedural wins to the Trump administration. 
New challenges to Trump mail-in voting order arrive after US Supreme Court ruling

A U.S. Supreme Court opinion issued Monday said that the Trump administration is likely to prevail on its argument that 23 Democratic-led states do not have standing to stop his executive order to change how the U.S. Postal Service processes mail-in ballots.Then on Wednesday, U.S. District Judge Indiria Talwani removed her nationwide preliminary injunction blocking the administration from implementing the executive order that directed the USPS to create new restrictions and standards for mail-in ballots. 
The rule sets new ballot-design requirements and mandates that states collect information from voters and send that information to the federal government. It also bans the Postal Service from delivering or collecting mail-in ballots from people who haven’t been confirmed as eligible voters. 
The U.S. Postal Service said on Thursday that its new requirements for mail-in voting are now in effect, requiring the post office to refrain from delivering by-mail ballots to voters deemed ineligible. 
But a new round of legal challenges have been filed, including from Democratic officials in 24 states and the District of Columbia challenging the new Postal Service rule as unconstitutional. Monday’s U.S. Supreme Court ruling determined that the injunction on the rule should be lifted at least until the Postal Service had started implementing the new rule. Notably, it didn’t address the legality or constitutionality of the rule. 
Too late
While those legal issues continue to play out, Hatch said given the tight timeline between now and the Nov. 3 election, logistically it’s too late for those rulings to have any impact on Utah’s elections. 
“That ruling, the way I read it, it’s just a procedural hurdle that had to be cleared, and so now the Postal Service’s rule is being challenged in court, now that it’s final,” he said. “There’s certainly nothing that’s been decided.” 
Postal Service pushes ahead on Trump order limiting vote-by-mail

He also pointed to a legal principle known as the Purcell principle, which makes clear that courts should not change election rules too close to an election in order to avoid voter confusion. 
“And this clearly falls within the Purcell principle,” he said. “I just see tremendous risk in introducing a technology or an intermediary like the Postal Service this close to the election.” 
Even though the federal lawsuit is ongoing and it’s not yet clear how it will end, Hatch said he doesn’t foresee how Utah election officials could even implement the new Postal Service rule at this point, so close to the November election. 
“There are just too many question marks for us to dive in to make a risky change this late in the game,” he said. 
The office for Utah’s top election official, Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson, didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on how this week’s rulings, including the lifting of the injunction on the Postal Service rule, would impact Utah. 
Hatch said he and other clerks hadn’t yet received any guidance from the lieutenant governor’s office on next steps, but he said “their non-response kind of supports the fact this is still very much up in the air and it’s kind of a wait-and-see approach.” 
An ‘unmitigated disaster’
Online, Henderson has remained a vocal critic against the Trump administration’s attempts to force states to hand over sensitive voter information while continuing to note that the Constitution clearly says states control election administration. 
 


View on Threads

 

“This will be an unmitigated disaster if the injunction is lifted,” Henderson posted on social media earlier this week in response to the Postal Service’s rule. “The Postal Service could not concoct a better way than this to obliterate the last crumbs of confidence the public once had in the institution. Shameful.”
In response to Monday’s U.S. Supreme Court ruling, Henderson wrote another post that said the decision “has no effect on Utah,” noting the injunction against the rule stemming from a different lawsuit remained in place at the time. 
“In the meantime, Attorney General Brown and I are in close communication as his office works through all our legal options,” Henderson wrote. “I assure all Utah voters that they will be defended. We will run a secure election in accordance with state and federal law.”
But after the injunction on the Postal Service rule was lifted Wednesday, Henderson has not responded to a request for comment. 
Brown’s office declined to comment Thursday, but the attorney general told KUER on Wednesday he and his legal team are still analyzing the U.S. District Court judge’s ruling and determining what — if any — impact it will have. He also noted that the decision, like the U.S. Supreme Court opinion, was procedural and did not address the legality of Trump’s executive order. 
“This is really a decision on process as opposed to the substance, and that’s really what it comes down to,” Brown told KUER.
Brown also told the radio station that he wants to ensure “predictability in terms of the system” as the November midterm elections approach.
Mail ballots will go out as normal despite Supreme Court ruling, Colorado election officials say

“Our election officials do a good job of making sure that that is the case and having secure elections,” Brown said. “Ultimately, I think that is the responsibility, and that’s the aim. And so my job as the attorney general is to work with them to make sure that they follow the laws.”
Hatch agreed with Henderson’s comments that the new Postal Service rule would bring “absolute chaos” to the upcoming election — but also create problems for future ones if it’s allowed to stand. 
“The post office delivers mail. That’s their job. It’s not their job to vet who should and should not receive a ballot,” Hatch said. “They shouldn’t be involved in this at all.” 
Still, because of the tight timeline, Hatch doesn’t think states or local election officials are in any practical position to adhere to the new rule ahead of November, even with the injunction lifted for the time being. 
Even if the rule went into effect six months before the election, he said, there would be some “significant complications” that would need to be figured out, “one of which being this massively huge organization now needing to become a data sharing partner and intermediary between election officials and the voters.”
“That just invites all sorts of complications that aren’t necessary,” he said. 
Election officials are “naturally cautious when it comes to any kind of change that could impact the voters or the election,” Hatch added. “So we’re cautious because everything is so tentative surrounding the rule and the lawsuit.”
Above all, Hatch said clerks “really want to do what’s right for the voters” and ensure the election is run “accurately, securely and fairly.”
