name: Florida Phoenix
title: Florida pushes publishers to play down climate change in textbooks
description: NEWS HEADLINE:  How Florida quietly removed climate change content from textbooks “Good morning, class! Please take your seats. I’m your new science teacher, Mr. Ilg. “You’re probably wondering what happened to your old teacher, Ms. Glowasky. She made one factual comment on Facebook about Charlie Kirk, got fired, sued the school board, and collected a […]
text:
Victims of Hurricane Helene wade through flood waters made worse by sea level rise. But Florida education officials have pushed textbook publishers to play down the dangers of climate change. (Photo via Venice Police Department)NEWS HEADLINE:  How Florida quietly removed climate change content from textbooks
“Good morning, class! Please take your seats. I’m your new science teacher, Mr. Ilg.
“You’re probably wondering what happened to your old teacher, Ms. Glowasky. She made one factual comment on Facebook about Charlie Kirk, got fired, sued the school board, and collected a $650,000 settlement. She told the vice principal it was like winning the First Amendment lottery.
“Anyway, please open your textbooks to page 77. Yes, you in the third row, you have your hand up. What’s your question?”
KID IN THIRD ROW: “Mr. Ilg, why aren’t we starting at the beginning of the textbook?
TEACHER (speaking slowly): “Good question. This is science class, and science is all about asking questions and looking for answers. In this case, the answer is, ‘Because the state Education Department wants me to skip over all that stuff about evolution.’ Now let’s get back to today’s lesson, which is about climate change. How much do you already know about that subject? Yes, you in the fifth row?”
KID IN THE FIFTH ROW: “It’s making, like, our world a hella lot hotter. Even at night.”
TEACHER: “Yes, anyone else? You in the second row?”
KID IN THE SECOND ROW: “The higher temperature is heating up the water and making hurricanes much more intense.”
TEACHER: “Excellent. You in the fourth row, your hand is up.”
KID IN THE FOURTH ROW: “Because of sea level rise, the storm surge goes much further inland. My mom’s in real estate and she says it’s changing where people are moving to in Florida.”
TEACHER: “Very good. Anyone else? You in the front row?”
KID IN THE FRONT ROW (holding up the textbook): “Mr. Ilg, while everyone’s been talking, I’ve been skimming this part of our textbook, and it doesn’t say climate change is bad. It even claims the excess carbon dioxide that’s killing our planet can actually HELP plants! What’s up with that?”
TEACHER (taken aback): “Oh, uh… You noticed that, huh?”
KID IN THE FRONT ROW (sounding disgusted): “Well c’mon, Mr. Ilg, we LIVE in this world. We can see what’s happening. We’re not stupid. Although this textbook seems to think we are.”
Hurricane Helene makes landfall in Florida as one of the most powerful to ever hit the U.S. (Photo via NOAA)
 A world of information
TEACHER: “Okay, let me try to explain.” (Inhales deeply, then exhales.) “The Florida Department of Education is the branch of state government that oversees the selection of textbooks you get. A couple of years ago, the department told publishers they should play down the climate change stuff in Florida’s textbooks because the science isn’t settled.”
(Someone makes a derisive raspberry sound.)
TEACHER (narrowing his eyes at the sound): “You in the back, did you have something to say?”
KID IN THE BACK ROW: “Yeah, I said (makes rasberry sound again). That’s a bigger bunch of bull than the University of South Florida mascot.”
TEACHER: “What makes you say that?”
KID IN THE BACK ROW: “Because the scientists DO agree that climate change is real and it’s real bad. It’s the politicians who refuse to accept reality.”
KID IN THE FRONT ROW: “Yeah, like that 80-year-old loser in the White House who keeps saying it’s a hoax. Everybody knows he’s just trying to suck up to the oil industry dudes who helped him get re-elected.” (Multiple kids nod their heads.)
KID IN BACK ROW: “Yeah, him saying it’s a hoax is about as believable as him blaming vandals for what he did to the Washington Reflecting Pool.”
TEACHER: “Now wait a minute. Back up a second. How do you know the scientists are all in agreement?”
KID IN THE BACK ROW <rolls his eyes>: “Do you think we get all our information from our textbooks like kids back in the ’50s used to do?”
TEACHER: “I … uh, you know I never thought about it.”
KID IN THE BACK ROW: “Well, we don’t. We have access to the internet and we use it. And I mean use it a LOT.”
KID IN THE SECOND ROW: “Right. Like, we know how to search for answers online. We’ve been doing that for years. Plus, there’s a lot of social media we can use now. We can get information from Tik Tok, Instagram, and YouTube. We’ve got a world full of sources to tell us what’s going on beyond the classroom and these textbooks.”
KID IN THE BACK ROW: “Right. For instance, I follow Greta Thunberg on Instagram and Hank Green on Tik Tok.”
KID IN THE THIRD ROW: “Oh, you should try Ecotok Collective! They’re awesome.”
KID IN THE FRONT ROW (waving a hand around, making her bracelets clink together): “See? All these accounts act like an instant fact-check about what’s in these weaselly textbooks.”
TEACHER (in a voice full of wonder): “I had no idea.”
KID IN THE BACK ROW: “Heck, there are even videogames about climate change, and, like, not one of them tries to claim that it might be a GOOD thing.”
KID IN THE FOURTH ROW: “Is there one with Mario and Luigi?”
KID IN THE BACK ROW: “No — and don’t even ask about Minecraft.”
Loggerhead sea turtle hatchlings via FWC
 The tell-tale turtles
KID IN THE THIRD ROW: “You know, Mr. Ilg, we have, like, an environment club here in school. We talk about issues and bring in special speakers. We were just talking about climate change, like, I dunno, two weeks ago.”
KID IN THE SECOND ROW: “Yeah, like, my aunt came in and talked to the club about what it’s like volunteering with her sea turtle rescue group. She said the temperature of the sand, like, determines whether sea turtle eggs hatch out as male or female turtles. And she said that the sand has been, like, sooooo hot over the past 15 years that they’ve seen all or mostly all female sea turtles — hardly any males.”
KID IN THE THIRD ROW (nodding vigorously): “Oh man, that was so weird!”
TEACHER (speaking slowly): “I didn’t know that was happening. That’s a biological marker of climate change that’s pretty hard to ignore, isn’t it?”
KID IN THE BACK ROW: “You’re right it’s hard to ignore, Mr. Ilg. But even though it’s been happening for so long, she told us the politicians continue to ignore it because it doesn’t fit what they believe.”
KID IN THE FRONT ROW: “You shouldn’t be surprised at us being aware of this stuff, Mr. Ilg. Kids like us have been, like, on the front lines of the fight against climate change. A few years ago, a bunch of kids filed a lawsuit over it. One of them was a 10-year-old from Florida.”
TEACHER (nodding): “I kinda remember that. Whatever happened to that case?”
KID IN THE BACK ROW (consulting his phone): “Says here the Supreme Court shot ‘em down last year.”
KID IN THE SECOND ROW (sounding angry): “That bunch of creeps! They’re gonna kill us all. How many of them own stock in fossil fuels?”
 Fossil fuel fooling
KID IN THE FRONT ROW: “Hey, do you remember the Great American Teach-In last year? One of our speakers was Dawn Shirreffs from the Environmental Defense Fund.”
Dawn Shireffs via Environmental Defense Fund
KID IN THE BACK ROW: “The Environmental Defense Fund has a cool Tik Tok too.”
KID IN THE FRONT ROW: “Right. So anyway, she was talking about how we’ve got to be ready for this kind of stuff, because the fossil fuel industry has spent years spreading misinformation about the climate. They’re desperate to fool people so they can keep selling this product that’s polluting the atmosphere, ruining the world, and killing people.”
KID IN THE BACK ROW: “Yeah, plus they’ve been spending beaucoup bucks on campaign contributions, too. Buying loyalty.”
KID IN THE THIRD ROW: “She also talked about how politicians who sell out to these people wind up undermining, like, the confidence we have in government and in education.”
TEACHER (appalled): “Oh, I hope that’s not true.”
KID IN THE FRONT ROW: “She warned us to be careful about anyone trying to mislead us about what fossil fuels are doing to our future. Especially the way they influence politicians. And, apparently, textbooks.”
KID IN THE BACK ROW: (Clears throat.) “So, let’s talk about which politicians have been pushing for weakening Florida textbooks and trying to fool us students.”
 A current events discussion
TEACHER (looking uncomfortable): “I’d rather not get into any political stuff. I’m not Ms. Glowasky.”
KID IN THE FRONT ROW: “Think of it as, like, a current events discussion. We’re supposed to have those from time to time, right? So, what we’re wondering is, who twisted the arm of the textbook publishers to play down the role climate change has in everything that’s going wrong?”
KID IN THE THIRD ROW: “I wonder if it was the Florida Legislature. My uncle is a pilot at MacDill Air Force Base, and he was cracking up last year when the Legislature banned ‘chemtrails.’ He was laughing so hard he was falling over. They cut climate change out of the law like it’s no big deal, but they’re freaking out about chemtrails? He said anyone with any sense knows those don’t exist. Banning them was like banning the Skunk Ape.”
KID IN THE BACK ROW: “No, I bet it was the governor. That smells like his work.”
TEACHER (speaking cautiously): “The Education Department is under Gov. Ron DeSantis.”
KID IN THE FRONT ROW: “Figures. I remember he’s the guy claiming that slavery wasn’t all that bad.”
KID IN THE FOURTH ROW: “Didn’t DeSantis work as a teacher somewhere?”
KID IN THE BACK ROW: “Yeah, I think it was in Georgia.”
KID IN THE FRONT ROW (looking at her phone): “Yeah, here’s a New York Times story about that. Says he spent a year working as a teacher at a private school. Some students thought he was cool because he was a jock, but some said he came across as smug and superior. One Black student said he treated her badly because of her skin color. And he liked partying with the seniors, even though that was against the rules.”
KID IN THE THIRD ROW: “Can you imagine what would happen if he tried that now?”
KID IN THE FRONT ROW: “Oh man, this is wild! Listen to this: The story says he made some weird comments about the Civil War and so, for the school’s video yearbook, some of the kids made a video that made fun of him.”
KID IN THE BACK ROW (in a speculative voice): “I wonder if he’s devoted the rest of his life to getting revenge.”
TEACHER (sounding skeptical): “That seems a trifle far-fetched.”
KID IN THE BACK ROW: “No, no, hear me out! He decides to get vengeance on the whole education system. He works his way up to being governor, then takes a wrecking ball to the schools. He pays teachers so poorly they leave. He shuts down their unions so they can’t fight back. He turns the censors loose on the school libraries. He gives so much money to private schools that a lot of public ones have to close. Then, as the finishing touch, he undermines confidence in the textbooks.”
TEACHER (shaking his head): “That’s crazy. What’s your name, young man?”
KID IN THE BACK ROW: “My name is Danny — Danny Glowasky.”
TEACHER: “You mean …”
KID IN THE BACK ROW: “Yeah, that was my mom who used to teach this class.”
TEACHER: (Stands with his mouth open, then closes it and clears his throat.) “OK, this concludes our discussion of climate change. Let’s move on to the next section of our textbook which is about — oh shoot. It’s about sexual reproduction.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Don’t let St. Stephen’s Road become a sacrifice zone
description: We suggest an immediate formal rerouting designation; thus protecting the vulnerable populations of St. Stephen’s Rd.
text:
It is 3 p.m. on a Friday, and Bridgeport’s Geraldine Claytor Elementary School opens its doors. Students pour out and run across St. Stephen’s Road to greet their awaiting parents and grandparents. 
Their excited voices trail down the road toward the aquaculture school, where busloads of high school students from Fairfield, Trumbull, and Stratford arrive for the hands-on after-school program. Senior Citizens stroll down St. Stephen’s for an afternoon walk, children play at the park, and people cheerfully greet one another. Such is a typical day in a quiet corner of the Black Rock neighborhood of Bridgeport -– residents, young and old, confidently crossing without giving it a second thought, but this all will change. 
“The Last quiet corner of our neighborhood” is under attack.
St. Stephen’s Rd. is home to two schools, a senior apartment complex, playgrounds, and an affordable housing community with over 1,200 residents. This densely populated corner of Bridgeport sits adjacent to the Water Pollution Control Facility (WPCF), which is days away from committing an industrial intrusion in this neighborhood. 
The Water Pollution Control Authority (WPCA) wants to transform the peaceful residential area into a polluted haul road – compromising safety, degrading health and air quality, and disrupting tranquility for locals. PT Partners, a grassroots resident-led nonprofit based in Bridgeport public housing, is actively protesting the aspect of construction that intrudes unnecessarily into their livelihood. They are fighting for the health and well-being of P.T. Barnum residents – echoing their continual “demand to be heard.”
Zenida Gonzalez puts it this way: “St. Stephen’s Road is very important to PT Barnham and to the rest of our community, and we just want to be heard. We want to make sure we can save one piece of Bridgeport for our community because you’re taking everything else from us.”
WPCA’s proposed construction is essential to comply with the Connecticut Department of Energy & Environmental Protection and to reduce sewer overflows. The necessary modernization of Bridgeport’s WPCF is indisputable, and our goal is not to dissuade you from supporting this upgrade. Rather, we suggest an immediate formal rerouting designation; identification and utilization of specific alternate roads, thus protecting the vulnerable populations of St. Stephen’s Rd. 
Furthermore, a legally binding agreement among Bridgeport city officials, WPCA, and all contractors should be established to prohibit construction vehicles from entering the street.
Tantamount to preserving quality of life, upholding human rights, and prioritizing environmental justice is ensuring optimal health outcomes for residents and students. A fenceline community should never be forced to choose between environmental progress and human health. Bringing massive construction vehicles into a residential community poses obvious risks to pedestrian safety. Furthermore, consistent exposure to the detrimental air quality produced by the diesel trucks would pose a risk of respiratory distress and, over time, can increase risks of infant mortality and preterm birth.
The health risks posed by this industrial intrusion are avoidable if the WPCA would seek an alternative route for the trucks:
Running parallel to St. Stephens Road on the other side of PT Barnum is Bostwick Avenue. This is a street that the community does not relate to as it is an industrial zone. It creates pollution, and it isn’t a safe environment for our children to play. The asphalt factory is on Bostwick as well as “the incinerator”. The WPCF already has an entrance on Bostwick. This sewage treatment plant is known to be unsafe to our community because of the passing of Gary Crooks. As a young child, he died in their cesspool. This is not a future we want for our children.
The value of Bridgeport should be measured by its efforts to protect its residents. This means not only conducting the imperative upgrades that the WPCF requires but also safeguarding those who live alongside it. Some places are worth protecting; St. Stephen’s Road is one of them, and this is only possible when we raise our voices. We urge readers to sign our petition to grab the attention of Bridgeport City Council members- and to contact PT Partners for more information on how to support the movement. Saving St. Stephen’s Road requires immediate action. Act now to help protect our lives, homes, and health.
Razul Branch and Zenida Gonzalez are members of PT Partners.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Danbury residents express fear, anger as ICE arrests escalate
description: Activists in Danbury shouted at CT officials Wednesday as emotions ran high over dozens of arrests by ICE in the city each day this week.
text:
For more than a year, activists in Danbury have mobilized to support the local immigrant community as U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity has ramped up in one of the country’s most diverse cities. 
Members of immigrant rights groups and their families have helped people compile custodial paperwork to prepare for the possibility that parents could be separated from their children. They’ve handed out red cards to members of the immigrant community, to help people understand their rights if they are approached by ICE agents. And they’ve filmed ICE vehicles they see on town streets.
But this week, activists say they are facing the nightmare scenario they hoped would never come: massive raids that have resulted in parents detained in front of their children at school bus stops and dozens of people arrested in Danbury in just a few days.
ICE arrested two men outside of Kennedy Park in Danbury, Connecticut on August 24, 2026.  Credit: Ayannah Brown / Connecticut Public
Representatives of Danbury Unites for Immigrants, which works to protect, support and empower immigrant families, said on Wednesday that at least 25 people were detained in the city that day. That number that, if accurate, outpaces any single day of immigration arrests in the entire state of Connecticut since the Trump administration promised to crack down on illegal immigration.
According to CT Students for a Dream, which compiles counts of detainments based on arrests witnessed by activists, 16 more people were taken on Monday and 12 on Tuesday in Danbury, with additional arrests made in Stamford and Hamden on those days.
ICE officials did not return a request for comment on this week’s operation.
According to ICE data dating back to October 2022, which is processed and published by the Deportation Data Project at UC Berkeley and UCLA, Connecticut saw the most arrests recorded in a single day last August during Operation Broken Trust, a four-day string of arrests in Connecticut that ICE announced resulted in more than 60 arrests, including some in Danbury.
But Monday’s arrest count compiled by activists would top that.
And with no sense of when ICE activity will abate, activists are preparing for the days ahead. Some of those in attendance at a press conference held by state officials Wednesday afternoon in Danbury said they haven’t haven’t slept in days, and some were visibly shaken, shedding tears as they listened to the speakers.
Many expressed frustration related to what they say is a lackluster response from elected officials, sentiments that spilled over during the press conference on Wednesday, as activists shouted over speakers, including Gov. Ned Lamont who ultimately left the podium mid-response.
With protesters in the crowd calling for more direct action to combat ICE raids, Danbury Mayor Roberto Alves joined Gov. Ned Lamont, U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes, and U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy at Kennedy Park in Danbury, Conn. on Aug. 26, 2026 to condemn the actions of the agency, which has been detaining dozens of people Monday and Tuesday. “Everyone has constitutional rights in this country, regardless of immigration status,” he said, encouraging activists to record officers from a safe distance. Credit: Ryan Caron King / Connecticut Public
U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes, D-5th District, and Danbury Mayor Roberto Alves, who pressed a message of coalition building, also faced anger from the crowd, which demanded more action to protect immigrants from ICE and enforce the Connecticut Trust Act.
Some people also demanded an investigation into whether the Danbury Police Department has been cooperating with ICE in violation of the law, which outlines the circumstances under which local and state officials can work and communicate with the federal government’s detainment efforts.
The press conference was held in a place of layered and painful history for the Danbury community: Kennedy Park.
Speakers stood in front of a mural of Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr., John F. Kennedy, and Ruth Bader Ginsburg, which is near the site where 11 day laborers waiting to be picked up for work in 2006 were instead tricked by a police officer posing as a contractor and handed over to federal immigration authorities.
With protesters in the crowd calling for more direct action to combat ICE raids, Danbury Mayor Roberto Alves joined Gov. Ned Lamont, U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes and U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy at Kennedy Park on Aug. 26, 2026 to condemn the actions of the agency, which has been detaining dozens of people Monday and Tuesday. “Everyone has constitutional rights in this country, regardless of immigration status,” he said, encouraging activists to record officers from a safe distance. Credit: Ryan Caron King / Connecticut Public
The arrests resulted in a lawsuit that was settled in 2011. But by that time some men had been deported, and another had disappeared before receiving the settlement money, according to reporting from the Connecticut Post. 
Alves told the crowd that some of the arrests by ICE this week also occurred in Kennedy Park. “We are now seeing racial profiling, random people being picked up off the streets right here at this park, bringing back memories of a time in this city that we want to forget about,” he said.
Alves thanked the activists for their work, saying “you’re the reason we know what’s going on,” but also voiced his concerns that activists, who have been pepper sprayed and hit by ICE vehicles in recent days, according to accounts from members of Danbury Unites for Immigrants, could also be in danger.
“What I need you to do too is understand that these are dangerous actors who have killed people, and I want your safety just as much as I don’t want people deported,” he said. “Videotape them, yell, do what you need to do, but keep a safe distance…because I don’t want to see something happen to you either.”
Volunteers, like Bill and Karen Hunter, members of the Danbury Unites for Immigrants rapid response team, are trained to stay 6 feet back from ICE agents and to comply with their orders as they attempt to record the arrest. Their main goal as they go into the streets is to get the name of the detainee, and try to notify their family.
But these safety precautions don’t seem to be as effective anymore.
“They’re escalating,” Karen Hunter said. “Last summer, no one was pepper sprayed.”
Bill Hunter said activists have been approached and pushed while filming, and a recorded encounter from yesterday posted by Danbury Unites for Immigrants shows an ICE agent approaching an advocate.
Last year, Operation Broken Trust resulted in 65 arrests in Connecticut, according to ICE. The operation ran from Aug. 12 to Aug. 15.
Some of these arrests were conducted outside Connecticut courthouses, and some people arrested faced criminal charges. A press release from ICE alleged that 29 individuals arrested by the organization had been convicted or charged in the U.S. with “serious crimes.”
But this year, the arrests look different, activists said.
“Over the last year, there have been mostly targeted arrests,” Tabitha Sookdeo, executive director of Connecticut Students for a Dream, told the Connecticut Mirror on Tuesday. “Yesterday was out of trend with anything observed.”
The arrests Monday were seemingly more random, Sookdeo said, with ICE apprehending people at pickup sites for day laborers like Kennedy Park.
Juan Fonseca Tapia (right) and Clementina Lunar (center) of Danbury Unites for Immigrants speak to Congresswoman Jahana Hayes during a press conference on August 26, 2026 where officials condemned the actions of ICE officers in the city, who have been detaining dozens of people. Fonseca Tapia said ICE has been using aggressive tactics against immigrants in Danbury. “I saw the chains that they put on them. Not handcuffs. Literal chains,” he said.  Credit: Ryan Caron King / Connecticut Public
Hayes was also shouted over by activists on Wednesday, and she seemed ready for the criticism.  “I just want to start by saying we’re all on the same side. None of us want what we are seeing,” she said.
“Is that why you thanked ICE last year?” one person shouted, referring to a House resolution that Hayes voted for that also condemned antisemitism. As her speech went on, Hayes urged people to work with officials to keep community members safe.
She said that she’d been elected to sit at the table where decisions are made. “I promise you that I will work as hard as I can to keep your families safe, but once you gave me a seat at the table, it means you don’t want me yelling in the window,” she said. “It means you want me at those tables, doing the job that you sent me to do. So at a moment where the criticism of me is coming from both the left and the right, I know I’m meeting in the middle where the people are.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana secretary of state hopefuls clash over voting rules, office audit
description: Republican Max Engling found himself the outsider against three opponents on several key topics during the first debate between the four hopefuls for Indiana Secretary of State Wednesday night. Meanwhile, Democrat Beau Bayh, Lincoln Party candidate Greg Ballard and Libertarian Lauri Shillings often agreed. “When the facts and the law are on your side, maybe[...]
text:
Four candidates for Indiana Secretary of State squared off on Aug. 26, 2026 in downtown Indianapolis. From left to right, Max Engling, Lauri Shillings, moderators Dan Spehler and Lesley Weidenbener, Greg Ballard and Beau Bayh. (Photo By Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)

Republican Max Engling found himself the outsider against three opponents on several key topics during the first debate between the four hopefuls for Indiana Secretary of State Wednesday night.
Meanwhile, Democrat Beau Bayh, Lincoln Party candidate Greg Ballard and Libertarian Lauri Shillings often agreed.
“When the facts and the law are on your side, maybe it does feel like three to one,” Bayh told reporters afterward. “But you know, it was a nice discussion. I think we did a good job of sticking to the actual issues at play in this campaign, and hopefully, folks saw our vision.”
Lincoln Party candidate Greg Ballard answers a question during a debate for Secretary of State on Aug. 26, 2026 in downtown Indianapolis. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
The debate was part of the Indy Chamber’s annual HobNob event in downtown Indianapolis. Several hundred Hoosiers attended the event.
The secretary of state’s office is one of five statewide offices designated in Indiana’s original constitution. The agency oversees elections, securities, auto dealer and business services.
What is typically a low-profile, down-ballot contest has gained prominence in recent years as state leaders take cues from President Donald Trump’s administration and tightened voting laws.
Current officeholder Diego Morales lost the nomination contest at the Republican State Convention to Engling.
Engling’s late entry came as U.S. Sen. Jim Banks and Attorney General Todd Rokita pulled their endorsements from Morales, whose tenure has been plagued with questionable spending, traveling and contracting.
The 39-year-old Engling, who is on leave from Banks’ office to campaign full time, previously spent 12 years on Capitol Hill. He worked as a Republican staffer for a U.S. House committee and later as an aide to then-House Speaker Kevin McCarthy of California.
Engling was the only candidate to not pledge an audit of the office.
“Travel expenses would be a particular point of emphasis,” Ballard said. “What that office needs is stability. It needs some dignity.”
Shillings and Bayh also said they would support an audit.
But Engling didn’t join the trio. Instead, he said he challenged Morales at the convention as a way of reinstilling confidence in the office. And he also joked that he told his brothers-in-law he would not create a state job for them as Morales did.
Engling was also the only one to support the full SAVE America Act, a federal proposal that would require additional identification requirements for married woman and others to ensure only citizens cast ballots.
Indiana already has a photo ID requirement that is part of the proposal.
Republican Max Engling answers a question during a debate for Secretary of State on Aug. 26, 2026 in downtown Indianapolis. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
“It’s also important that we have only eligible citizens voting in our elections,” Engling said. “We have to know who’s voting in our elections. It is sacred, and if you think that it’s something that’s not important, I would say you fundamentally disqualify yourself for Secretary of State.”
But Shillings called the SAVE Act a barrier to voting.
“I believe that it disenfranchises people who absolutely should be able to vote. I think that it is an undue burden for individuals who have changed their name, married or adopted.”
Ballard said Indiana’s election security record is solid and he considers the proposal a federal intrusion.
Moderators asked the candidates about a controversial recount in Senate District 23. Spencer Deery of West Lafayette initially posted a three-vote win over challenger Paula Copenhaver in the Republican primary.
But the recount commission threw out several Deery votes because local election officials had not properly placed the clerk’s stamp on the absentee ballots. That gave Copenhaver a 6,332-6,329 victory.
The Indiana Supreme Court has accepted an expedited appeal of the case with arguments scheduled for Sept. 10.
Bayh said the votes should be counted because there are no allegations of fraud or wrongdoing.
“When a voter goes into the voting booth, they should have faith that their vote is counted if they’ve done everything right,” he said. “It doesn’t make sense to me to cast aside the intent of the voters. That doesn’t make sense, particularly when there’s been no alleged evidence of fraud.”
Bayh, 30, has never run for office before but had a bird’s-eye view growing up as his father, Evan Bayh, served as Indiana governor and senator. His grandfather also was a U.S. senator.
He has excelled in fundraising, and some believe he could be the first Democrat to win statewide office since 2012. He is already airing television ads in the race.
Democrat Beau Bayh answers a question during a debate for Secretary of State on Aug. 26, 2026 in downtown Indianapolis. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Ballard said the intent of the voter should be paramount, and he would have counted the voters. Shillings also agreed.
But Engling differed, saying the others are ignoring state law.
“I think when you look what happened with the recount commission, they followed the law,” he said. “They reviewed every ballot. They said, ‘Does this match the code?’ We have code for a reason.”
A significant part of the evening was spent discussing Ballard’s proposal to create and send a paper voter guide to every registered voter to help increase turnout. A software app would also be part of the program costing upwards of $2.5 million each election cycle.
Both Engling and Bayh believe the cost is too high and there are better ways to combat apathy and low voter turnout.
Ballard said afterward it’s clear the major political parties don’t want voters to be informed. He also said if the Republicans and Democrats pay the cost to run primaries rather than the state there would be money to cover that cost.
The foursome also touched on business services provided by the Secretary of State’s Office. Most of them criticized the website while Engling said it is straightforward but state agencies could communicate better between themselves to help businesses.
All four candidates supported adding transparency to business filings by requiring the owners of the company to be listed instead of registered agents. And all four said they would serve a full four-year term.
Ballard’s fledgling Lincoln Party also took some heat during the event.
Libertarian Lauri Shillings answers a question during a debate for Secretary of State on Aug. 26, 2026 in downtown Indianapolis. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Engling said parties should be clear about what they stand for and how they will govern.
After the debate, Shillings said the party might gain more traction “if they provided a platform so people knew what they stood for.”
Ballard said his party provides “hope to people who actually want to run for office without punitive signature requirements.”
Ballard is a wild card in the contest, having gathered more than 70,000 signatures to appear on the ballot as an independent under the Lincoln Party label. The 71-year-old has raised significant cash but spent most of it to get on the ballot.
Both Ballard and Bayh are Marine Corps veterans.
Ballard is disillusioned with his former party and wants to give Hoosiers an additional choice at the ballot. If he receives at least 2% of the vote, the Lincoln Party will have automatic ballot access for the next four years.
Shillings also hopes to hit that mark to maintain ballot access for Indiana Libertarians.
She is creative director at the University of Indianapolis, and CEO of Pirate Smile Media — a small business she has run since 2000.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: East entrance to Zion National Park to stay ‘serene and pristine’ under new deal
description: A nonprofit supporting Zion National Park says it's made a big step for preservation.
text:
The view from the floor of Zion Canyon in autumn. (U.S. National Park Service/Christopher Gezon)

A nonprofit supporting Utah’s most-visited national park is celebrating a milestone for preservation at its scenic, winding East entrance.
The Zion Forever Project announced Wednesday it has secured a conservation easement to protect 145 acres just outside Zion National Park in southwestern Utah. Under the agreement, a private landowner is keeping title to the property but handing over rights to develop it, with Zion Forever as its steward going forward.   
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Chris Horton, the nonprofit’s chief operating officer, said it’s a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity for conservation. It means no hotels, condos or restaurants will pop up there, although visitors will be able to take advantage of a planned, expanded trail network running through the newly protected area, which is a little smaller than one square quarter-mile. 
“There are a lot of people that really enjoy that drive in from the east side because it’s so serene and so pristine compared to a lot of other gateway communities surrounding national parks across the country,” Horton told Utah News Dispatch. “People can be very happy to know that that stretch of land is going to look the way it does now forever.”
Zion Forever is calling the move a monumental step, saying it won’t just protect the views and watersheds, but also wildlife corridors along the park. Horton declined to disclose the exact cost, but noted easements aren’t cheap, generally matching the price of the land if it were to go on the open market. 
Horton said it was philanthropist Brian Donnell and the landowner who approached the group about working together to protect the patch of land within a half-mile of the park. 
“Zion belongs to all of us, and preserving it takes people who are willing to think beyond their own lifetime,” Donnell said in a prepared statement issued by the nonprofit Wednesday. 
Donnell went on to say that “my hope is that future generations will experience this treasured landscape with the same sense of wonder that we have today.”
The group already has a separate conservation easement for land close to the new site, though not right next to it, Horton said. That’s in addition to six other properties it owns outright along the park’s boundary.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy focuses on ICE during ‘In The Room’ visit
description: Immigration was bound to come up during CT Mirror's visit with U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy on Wednesday. But ICE activity delayed his arrival.
text:
There was little doubt that President Donald Trump’s immigration policies would come up at some point during CT Mirror’s “In The Room” session with U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy on Wednesday. 
Few, however, anticipated those policies would affect the event itself.
The plan was for Murphy to arrive at 5:15 p.m. and spend the next 45 minutes mingling with attendees at a reception before the webcast. Instead, he spent that time on the road from Danbury before finally walking onstage at roughly 6:07 p.m. 
Shortly after sitting down, Murphy told the crowd what had happened: There had been “extraordinary ICE activity” that day in Danbury, and he had been visiting the city at the request of its mayor.
ICE’s presence, Murphy told the audience, was “not coincidental to the beginning of the school year.”

U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy answers a question from host John Dankosky during Connecticut Mirror’s “In the Room” series at Connecticut Public Broadcasting in Hartford on Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

“If you can sort of imagine how one would design a system intended to terrorize a community — not intended to keep the community safe — you would design what they’re doing in Danbury right now,” Murphy said.
He went on to explain: That morning, ICE agents had waited at a bus stop in Danbury as parents dropped off their children. Once the children were on the bus, the agents arrested their parents. This, Murphy said, was intentional.
“They knew what would happen when the bus came back, right? The kids don’t know that their parents are gone. The bus comes back … this little 7-year-old gets dropped off expecting to be greeted by their parent, and there’s no parent,” Murphy said, drawing muffled exclamations from the crowd.
He described this as a new “scale” of ICE enforcement for Danbury. 
“I fear that, you know, this is a sign of what’s to come for the fall in Connecticut cities,” Murphy said.

U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy answers a question from host John Dankosky during Connecticut Mirror’s “In the Room” series at Connecticut Public Broadcasting in Hartford on Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

So what can and should be done to solve the problem? asked the host of the event, CT Mirror’s John Dankosky.
Murphy said the first step is to define what the problem is. The Trump administration, he said, defines it as an invasion of people from other countries coming to the U.S.
“That is a fake problem,” Murphy said. “Immigrants, first generation immigrants and undocumented immigrants, both commit crimes at rates lower than natural-born Americans. … So if you want to live in a safe community, you are actually better off living in a community with people that just got to the United States of America.”
He said the real problem is that Americans perceive the U.S. immigration system to be lawless — something that would have been solved, he added, if Congress had passed an immigration reform bill he sponsored in 2024. Trump, facing multiple criminal investigations and running for a second term, urged Republicans to kill the bill, which had enjoyed bipartisan support.
“You can ask the question: Had we passed that bill, would Donald Trump have been elected?” Murphy mused.

U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy answers a question from host John Dankosky during Connecticut Mirror’s “In the Room” series at Connecticut Public Broadcasting in Hartford on Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

When they finished discussing immigration, Dankosky asked Murphy about the recent primary defeat of U.S. Rep. John Larson, whom Murphy had endorsed. Murphy replied that he also likes Luke Bronin, the former Hartford mayor who defeated Larson in the primary, but defended his support for outgoing representative.
“I definitely have seen people who have outlived their effectiveness. I just didn’t think that that was true of John,” Murphy said.
But you think some politicians hang on too long? Dankosky asked.
“Well, sure. I mean, I still, I haven’t seen Mitch McConnell in months,” Murphy said. “Diane Feinstein on the Democratic side was another example … and obviously, the American public judged that Joe Biden had stayed too long, and, you know, it took far too long for the Democratic Party to come to terms with” that.
But when asked whether his Senate counterpart, Richard Blumenthal — who will be 82 if reelected in 2028 — should take a hint from Biden’s example, Murphy demurred.
“That’s Dick’s decision to make,” Murphy said. “As to the question of whether Dick Blumenthal still has the energy to be a United States senator — I am still trying to keep up with Dick Blumenthal.”
He said he doesn’t like the idea of term limits for members of Congress, citing the argument that it gives too much power to unelected staffers and lobbyists. First-term members of Congress, he said, are forced to spend most of their time raising money because of what he described as a broken campaign finance system.
Giving term limits to Supreme Court justices, however, was something Murphy said is worth considering, because there are fewer ways to remove justices than to remove legislators.

U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy answers a question from host John Dankosky during Connecticut Mirror’s “In the Room” series at Connecticut Public Broadcasting in Hartford on Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Murphy also discussed the divisions within the Democratic party and pushed back on the typical framing of “progressive versus moderate.”
“I think there’s a market fundamentalist wing of the Democratic Party that thinks the market can solve everything … and then there are Democrats like me who think that the market is fundamentally broken and corrupted, and that we need much bigger changes,” Murphy said.
He added, “I see the world as worker power versus corporate power. I don’t necessarily see it as left versus right.”
His vision for the Democratic Party, he said, is built around two “tentpoles”: unrigging the economy and unrigging democracy.
“If you agree, I want you in the tent,” Murphy said. “And if you disagree with me on other issues that I feel are really important, like guns or climate or gay rights, let’s have that conversation.”
He said he thinks it’s easier to persuade people once they’re “in the tent” than otherwise.
On Iran, Murphy expressed harsh criticism of how the Trump administration has managed the conflict.
“It’s really hard to overhype the incompetence, the gross incompetence, of the crowd that is in charge,” Murphy said.
He said at this point, he doesn’t think Washington can get a good deal with Tehran. He urged the president to unilaterally halt the war and said U.S. allies — namely Europe and the Gulf states — would likely have to negotiate an opening to the Strait of Hormuz.
The last part of the evening’s conversation touched on Murphy’s new book, “Crisis of the Common Good.” The senator seemed surprised when Dankosky began by drawing a comparison to, of all people, Ralph Nader.
No, Murphy said, he had not drawn from Nader in writing his book. But, he said, it is “a pretty universal conversation” — how the U.S. is becoming more isolated and people feel increasingly disconnected and powerless.
His idea of the common good: “We should have a society that makes it easier for us to care about the common good. About how the community is doing.” That’s something he said the country has lost in recent decades and which he believes government can help restore.
When Dankosky suggested the book might be a policy platform for someone considering a run for president, Murphy pushed back — slightly.
“Other people have had the opposite view … because it is a book that’s not about me,” Murphy said.
But does he think about it? Dankosky asked.
“I can’t say that I don’t think about it, in part because I get asked about it all the time,” Murphy said. But he also has “a pretty powerful job” now, and it’s one that he enjoys.
His closing remarks were, “I don’t know what I’m going to do after this election. I don’t. But I don’t need to run for president to make a difference.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Maryland hopes to pick all new Key Bridge contractors by spring 2027
description: After parting ways with the contractor once expected to build the new Francis Scott Key Bridge, Maryland has started requesting bids for four separate contracts, which it hopes to award by late next spring.
text:
A construction worker descends a stairway Wednesday at the construction site for the replacement Francis Scott Key Bridge. Crews are continuing to drive piles into the Patapsco riverbed for the new bridge as the state seeks new contractors for the bridge's construction. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)After parting ways with the contractor once expected to build the new Francis Scott Key Bridge, Maryland is aiming to select four replacement contractors by late next spring.
Disagreements over cost compelled the state to break ties in April with the Kiewit Corp., the large Nebraska-based firm that designed the new bridge, and split the construction project into four separate parts.
“It enables us to have more competition among contractors,” said Jim Harkness, chief engineer for the Maryland Transportation Authority, during a news conference at the bridge site Wednesday. “It also gives us the benefit to encourage and expand opportunities for our local workforce.”
So far, the state has opened two of the four contracts to new bidders, including the largest one, which will cover the main span of the bridge running over the Patapsco River. The state isn’t expecting to award that contract — which has an estimated value between $3.5 billion and $4 billion — until next spring.
The state advertised another, much smaller contract Tuesday, for the demolition of several remaining bridge structures, both in the water and over land, which is valued at $50 to $100 million. That work could start before the end of this year.
The final two contracts will cover the portions of the bridge that will be built over land, approaching the river from the north and south sides of the river. Both are currently valued between $200 and $400 million.
A construction worker examines a steel pile that will form part of the new Francis Scott Key Bridge on Aug. 26, 2026. Work is continuing at the site even though Maryland parted ways with its initial contractor, the Kiewit Corp. and is seeking replacement contractors. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)Crews can now use a large trestle, pictured on Aug. 26, 2026, to access the construction site for the new Francis Scott Key Bridge from Fort Armistead Park. Work continues at the site although the state dumped its original bridge contractor amid cost disagreements and is still seeking replacements. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)Crews can now use a large trestle, pictured on Aug. 26, 2026, to access the construction site for the new Francis Scott Key Bridge from Fort Armistead Park. Work continues at the site although the state dumped its original bridge contractor amid cost disagreements and is still seeking replacements. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)Construction crews adjust massive steel piles in the Patapsco riverbed for the new Francis Scott Key Bridge on Aug. 26, 2026. Work continues at the site although the state dumped its original bridge contractor amid cost disagreements and is still seeking replacements. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
Rising cost estimates and shifting timelines for the bridge have been points of tension between Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) and President Donald Trump (R) at various times during Trump’s second term. After the bridge collapsed due to a ship strike in 2024, killing six construction workers, the federal government pledged to fund its replacement.
The state initially hoped to complete the new span in 2028. Currently, the goal is for the bridge to open to traffic by the end of 2030, Harkness said.
“We have to wait for our proposals to come in. We still have a goal of the end of 2030,” Harkness said. “Ultimately, we need those proposals to tell us what they can build it in.”
Though Kiewit will not be building the new bridge, its crews remain on site, continuing to drive massive 8-foot-wide piles into the riverbed, which will serve as a foundation for the new bridge, and for its new protection system against ship strikes.
Kiewit is also building a large pier over the river — called a trestle — for construction workers, vehicles and cranes to access the bridge site. The southern portion of the walkway is complete, allowing crews to walk or drive onto the worksite from the shoreline at Fort Armistead Park.
When all is said and done, some 104,000 square feet of timber will form the deck for the trestle, and it will be supported by 35,000 linear feet of steel piles, said Brian Wolfe, director of project development at the transportation authority.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Turek highlights cancer advocacy, pledges support if elected to U.S. Senate
description: Iowa Rep. Josh Turek said Wednesday his work across the aisle to support pediatric cancer research and funding in the state Legislature shows he would be the best candidate to advocate for these priorities in the U.S. Senate. Turek, the Democratic nominee for Iowa’s open Senate seat, spoke to cancer patients, advocates and volunteers at […]
text:
Iowa Rep. Josh Turek, D-Council Bluffs, spoke with Gary Streit, right, and other advocates working with the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network at a "cancer coffee chat" in Cedar Rapids Aug. 26, 2026. (Screenshot via CSPAN)Iowa Rep. Josh Turek said Wednesday his work across the aisle to support pediatric cancer research and funding in the state Legislature shows he would be the best candidate to advocate for these priorities in the U.S. Senate.
Turek, the Democratic nominee for Iowa’s open Senate seat, spoke to cancer patients, advocates and volunteers at a “coffee cancer chat” in Cedar Rapids, hosted by the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network (ACS CAN). It was part of a nonpartisan series of events the group is holding with members of both parties ahead of the midterms in Iowa.
Cancer has become a top issue on the Iowa campaign trail this election season because of the state’s position as having the fastest-rising cancer rate and the second-highest number of new incidences of cancer in the nation. Turek said Wednesday his work to address cancer in Iowa began well before his 2026 campaign for U.S. Senate, as he worked on legislation related to cancer as a member of the Iowa House.
Turek said the first year he was in the Iowa Legislature, 2023, he advocated for a bill to dedicate $1 for every Iowan toward pediatric cancer research at the University of Iowa — a similar proposal to the measure supported by Iowa House Republicans this session. Ultimately, Gov. Kim Reynolds signed a law providing $3 million in funding for pediatric cancer research through a 5-cent tax on vapes and alternative nicotine products, which Turek said represented “a form” of his proposal.
None of these bills passed by the Iowa House or Senate in 2026 featured his name, Turek said. “I’m in a trifecta minority, so you don’t always get the credit for some of the work that you did.” If elected to the U.S. Senate, the Democrat said he would take a similar approach to working across the aisle on issues like cancer research.
“As you’ve heard me say, even here today, with some of the examples that I gave you, sometimes you don’t end up getting credit for the work that you end up doing on these bills, but what I’ve learned in the Legislature is, it’s amazing what we can get done with people who don’t care who takes credit,” Turek said. “And when we’re willing to work to do the hard work behind the scenes, to work in a bipartisan manner, to get results. And that’s what I’d like to do. I’m not going up there to play political games, I’m going up there to make sure that people have healthcare, and people are taken care of.”
The Democrat had also introduced a measure in 2023 called “Better Caths for Iowa,” which would have called for Iowa Medicaid to not reimburse for catheters made with DEHP, a manufactured chemical linked with higher instances of bladder cancer, until a review was conducted. Though the bill was not taken up by the Iowa House, it received a subcommittee hearing — something that often does not happen for bills presented by the minority party.
Even though the bill did not pass, Turek said having the discussion still had an impact.
“Because of the work and advocacy that we did on this, we had the five largest providers, actually, pull out the DEHP,” Turek said. “So now, there is 20 million catheters that are made annually that no longer contain this cancerous compound that was leading to a bladder cancer epidemic. So, it has taught me how much advocacy can really move the needle in the right direction.”
Turek said healthcare was a top priority for him at the Statehouse, and would continue to be a major focus in Washington, D.C., if elected.
“If I only got one thing done in the U.S. Senate, I would love to arrive at a public option, so every American, every Iowan, has access to care,” Turek said. “And I would love to (be) — even if it means only six years in the U.S. Senate — coming back and saying, ‘We made meaningful progress on this cancer issue, and Iowa no longer lead the nation in cancer rates.'”
Turek faces U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, a Republican, in the general election. Hinson also plans to speak with ACS CAN advocates before the election about her priorities on addressing Iowa’s cancer rates and research funding.
Hinson’s campaign has criticized Turek for missing an April vote on the bill which would have provided $1 per every Iowan for pediatric cancer research funding.
Turek has previously answered questions from reporters about Hinson and Republicans’ criticisms that he missed a significant number of votes in 2026 by saying he was spending time “meeting Iowans all over the state” as he ran his primary campaign earlier in the year, and by saying he spent time working “really, really hard behind the scenes … to find strange bedfellows, build relationships across the aisle, and I was able to get a lot of policy to the finish line.”
Turek did vote in favor of the vape and nicotine product tax providing $3 million in pediatric cancer research that made it to the governor in May. He said he was happy to see the funding provision “get across the finish line” in 2026.
“I think it’s a great example of what we can do when we work together in a bipartisan fashion,” Turek said. “A lot of the times when you do this work behind the scenes, you don’t end up taking the credit. And something that I — really I’m proud of — is (that I’m) one of the most bipartisan members in the Iowa Legislature, and one of the most effective members.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Environmental groups take steps to sue to compel new protections for gray whales
description: Amid a decade of die-offs and a sharp decline in the population of gray whales that swim along the Pacific coast of North America, three environmental groups are preparing to sue the Trump administration over its failure to bring back Environmental Species Act protections for the animals. The Center for Biological Diversity, the International Marine […]
text:
A gray whale carcass washed up on a beach north of Ocean Shores, Washington, It was one of the 187 gray whales that, as of late August, have been found dead this year along West Coast shorelines from Mexico to Alaska. Environmentalists are seeking a return of Endangered Species Act protections for the population, and they cited recent years' die-offs as a major part of the justification. (Photo by Hal Bernton)Amid a decade of die-offs and a sharp decline in the population of gray whales that swim along the Pacific coast of North America, three environmental groups are preparing to sue the Trump administration over its failure to bring back Environmental Species Act protections for the animals.
The Center for Biological Diversity, the International Marine Mammal Project and Oasis Earth on Tuesday submitted a notice of intent to sue the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration over gray whale protections.
Oasis Earth submitted a petition a year ago to NOAA Fisheries for a threatened or endangered listing to be granted to the Eastern North Pacific gray whale population. But the agency neither issued a 90-day finding on the petition’s validity nor a 12-month finding on the population’s status, as required under the law, the groups’ notice said.
With its population halved over the past decade, the gray whales’ situation is dire, the groups said. Lapses in Endangered Species Act action put the whales “at greater risk of extinction,” their notice said. “These delays contribute to the decline of the gray whale population.”
A notice of intent to sue, which is filed at least 90 days before a complaint is filed, is required under the Endangered Species Act.
 

A graph shows the changes over time in the Eastern North Pacific gray whale population. The whales were delisted from endangered species protections in 1994. The population rose to a peak abundance of about 27,000 whales around 2016. They have since declined. NOAA Fisheries declared an unusual mortality event in response to hundreds of strandings from 2018 to 2023. Estimated calf production has remained low since then, according to NOAA Fisheries. (Graph provided by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Fisheries service)
 

	The Eastern North Pacific gray whale population was estimated at about 27,000 in the 2015-2016 period. Last year, the population fell to about 12,890, one of the lowest levels since counts began in the late 1960s, according to NOAA Fisheries. This year’s count indicated a bit of a rebound, with a median estimate of 17,750 animals, the agency said last month.
Despite that increase, Endangered Species Act protections are still needed, the environmental groups said.
“We’ve lost half of these Pacific gray whales in just a decade. It couldn’t be clearer that the population needs protections, but we’re just getting silence from the Trump administration as the crisis unfolds,” said Miyoko Sakashita, oceans director at the Center for Biological Diversity. 
“Gray whales are washing up dead all along the West Coast, and if federal officials keep dragging their feet, it could be too late for the species,” she said. “These majestic whales are starving and they face other threats we need to fix to save these creatures from extinction.”
Agency spokesman Michael Milstein declined to comment Tuesday on the environmental groups’ notice. He cited NOAA’s policies on pending litigation.
The Eastern North Pacific gray whale population has been struck by die-offs for several years, with beached animals found from Mexico to Alaska. NOAA determined that deaths from 2018 to 2023, with 690 documented cases, constituted an “unusual mortality event,” a finding that justifies further research. After a brief lull, the gray whale die-offs picked up.
 

A gray whale is seen (Photo by Merrill Gosho/NOAA Fisheries)
 

	There were 179 gray whales found dead last year along the Pacific coast, according to NOAA. This year’s toll has already exceeded that. As of Tuesday, 187 had been found dead this year, including 22 in Alaska, Milstein said.
The emaciated condition of the dead whales has supported scientists’ contention that the die-offs are tied to climate change. The whales spend summers feeding in Arctic and subarctic waters off Alaska, and long-term warming and changes in sea ice have affected supplies of the high-fat prey that gray whales need, scientists say.
Climate change and the resulting loss of suitable prey is the main threat facing the gray whales, the environmental groups said in their notice. But there are other threats, including ship strikes and entanglements in fishing gear and marine debris, the notice said.
A recent NOAA Fisheries report cites 31 documented cases of gray whale entanglements in fishing gear in Alaska from 1990 to 2024.
Eastern North Pacific gray whales were previously protected under the Endangered Species Act, but they were delisted in 1994 following a population increase that scientists attributed to the end of commercial whaling.
That delisting was premature, the environmental groups argue in their notice of intent to sue.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: How to get North Carolina students to love science and math? Ask a NASA astronaut.
description: NASA astronaut and Artemis II Mission Specialist Christina Koch was honored Wednesday with the Order of the Tar Heel, the highest award bestowed by the North Carolina Commissioner of Labor. Koch, a Jacksonville native and N.C. State University graduate, became the first woman to travel beyond low Earth orbit, and with her crew broke the […]
text:
NASA astronaut and Artemis II Mission Specialist Christina Koch tells a group of students to hold out their hand and imagine just how very small Earth looked from space.  (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)NASA astronaut and Artemis II Mission Specialist Christina Koch was honored Wednesday with the Order of the Tar Heel, the highest award bestowed by the North Carolina Commissioner of Labor. Koch, a Jacksonville native and N.C. State University graduate, became the first woman to travel beyond low Earth orbit, and with her crew broke the record for the farthest distance humans have ever traveled in space.
NASA astronaut and Artemis II Mission Specialist Christina Koch was honored Wednesday with the Order of the Tar Heel, the highest award bestowed by North Carolina Commissioner of Labor Luke Farley. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)
“Her accomplishments with NASA have made history, but her commitment to encouraging students to pursue STEM education may be among her most important contributions,” said Labor Commissioner Luke Farley, at the award ceremony at the historic Labor Building in downtown Raleigh.
The award recognizes Koch’s work with NASA as well as her ongoing advocacy for science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) education.
Koch said her mission would not have been possible without countless workers, all willing to contribute their unique talents to make the mission a success. A-B Emblem of Weaverville, North Carolina, was among the businesses recognized for producing the Artemis II patch, which was designed by the astronauts.
“I like to think we are a partnership because in NASA, so many jobs, high-skilled manufacturing and technical jobs, are created by a love of wanting to explore,” Koch said.
Developing a strong STEM workforce, starts with engaging students in science and math at a very young age.
As part of Wednesday’s special event, Koch took questions from two dozen enthusiastic elementary school students.
When you were my age, did you already know you wanted to be an astronaut?
“I did know I wanted to be an astronaut, but I also knew it was going to be really hard and probably not very likely,” Koch answered. “So, I went for my dream and I worked towards that goal. I also made sure that along the way I did things that I found really fun and that brought me joy.”
What’s your favorite planet, other than Earth?
“I like Jupiter! [It] has a huge magnetic field and beautiful lights like the auroras,” Koch said.
Just like the Northern lights, Koch said, the light will dance in the sky from the magnetic field of a whole planet.
“That happens on Jupiter just like it happens on Earth, and I think that’s pretty cool.”
What’s it feel like when you sleep upside down in space?
“Without gravity it feels the same as sleeping upside down as the right side up,” Koch said. “There’s no gravity to keep you in the bed. It’s just amazing.”
Could you see the dark side of the moon?
“It’s the far side of the moon. It’s never facing Earth, but the sun actually lights it up just as much as it lights up the side that faces us,” Koch said. “It was beautiful.”
Koch answered one last question from NC Newsline: What’s next for an astronaut who has seemingly achieved all her goals?
“I haven’t actually figured that one out,” she said.
NC State offers an out of-this-world homecoming for astronaut alum Christina Koch

In the short term, she plans to restore her family’s sailboat, a past time she enjoyed with her father growing up in Jacksonville.
“That actually has been one of the most exciting things that I’ve taken on recently — getting back to my family, and then trying something that scares me, which is what I always tell people they have to do.”
Koch said she hopes the students will embrace their own unique talents and find a way to give back to their community.
“You can make [it] happen when you’re supporting the people around you,” Koch said.
Artemis II Mission Specialist Christina Koch, a Jacksonville native and N.C. State University graduate, greets students who were fascinated by her journey to space. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)

title: Crowley has slight lead on Tiffany with likely voters in post-primary poll

text:
With less than three months until the midterm election Nov. 3, Democrat David Crowley, left, and Republican Tom Tiffany, right, have been criss-crossing the state to get their names out to voters and win over support.  (Photos by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Crowley polled slightly ahead of Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany in the first Marquette Law School poll conducted since the primary earlier this month. The poll results were released Wednesday.
The poll was conducted from Aug. 12, the day after the primary, through Aug. 20. Surveyors interviewed 891 Wisconsin registered voters, with a margin of error of 4 percentage points. The likely voter sample was 738, with a margin of error of 4.5 percentage points.
With less than three months until the midterm election Nov. 3, the candidates have been criss-crossing the state to get their names out to voters and win over support. 
 Crowley pulled in support from 49% of  likely Wisconsin voters, while Tiffany had 44%; another 7% of likely voters said they were undecided. Among registered voters, Crowley and Tiffany were tied at 44%.
The poll found a Democratic advantage among those who are certain that they’ll vote in November, with  84% of Democrats reporting they were certain compared with 82% of Republicans.
“You could either come away with a modest Crowley advantage, by about five points, or a dead tie, depending on whether you’re looking at everybody that’s registered to vote or looking at those absolutely certain to vote,” poll director Charles Franklin said.
The poll showed that 98% of likely voters who were Democrats planned to vote for Crowley, while 91% of likely Republican voters said they planned to vote for Tiffany. 
The biggest percentage of undecided voters were independents: 30% of independents who said they were likely to vote were undecided. Among registered voters, undecided independent voters jumped to 47%.
Among likely voters, Crowley had an advantage with independent voters. About 55% said they supported him, while 16% said they would support Tiffany.
Following the divisive and chaotic primary campaign, Crowley called on Democrats to unify to win in November and campaigned with state Rep. Francesca Hong, who finished a close second in the primary.  
“It’s interesting that the Democrats do appear to be completely unified behind their candidate and Republicans, quite unified, but not quite as much as Democrats,” Franklin said. 
Tiffany and Crowley will be working to win over undecided voters and flip people to support them over the next 10 weeks, especially as Wisconsin’s statewide races are typically decided by close margins. In 2018, Gov. Tony Evers defeated Gov. Scott Walker by about 30,000 votes.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Data centers in North Dakota have received millions in sales tax breaks
description: Data center owners in North Dakota have reaped tens of millions of dollars in state sales tax breaks in the last two years, figures that have ballooned as public scrutiny has intensified on data center projects. The Legislature’s interim Tax Reform and Relief Advisory Committee on Wednesday heard a series of reports about data center […]
text:
North Dakota Republican Tax Commissioner Brian Kroshus gives a presentation on Aug. 26, 2026, to legislators. 
(Photo by Jack Dura/North Dakota Monitor)Data center owners in North Dakota have reaped tens of millions of dollars in state sales tax breaks in the last two years, figures that have ballooned as public scrutiny has intensified on data center projects.
The Legislature’s interim Tax Reform and Relief Advisory Committee on Wednesday heard a series of reports about data center tax exemptions and incentives, including what North Dakota and other states offer. State Tax Commissioner Brian Kroshus outlined exponential growth in sales and use tax exemptions for data center owners on information technology equipment, such as computer hardware, servers, routers, cooling systems and other infrastructure. 
Those sales tax breaks, which are not for construction, ranged from $5.4 million in 2021 to $7.8 million in 2023, then leapt to $15.3 million in 2024 and more than $65 million last year. 
“It’s a number that I think will grow without question,” Kroshus told the panel.
Residents voice concerns over Mandan data center during town hall

Data centers are huge facilities housing computers that handle everything from financial transactions to email to artificial intelligence.
The 2015 Legislature approved the original tax exemption, with the current version set by the 2021 Legislature, Kroshus said. 
“I don’t think anyone at the time, the Legislative Assembly, could have envisioned what this would become just 11 years later,” Kroshus said. 
In a 2015 House floor debate, bill sponsor Rep. Mark Owens, R-Grand Forks, who died in 2024, said he brought the bill to make North Dakota more attractive for data centers looking to relocate. He said he had precision agriculture, drones, banking, finance and jobs for North Dakota college and university graduates in mind with the bill. 
North Dakota’s cold climate and a reliable source of electricity in the state are draws for data center companies, Sen. Mark Weber, R-Casselton, said Wednesday. North Dakota is “on the radar” across the U.S. for data centers, he said. 
“I’m wondering if the time at the next legislative session is to have some of this discussion,” Weber said. “Are we – I don’t want to say giving away the store, but I think it warrants some discussion amongst all of us.” 
Data center developers have emphasized the significant property taxes they pay to local communities as a benefit to the state.
In addition, data centers also created or retained 332 permanent jobs from 2021 to 2025, Kroshus said.
Data center companies evaluate states for years prior to locating their projects, said Matt Marshall, an economic development manager with Minnkota Power Cooperative.
“They’re looking at lots of different metrics, and by the time we get the call, you’d be amazed at how educated they are about our area,” Marshall told the panel. 
North Dakota has a number of data centers, including ones built near Ellendale and Williston, under construction near Harwood or in planning stages near Mandan and Center.
Data centers have drawn scrutiny and criticism from citizens for their size, water usage, noise and other factors.
No pause on data centers but North Dakota special session to debate nondisclosure deals

In its upcoming special session, North Dakota’s Republican-led Legislature will consider a bill to temporarily ban nondisclosure agreements between industrial projects and government officials. Critics say those agreements keep the public in the dark about data center projects.
At least 38 states offer a dedicated tax exemption or incentive for data centers, some dating back to the early 2000s, said Nicholas Miller, a policy associate with the National Conference of State Legislatures’ Fiscal Affairs Program, who presented to the panel.
States see jobs, economic benefits and property tax revenue as reasons to create the incentives, though some states have considered walking back or adding requirements to their incentives, Miller said. Concerns related to data centers’ energy use and water use and the loss of tax revenue might be why some states are pumping the brakes on their incentives, he said.
“And I think increasingly data centers are a hot topic just in general,” Miller told the panel.
The data center presentations will be helpful for lawmakers in their upcoming special session and in the 2027 Legislature, said committee chair Sen. Brad Bekkedahl, R-Williston. He pointed to community benefit agreements with developers as one potential topic.
“They need to engage the communities. They need to provide a direct benefit to the communities,” Bekkedahl told the North Dakota Monitor. “They’ve talked about property tax benefits, but there’s other things involved with that as well.” 
North Dakota Monitor reporter Jack Dura can be reached at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.

title: New Mexico sues feds, contractors over water wells drilled to aid border wall construction
description: New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham on Wednesday announced a lawsuit against the U.S. government and its contractors over unauthorized water wells that federal agencies used to construct a wall along the state’s border with Mexico.
text:
New Mexico leaders announced Aug. 26, 2026, that they had filed a lawsuit against the federal government, along with its primary contractor and subcontractors, for unauthorized water wells drilled as part of a border wall construction effort along the U.S.-Mexico border. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham on Wednesday announced a lawsuit against the U.S. government and its contractors over unauthorized water wells that federal agencies used to construct a wall along the state’s border with Mexico. 
The New Mexico Office of the State Engineer had previously documented multiple sites in protected underground water basins and cited federal subcontractors for drilling wells without state authorization. The office also alleged that contractors’ failure to construct or plug wells properly had created an “imminent risk of groundwater contamination.”
