A news release from the governor’s office announcing the lawsuit from Wednesday names as defendants the subcontractors, Wyatt Drilling Arizona, LLC, and Cascade Drilling, LP., as well as their prime contractor, Montana-based Barnard Construction Company. It also names the United States of America.
A copy of the lawsuit was not immediately available in court records, because court staff were still processing it as of late Wednesday afternoon, according to Leah March, a spokesperson for the governor’s office. Source NM has a pending request to the governor’s office for the name of the federal agency being sued.
“Water is a precious resource in New Mexico, and the residents, ranchers, and farmers whose water is being stolen by the federal government deserve justice,” Lujan Grisham said in a statement.
Officials from Barnard Construction and Cascade Drilling did not immediately respond to Source NM’s calls and emails seeking comment Wednesday afternoon. Vincent Wyatt, owner of Wyatt Drilling, declined to comment. 
The lawsuit adds a new allegation against the contractors and the federal entity that hired them, according to a news release from the governor’s office. The lawsuit claims “improper tampering” with a water meter, an illegal practice that state officials said can obscure the amount of water diverted from a wall. 
A copy of the lawsuit was not immediately available in court records, because court staff were still processing it as of late Wednesday afternoon, according to Leah March, a spokesperson for the governor’s office. 
But State Engineer Elizabeth Anderson said in a statement that the lawsuit aims to ensure that the state’s permit procedures are followed and that the federal government pays for any water it was not authorized to take. 
“Our permit procedures exist to protect water rights holders, and we are not going to allow the federal government to evade those protections and threaten our groundwater,” Anderson said. “We are also demanding double repayment for all illegally diverted groundwater.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Tougaloo College President Corey Wiggins promises transparency after years of leadership  concerns
description: Tougaloo College President Corey Wiggins delivers his convocation address, Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026, at the campus in Jackson.
text:
At his first convocation as Tougaloo College’s president, Corey Wiggins reflected on a question he’d asked himself before the event: What prepared him for this moment?
“And strangely enough, my mind didn’t go to a job I had, a title I’ve carried, or even a degree I’ve earned,” Wiggins said during his speech. “It went home.” 
Wiggins, who took over as the college’s president on July 1, talked about growing up in Copiah County, and how his experiences led him to his new role. He also recounted the college’s storied civil rights history and its connection to the institution’s future. 
Nearly 250 Tougaloo alumni, faculty, students and local high school students and community residents filled the Kroger Gymnasium in the Owens Health & Wellness Center for the convocation Wednesday. The event opened with brief remarks and prayers from campus student leaders followed by the college’s concert choir singing “Lift Every Voice and Sing,” which is often called the Black national anthem. 
Wiggins recounted Tougaloo’s history before talking about his role in its future.
Founded in 1869, four years after the Civil War, the American Missionary Association bought 500 acres of a former plantation and established Tougaloo College. Nearly a century after the college’s founding, nine Black students — later dubbed the Tougaloo Nine — staged a sit-in at the segregated Jackson Municipal Library on March 27, 1961. 
Tougaloo College President Corey Wiggins delivers his convocation address, Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026, at the campus in Jackson. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
That moment and other events during the Civil Rights Movement, Wiggins said, defined the college’s mission: to learn, lead and serve.
For Wiggins, the college’s legacy will require new and prospective students to show the same courage by embracing change. It will ensure Tougaloo remains strong for future generations, he said. 
“You have to show up. You have to do the work. You have to be curious,” Wiggins said to applause. “Whatever path you take, your Tougaloo education should prepare you for your moment to think critically, to act courageously and serve something larger than yourself.”  
Those commitments come as Wiggins inherits lingering concerns about the college’s leadership. 
In March 2025, the college’s faculty senate issued a series of no-confidence votes for former President Donzell Lee, Provost Josiah Sampson III and Registrar Pam England.
The faculty senate previously voted no confidence in Sampson and England in May 2024. Lee was interim president of the university at the time. 
The dissatisfaction also predates Lee. 
In 2022, Tougaloo students voted no confidence in President Carmen Walters. That year, a group called the Tougaloo College Alumni Coalition for Change garnered more than 1,500 signatures on an online petition calling for Walters’ removal.
On Tuesday, Wiggins told Mississippi Today he can’t speak to what happened on campus before his arrival. But he has attended alumni events, faculty senate meetings and walked the campus with students. 
Read more: Who is Corey Wiggins? Learn more about Tougaloo College’s new president
“I think that’s how we build camaraderie,” Wiggins said. “That’s how we build and create the healthy tension that you need to create an institution that’s forging a way ahead.” 
Wiggins said Tougaloo faces challenges competing with public institutions for faculty, an issue he plans to address as he develops the college’s strategic plan. 
Meherun Laiju, vice chair of Tougaloo’s faculty senate, said she was a member of the selection committee for the president and believes they chose the right candidate. 
“We believe that he will be transparent,” Laiju said. 
Wiggins asked faculty to work directly with Pamela Foster, the college’s new provost and vice president of academic affairs, to address their concerns, Laiju said. 
Jalynn Sanders, a senior physics major, said students have felt unheard by college administrators, particularly around campus infrastructure. But Wiggins has reached out to student groups since the start of the semester to create a positive impact on their campus experiences, Sanders said.
Tougaloo College President Corey Wiggins speaks with attendees during a meet-and-greet at the school in Jackson on Wednesday, July 1, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
The institution has had too much change, said Blondean Y. Davis, who chairs the college’s board of trustees. Wiggins will provide the leadership that the college needs, she said. 
“With change comes a sense of unrest,” Davis said. “He also has the aggressiveness in terms of facilitating financial stability that we need to lead us into the world.” 
Wiggins has a deep understanding of the college’s community and the potential to elevate the institution nationally, said Michael J. Cleveland, vice chair of the Tougaloo College National Alumni Association board of directors. It is important that Wiggins involves alumni, the community, and faculty, in shaping the institution’s future, he said. 
Wiggins and his administration should also address faculty and student recruitment, retention, fundraising and donor retention, Cleveland said. 
“I think he’s coming at the right moment to do what needs to be done,” Cleveland said.
 “And if he isn’t,” he said. “We’re going to hold him accountable.”

name: Nevada Current
title: Nevada could get up to $256 million from Meta settlement over youth social media addiction
description: Nevada could receive as much as $256 million from multibillion dollar multistate settlement over claims that Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, is addictive and lacks child safety protections. Under the settlement announded Friday, the social media company agreed this week to pay 47 states and the District of Columbia up to $17.1 billion in […]
text:
(Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Nevada could receive as much as $256 million from multibillion dollar multistate settlement over claims that Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, is addictive and lacks child safety protections.
Under the settlement announded Friday, the social media company agreed this week to pay 47 states and the District of Columbia up to $17.1 billion in penalties and pledged to implement changes to bolster protections for children using social media platforms. 
Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford called the settlement a historic win and a “first step toward a future in which social media companies do not treat our children as disposable products.”
“This settlement will bring money into Nevada that will go directly toward educating and protecting our children, but, most importantly, it will implement changes that will drastically change how children can interact with Meta’s products,” Ford said in a statement Wednesday. “This settlement is strong, but it is not the end. I will continue to work to hold accountable the remaining social media companies who have unlawfully neglected to protect our children.”
Nevada is guaranteed to receive $178 million over the next 10 years though the amount could be larger, according to a statement from the attorney general’s office. 
A lawsuit filed in 2023 claimed that Meta purposely designed its platforms to be addictive while knowingly exposing children to serious mental harms. The suit also claimed the company had intentionally misled the public about the safety of those platforms.
Ford, along with state officials across the country, echoed social media critics and legal observers who have suggested the suits against the platforms could have an impact similar to the lawsuits against Big Tobacco in the 1990s. Those suits resulted in huge monetary awards to states to fund public health programs, and also severely curtailed cigarette marketing and advertising. 
In addition to the settlement, the company also has to to implement a series of safety protocols including “Nighttime blocks” restricting children’s access from 12:00 a.m. to 6:00 a.m., limits on school-time access for children, stronger safeguards against bullying, and eliminating push notifications on weekdays during the school year.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Researchers expect ‘biggest year yet’ for energy siting bills in 2027
description: An analysis of renewable energy siting bills across the U.S. during 2026 legislative sessions found the majority of introduced bills were aimed at restricting renewable energy infrastructure, though most of the enacted bills were permissive to the industry.  Researchers who worked on the report with the Siting Solutions Project, a nonpartisan initiative focu[...]
text:
Wind turbines along west-bound Interstate 80 on March 29, 2025. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)An analysis of renewable energy siting bills across the U.S. during 2026 legislative sessions found the majority of introduced bills were aimed at restricting renewable energy infrastructure, though most of the enacted bills were permissive to the industry. 
Researchers who worked on the report with the Siting Solutions Project, a nonpartisan initiative focused on energy siting and permitting, said in a webinar Wednesday they anticipate data center growth and continued concerns around energy affordability will make 2027 the “biggest year yet” for state bills related to energy siting. 
The policy analysts anticipate Iowa renewable energy advocates will have to take a defensive position on siting policy at the Statehouse in 2027.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Siting Solutions Project looks at bills that pertain to renewable energy regulation and categorizes the bills as either very restrictive, somewhat restrictive, neutral, somewhat permissive or very permissive. 
Of the more than 200 bills tracked this legislative session, 43% were restrictive and 36% would have “had a positive impact” on renewable energy deployment. The project’s report from 2025 similarly showed a trend toward restrictive bills, but a smaller share, 22%, of 2025 bills were permissive. 
Less than 30 of the bills tracked by the organization have been enacted, and of those, just two were categorized as restrictive policies. 
Nelson Falkenburg, one of the authors on the report and a siting policy manager with Clean Tomorrow, the parent organization of the Siting Solutions Project, said this means that defensive strategies protecting renewable energy are “adept and strong” or some of the proposed bills were used as political messaging. 
 
How bills were classified
Restrictive bills tended to include policies that: increased local zoning authority, increased the procedural burdens on the permitting process, made the decommissioning process more costly, expanded setbacks or restricted projects based on agricultural or environmental impacts.
Permissive bills tended to include policies that: created statewide standards in line with industry standards, streamlined permitting processes, created financial incentives for projects or reduced the barriers to build projects on certain types of locations. 


“It’s possible that many of the restrictive bills introduced in 2026 were messaging bills, where legislators were scoring political wins for their constituents by beating up on wind and solar,” Falkenburg said, noting that these bills often don’t make it out of committee.
Utah enacted a bill that removes incentives for solar on agricultural land and took a “restrictive approach” to decommissioning standards. In Kentucky, a new law creates “punitive” siting standards for renewable energy projects in unzoned counties, according to Falkenburg. 
Permissive bills that were enacted updated standards for renewable energy siting and decommissioning, or streamlined permitting for co-located battery storage laws. Lawmakers in Alabama passed a law that made it easier to convert oil and gas wells into renewable energy sites. 
In the 2026 report, each U.S. state that had an active legislative session was similarly categorized based on the consequences of each introduced energy siting bill. 
Some states, like Missouri, Oklahoma, Arizona, Mississippi, Alabama and New York, had predominantly “very restrictive” policy proposals, including outright or de facto moratoriums on renewable energy projects. Washington, Oregon, California, Maine, Virginia and New Jersey had mostly permissive policies, though researchers said the permissive policies only made “incremental progress” whereas restrictive policy tended to propose more drastic changes. 
States with a balance of restrictive and permissive policies, like Iowa and several other Midwestern states, were labeled as “neutral” for the 2026 legislative session.
The Siting Solutions Project mapped renewable energy siting bills introduced in each state based on their potential impact. (Map courtesy of Siting Solutions Project)
This categorization, based on 2026 introduced legislation, does not necessarily correlate with the overall nature of renewable energy siting in a state, according to Zona Martin, an analyst with Siting Solutions and author on the report. 
For example, Martin said that while Oregon and Washington passed and introduced mostly permissive energy siting bills this session, the permitting and development processes for renewable energy projects are still “very slow” and “costly.” 
How did Iowa stack up? 
Martin noted states with significant renewable energy infrastructure, like Iowa, Arizona and Oklahoma, had legislation that reflected a “backlash” to renewable energy project buildout. She said these states proposed policies like restrictive statewide standards, capping development to preserve farmland and expanding local control.
The analysis flagged seven bills in Iowa, three that were considered permissive, three that were restrictive and one neutral bill. None of the Iowa bills tracked by the project were enacted in 2026.
Iowa’s restrictive bills fit similar descriptions, including a bill that would have required certain environmental studies, insurance and proof that the project would be a benefit to the community. A neutral bill from the Statehouse would have addressed landowner complaints about blinking red lights on wind turbines by requiring the structures to have aircraft detection lighting systems.
A notable permissive bill would have created renewable energy siting language for counties to adopt which would set a standard for initiatives like moratoriums, setbacks, property tax and other considerations. While similar bills advanced from committees in both chambers, neither was heard on the floor. 
The report said Iowa’s siting policy was “turned on its head” following a decision from the Iowa Utilities Commission to approve the generation certificate for a solar project in Cerro Gordo County, which preempted the county’s ban on wind, solar and battery storage projects. 
Falkenburg said because of the IUC’s decision on this case, he anticipates renewable energy advocates will shift their focus in 2027 from pushing for more permissive policies, to trying to defend the right of the IUC to preempt local ordinances. 
2027 projections 
The report notes that clean energy advocates will be “on the defense” in Iowa and Texas this year to “shore up” permitting paradigms in the state. 
Falkenburg said he anticipates it will be effective to “make the business case” to Republican leadership in Iowa about renewable energy projects. 
“Advocates are going to have to be really closely tracking any renewable energy legislation that’s introduced or advancing in the state, and making the case to the IUC, to Iowans, and to the Legislature that the projects that are coming online in Iowa, are addressing the needs of Iowans and the business community,” Falkenburg said. 
Iowa groups ramp up campaigns for and against data centers

While the report shows that Republicans tended to introduce more restrictive bills and Democrats tended to introduce mostly permissive bills, Alex Brekel, the senior director of programs for Clean Tomorrow, said there’s a “poor correlation” between the voting color of a state and its clean energy policy. 
“Or at least the partisanship of a state tells you very little about the quality of the wind, solar, battery siting policy regime,” Brekel said. 
Falkenburg said Texas is a “prime example” of a Republican-dominant state that has a lot of renewable energy and “very little” siting regulation.
In other red states, Falkenburg said bills to “constrain” local governments from enacting restrictive ordinances have been common. States with a mostly Democratic base tend to favor clean energy policies that create an “effective state siting regime.” 
The report said notable permissive bills are anticipated in Pennsylvania, Virginia, and Indiana and restrictive bills that didn’t make it across the finish line this year in Oklahoma, Alabama and Arizona are expected to return in 2027. 
Overall, researchers on the call said data centers and energy affordability will likely drive conversations around renewable energy siting policy. 
“2027 is going to be the biggest year yet for renewable energy siting and permitting legislation, considering both the trends of data center buildout and the rising electricity bills that Americans are seeing that are affecting their wallets,” Falkenburg said. 
The Siting Solutions Project maintains a legislative tracker that is updated weekly with renewable energy siting policies across the country. The interactive tracker also shows more state specific information, down to the bills the project is watching.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: District judge won’t force Nebraska Democrats to replace Senate candidate
description: District Court Judge Susan Strong said in her order that she “respectfully disagrees” with William Forbes' interpretation of state law.
text:
Lancaster County District Judge Susan Strong presides over a hearing in a case revolving around legislative authority and lottery proceeds from the Nebraska Environmental Trust. June 29, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN —  A Lancaster County district judge dismissed an effort from the loser of the Democratic Senate race trying to force the Nebraska Democratic Party to replace its nominee who dropped out.
Lancaster County District Court Judge Susan Strong said in her order Wednesday that she “respectfully disagrees” with William Forbes’ interpretation of state law. 
“In sum, under the plain language [of the state law], a political party has the discretion to fill a vacancy after a candidate declines their nomination,” Strong wrote.
Forbes’ lawyers argued the law’s language requires a replacement. During a court hearing on Monday, his lawyers reiterated their contention state law prohibits what they described as a “scheme” — referring to the Democratic Party’s strategy to clear the field for nonpartisan U.S. Senate candidate Dan Osborn.
Lawyers for the Nebraska Democrats said Forbes is misreading state law because the statute he cited addresses the process that must be followed if a party chooses to replace a nominee, whereas the law about a candidate declining the nomination says a party “may” replace the person.  
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The state Democratic Party continued the strategy when its central committee voted against filling the vacancy last week. Its strategy wasn’t a secret, as it was widely reported that the Democrats’ plan was not to actively recruit a Senate candidate.
Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers weighed in on the case with a brief, saying the state “has an interest in preventing gamesmanship and manipulation of the electorate.” Hilgers, in his brief, wrote that Forbes correctly interpreted the law as it “ensures that all the Democratic voters who wanted a candidate on the general-election ballot when they voted for someone in the primary will have one.” 
Strong, in her order, said she has “serious doubts” that Forbes’ inability to consider voting for a Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate constitutes “an injury.” 
Forbes was registered as a Republican until 2008 but has been a Democrat since, according to records obtained by the Examiner. In his affidavit for the lawsuit, he said he was a “longtime registered Democratic Party voter in Nebraska.”
There were allegations that both candidates in the Democratic Senate primary, Forbes and Cindy Burbank, were “plants” to help either incumbent Sen. Pete Ricketts or Osborn. Both Ricketts and Osborn have denied any involvement with Forbes or Burbank.
Burbank dropped out of the race one day after the secretary of state verified Osborn’s signatures to be on the fall ballot. 
Democratic Party Chair Jane Kleeb said in a statement that the ruling “recognizes an essential principle: Nebraska political parties retain the discretion to determine whether to fill a ballot vacancy when a nominee withdraws.” 
It is unclear if there will be an appeal to the state Supreme Court. 
The general election is Nov 3.

title: Kansas to receive $134 million in transformative Meta settlement
description: TOPEKA — The parent company of social media platforms Facebook and Instagram agreed to one of the largest state consumer protection settlements in American history, paying $17.1 billion to most U.S. states and territories and promising to implement sweeping safety features to protect kids. Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach said Wednesday the state’s $134 m[...]
text:
The parent company of Instagram and Facebook agreed to settle a nationwide lawsuit by paying up to $17.1 billion and implementing safety features on its platforms to protect children. (Photo by Anna Kaminski/Kansas Reflector) TOPEKA — The parent company of social media platforms Facebook and Instagram agreed to one of the largest state consumer protection settlements in American history, paying $17.1 billion to most U.S. states and territories and promising to implement sweeping safety features to protect kids.
Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach said Wednesday the state’s $134 million portion of the settlement with Meta “marks a down payment on an industry-wide transformation that will finally prioritize our children’s well-being over corporate profits.”
“For too long, Meta deliberately designed Instagram and Facebook with addictive features that preyed on kids’ developing brains, exposed them to serious mental-health harms, and then misled parents about the dangers,” he said in a news release.
The settlement ended a case that 47 states, Washington, D.C., and three territories filed against Meta Platforms Inc. in 2023, arguing the social media giant designed its platforms to be addictive, knew it mentally harmed children, and misled the public about the platforms’ safety.
Meta must now roll out a list of protections, including daily time limits, mandatory pauses to reduce continuous scrolling, nighttime blocks, limited access during school hours, age verification measures, content controls, parental controls and limits on beauty filters and like counts.
Kobach said child safety on social media extends beyond one company. Meta will pay out just 70% of the settlement amount — $12.7 million — unless TikTok and Alphabet, which owns YouTube, adopt comparable measures.
The settlement’s magnitude is second only to the big tobacco settlements of the 1990s, Kobach said.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Rhode Island to receive at least $49.4 million in landmark Meta settlement over addictive features
description: A yearslong court battle against Meta will see Rhode Island receive a payout of at least $49.4 million as part of the windfall won by a multistate effort alleging the social media behemoth knowingly designed Instagram to addict young users while misleading the public about the risks involved. Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha joined […]
text:
A smartphone shows Instagram's settings page. The photo-sharing platform's owner Meta agreed to pay nearly $18 billion to an array of U.S. states over claims its platforms intentionally addicted teens. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)A yearslong court battle against Meta will see Rhode Island receive a payout of at least $49.4 million as part of the windfall won by a multistate effort alleging the social media behemoth knowingly designed Instagram to addict young users while misleading the public about the risks involved. 
Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha joined his counterparts in 46 other states and several U.S. territories Wednesday in announcing the approximately $17.1 billion settlement.
Rhode Island’s share of what Neronha’s office called “one of the largest state consumer protection settlements in history” will be at least $49.4 million but could be as high as $64.5 million
“While there is still much work to be done, this agreement is a significant step forward safeguarding our children from the well-documented harms of social media use by young people,” Neronha said.
The much higher ceiling on Rhode Island’s payout is not a sure thing. The settlement has a guaranteed portion and a contingent portion, and notes Meta will disburse about 70% of the money over 10 years — the guaranteed portion.
The internet is putting kids at risk. These mom lawmakers want to force tech firms to make it safer.

But the payout for the remaining 30% or so depends on if “all Core Industry Members with annual profits above $10 billion” — or Snap, TikTok and YouTube, per the settlement text — adopt comparable protections and settlements with participating states. 
“The ways in which our children engage with social media, and technology generally, are constantly changing,” Neronha said, “and as such, we must continue to adapt our approach to online safety.”
In addition to the cash, Meta must also make changes to its flagship platforms, Facebook and Instagram, for users ages 13 to 17.
New limits on use
The 130-page consent decree will have Meta introduce a number of stipulations on teens’ use of its platforms, including a combined two-hour daily time limit across the company’s products for most uses. If a teenager uses up all their allotted time, they will be locked out until midnight, barring the intervention of a parent or guardian, who will be able to link their account to their child’s and unlock a less (or more) restrictive setting if desired.

Messaging, account settings and “longform content” — which the settlement defines as “a piece of video or audio content with a duration of at least 22 minutes that Meta has determined with a high degree of reliability to not have been artificially extended” — are all exempt from the two-hour time limit.
Should Meta’s competitors and “core industry members” Snap, TikTok and YouTube also enter into similar agreements, the time allotment would drop to an hour daily — and also trigger the remainder of Meta’s payment. 
Messaging will also remain available between midnight and 6 a.m. in the user’s local time, when access to most functions of the platforms are otherwise blocked. Most push notifications, meanwhile, will be blocked daily from 10 p.m. to 7 a.m., as well as during school hours. 
Within four months, Meta must provide teens with the option for a non-personalized home feed. The settlement also mandates that teens not be allowed to use certain beauty filters on their photos, which the settlement specifically defines as an “effect that distorts, sculpts, redefines, or idealizes a user’s face in a way that cannot be achieved without cosmetic surgery or extreme makeup.”
Meta will need to fortify its age verification process, and can draw on methods including identification documents, facial age-estimating technology, third-party verification services and Meta’s own age-prediction models. Accuracy benchmarks for those systems — as well as a separate set of standards to detect accounts belonging to children under 13, which the company already prohibits — are specified in the settlement.
As for enforcement, the attorneys general are not leaving it up to Meta, at least not without an additional watchman providing oversight. Per the settlement terms, an independent auditor will be given access to relevant company data, documents, systems and personnel as part of a regular assessment of compliance.
The nationwide investigation began back in 2021, when dozens of attorneys general banded together to scrutinize Meta’s platform design. Over the course of the suit, the states alleged that Meta knew Instagram’s design could harm young users and their mental health.
As is the case with many settlements, Meta’s agreement to the terms does not “constitute an admission by Defendant of any liability, wrongdoing, or violation of any local, state, federal, or international law,” according to the settlement.

title: US House Speaker Johnson stumps for GOP congressional hopeful Cunningham in Albuquerque
description: U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) on Wednesday told a group of reporters gathered in the back room of Albuquerque’s Rio Bravo Brewing Company that he started his day with a phone call to President Donald Trump, who agreed that Republican congressional challenger Greg Cunningham is “straight out of central casting.”
text:
U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) addresses the media inside Albuquerque's Rio Bravo Brewing Company during a campaign stop for Republican congressional candidate Greg Cunningham, who is challenging incumbent U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.). (Joshua Bowling/Source NM)U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) on Wednesday told a group of reporters gathered in the back room of Albuquerque’s Rio Bravo Brewing Company that he started his day with a phone call to President Donald Trump, who agreed that Republican congressional challenger Greg Cunningham is “straight out of central casting.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Johnson visited New Mexico to stump for Cunningham, a retired Marine and Albuquerque detective who is challenging incumbent U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.) for the state’s southernmost congressional district.
Vasquez first won the seat to the 2nd Congressional District in 2022, when he ousted Republican Yvette Herrell by less than one percentage point. Although he won re-election in 2024, Trump defeated Kamala Harris in that district the same year. The race for the seat this year is considered among the most contested in the state. It’s become a key race nationally, as well — conservative and progressive organizers have identified it as a “must-flip” and “must-hold” seat, respectively, as Republicans hold a narrow 218-212 majority in the U.S. House of Representatives.
Johnson said he believes Cunningham is “overqualified” to flip CD2 back to Republican control for the first time in four years.
“We’re gonna flip a number of seats from California to New York,” Johnson said. “They will become red on election night. The reason is very simple — we fulfilled our promises, we’ve done what we said we were going to do…Ronald Reagan used to remind us that you can trust the American people. When they have the facts, they’ll make the right decision.”
He said the upcoming Nov. 3 general election offers New Mexicans a “contrast between common sense and crazy,” arguing that Vasquez has voted against Republican-backed economic and immigration policies and represents a Democratic Party of “woke, kind of DEI nonsense.”
Johnson referenced the latest data from the Cook Political Report, which rates New Mexico’s Congressional District 2 as “leans Democrat,” as evidence of how close the race is.
Cunningham, for his part, delivered brief remarks and did not take questions from the media.
Greg Cunningham, a retired Marine and Albuquerque detective, speaks alongside U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) at an Albuquerque campaign event on Aug. 26, 2026. (Joshua Bowling/Source NM)
Protesters set up outside the Albuquerque brewery and their cries of, “Hey hey, ho ho, MAGA Mike has got to go” were audible from inside as Cunningham and Johnson spoke.
“I raised six children and have nine grandchildren, so I’m actually used to speaking over stuff like this,” Cunningham said while standing alongside Eddy County Sheriff Matthew Hutchinson and members of the state Fraternal Order of Police. “I’m not a politician that is telling police officers and detectives that I like them or I’m listening to them. I am one of them.”
Outside, protesters from around Albuquerque decried the pair for their support of Trump, who earlier this year endorsed Cunningham.
Lisa Christopherson, the executive director of NM Stronger Together Coalition, held up a sign that read, “Jesus was a brown immigrant. Matt 2:13-15,” a reference to a Biblical passage that describes God telling Joseph to take Jesus to Egypt shortly after his birth.
Behind her, a sign that read, “pedo protectors not welcome” hung off a chain-link fence.
“Trump and his friend Epstein have not been held accountable,” she said, adding that she believes Johnson has failed to provide any meaningful check on the president’s power in his role as speaker of the U.S. House. “Mike should work for the American people and not the pedo-in-chief.” 
Earlier this year, Cunningham’s campaign narrowly raised more money than Vasquez’s, according to campaign finance filings. However, Vasquez has maintained a significant cash-on-hand advantage. 
In a statement Wednesday, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee attacked Cunningham’s alliance with Trump.
“You are the company you keep. Greg Cunningham has made Donald Trump and Mike Johnson’s extreme Washington agenda his ‘number one priority,’ so it’s no surprise he’s rolling out the red carpet for the architect of Republicans’ Medicaid cuts, reckless tariffs, and costly war in Iran,” DCCC spokesperson Anna Elsasser said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Making homeownership in Litchfield County affordable, one house at a time
description: Homeownership in Litchfield County isn’t a reality for many families in western CT. Efforts are under way to change that.
text:
Homeownership in Litchfield County isn’t a reality for many middle- and low-income families in western Connecticut. But efforts are under way to make new homes more affordable.
The latest example is a brand-new Cape Cod-style home, which was sold for $280,000 — far below the average price in the area.
The Washington Community Housing Trust helped make it happen.
The house is the eighth of 10 in the works in western Connecticut as part of an affordable housing effort spearheaded by the Litchfield County Center for Housing Opportunity. The initiative also involves nonprofit housing developers in four towns.
The final two homes are expected to be complete by the end of the year, according to center director Jocelyn Ayer.
As the cost of housing has increased statewide, it’s become more difficult to construct homes, Ayer said.
“A long time ago, our local housing nonprofits were able to build these types of homes and then raise just a little bit of money locally and sell them affordably,” Ayer said.
Litchfield County, like all of Connecticut, has an affordability and housing crisis. The four towns included in the Litchfield County Affordable Homeownership Program are Salisbury, Norfolk, Washington and Cornwall.
Eligible families were required to earn below the area median income (AMI) and pre-qualify for a mortgage of at least $200,000.
All the homes are selling between $250,000 and $330,000. That’s compared to an average home sale price between $882,500 and $1.2 million in the four municipalities in 2024.
Homes that sell below these prices are often older, requiring costly renovations and upgrades, Ayer said.
“Because of the cost of construction, the challenging sites in our rural towns, where we have to put in wells and septics, we just really need the additional partnership,” Ayer said.
Washington is home to many New Yorkers with second homes, making the town even less affordable, according to Bill Fairbairn with the Washington Community Housing Trust.
“The old-time money in Washington has sort of died off,” Fairbairn said. “Now we have lots of people who have resources, but aren’t as connected to the community as some of these people back from the ‘50s and ‘60s and ‘70s.”
The housing trust helped make the Cape Cod house in Washington a reality.
The house is on wooded land, requiring land clearing and the installation of home infrastructure, like a septic system. It’s the fourth home built by the housing trust, and Washington’s only home included in the affordable homeownership program.
The house, with three bedrooms and two bathrooms, was bought by a New Milford family with three young children, Fairbairn said.
“The young man works for a roofing company, and they do a lot of work here. So now he’s closer to where he works,” Fairbairn said. “I always felt like you should be able to live in the town that you work in.”
This story was first published Aug. 25, 2026 by Connecticut Public.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Thousands of jobs will bring Space X skeptics around, higher ed leader says
description: Space X is the latest in a series of major projects coming to Louisiana touting numerous high-paying jobs that require specialized training. The state's technical college system is expected to provide much of that training.
text:
Richard Nelson, president of the Louisiana Community and Technical College System, told the state Board of Regents that opponents of the planned SpaceX launch facility in Vermilion Parish will be won over by the number of jobs the facility will provide. The workforce training programs in the LCTCS system are expected to provide the bulk of the training to SpaceX's new hires. (Photo by Greg LaRose/ Louisiana Illuminator)The head of Louisiana’s network of workforce training institutions said the thousands of jobs accompanying the new Space X launch facility in Southwest Louisiana will win over critics who have expressed concerns about the project’s impact on the environment and the immediate community. 
The aerospace company owned by Elon Musk announced plans Tuesday for its $100 billion self-sustaining spaceport in Vermilion Parish near the Pecan Island community, about 50 miles southwest of Lafayette. State officials say it is the largest capital investment in Louisiana history, with estimates for 3,000 permanent jobs at the facility itself — with Musk saying the number could reach 10,000 for the region. 
Richard Nelson, president of the Louisiana Community and Technical College System, told the state Board of Regents he understood that some people might be hesitant to embrace the space industry because of its perceived impacts. 
“The same people that may be resistant to something new probably support something that’s maybe a lot worse for the area, a lot worse for the environment … But it’s fine because it’s been there forever, and their brother-in-law works there or their son works there. So it’s fine,” Nelson said Wednesday at the Regents’ monthly meeting in Baton Rouge. 
“I think once you start seeing that employment actually go to the people that are there, that’s when it changes their life, and they’re going to get on board with it,” he said. 
SpaceX’s plans to launch thousands of rockets a year from what will be called Starbase Louisiana, which wildlife groups say could place native habitat and hurricane protection at risk.
Locals and environmental advocates are concerned about the development’s environmental impact to an already fragile region. Residents of Pecan Island fear noise, air and water pollution will bring to an end to the culture and livelihoods they have known for generations 
Musk’s company has promised to fund coastal restoration and habitat protection in the Acadiana region, along with an annual $25 million combined payment to Vermilion Parish’s school board, sheriff and police jury for the next quarter-century in the place of property taxes.
Space X is the latest in a series of major projects coming to Louisiana touting numerous high-paying jobs that require specialized training. Nelson’s campus network is expected to provide much of that instruction. 
But the workforce demands have also strained the state’s technical and community colleges to educate enough students to ensure the new jobs go to Louisianians. Many of the companies investing in the state have made donations to the schools that will train their local hires, but most of the cost of these new programs still falls on the institutions themselves. 
“We’re being called upon more and more to be responsive in an immediate time frame,” Kristine Strickland, chancellor of Fletcher Technical Community College, said Tuesday at legislative task force meeting on higher education funding. “We do know that standing up new programs is a more expensive venture than maintaining current programs, and then taking those to scale is even more expensive.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Minnesota Truth Council begins process of documenting impact of federal immigration operations
description: A truth council assembled by Gov. Tim Walz heard testimony for the first time Wednesday from people who say they were harmed by the thousands of federal immigration agents sent to Minnesota this winter.  Immigrants and community leaders shared stories, often through tears, about violence and abuse committed against themselves and others during Operation Metr[...]
text:
Pedro Dos Santos, a board member of immigrant rights nonprofit Fe y Justicia, describes immigration agents threatening to ram observers with their cars at a meeting of the Minnesota Truth Council on Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026. (Photo by Madison McVan/Minnesota Reformer)A truth council assembled by Gov. Tim Walz heard testimony for the first time Wednesday from people who say they were harmed by the thousands of federal immigration agents sent to Minnesota this winter. 
Immigrants and community leaders shared stories, often through tears, about violence and abuse committed against themselves and others during Operation Metro Surge and Operation PARRIS, which targeted recently-arrived refugees in Minnesota for re-verification, leading to arrests and deportations. 
Walz established the Minnesota Truth Council via executive order in March. Its mission is to “create a public record of both the harm endured and the generosity and resilience of Minnesotans across the state,” per the executive order. 
Truth councils have long been an important step in the reconciliation process in countries that have experienced human rights violations, said Madeline Lohman of the Advocates for Human Rights, which is running the council.
The council is chaired by retired Hennepin County Judge Peter Cahill, who presided over the murder trial of Minneapolis police officer Derek Chauvin, who was convicted in the killing of George Floyd. The council has no law enforcement power and will produce a report on its findings and policy recommendations for the governor, state Legislature and Congressional delegation.
Minnesota Truth Council Chair Peter Cahill and Vice-Chair Jennifer Prestholdt of The Advocates for Human Rights listen to testimony during the first full meeting of the Minnesota Truth Council on Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026. (Photo by Madison McVan/Minnesota Reformer)
Wednesday’s meeting focused on violations of the U.S. Constitution and the rule of law. 
Pedro Dos Santos, a board member of immigrant rights nonprofit Fe y Justicia, described agents posted outside of rural trailer parks, checking the papers of people driving in and out. Christin Crabtree, a Minneapolis parent who recently won a seat on the school board, recounted the violent arrest in January of a teacher outside of Roosevelt High School and the use of pepper spray on teenagers, hours after an ICE agent killed Renee Good.
Montha Chum, executive director of MN8, a southeast Asian political advocacy group, described an elder who couldn’t chew her food for months because she was scared to go to the dentist for new dentures. 
Imam Yusuf Abdulle, executive director of the Islamic Association of North America, described families experiencing extreme hunger as they sheltered at home for fear of ICE. Rachel Dionne-Thunder, CEO of Indigenous Protector Movement, decried the arrests of indigenous people in Minnesota and agents’ treatment of observers, including following her to her own home. 
“For the original people of these lands to be targeted by immigration enforcement is a testament and shows the truth that these were only and purely racially profiled stops and detainments,” Dionne-Thunder said.
Attorneys said it was difficult to reach clients in detention. Hanne Sandison, immigration and legal services director for The Advocates for Human Rights, described conditions at the Whipple Federal Building, where many immigrants were temporarily held during Operation Metro Surge. Sandison described broken phones and incorrect phone numbers for legal services.
“No one had any of their paperwork. Everyone I saw was shackled at the ankles, even while in the cell, and even while sleeping,” Sandison said. “The people I saw sleeping were on the floor, shackled and with no bedding.”
The council is still accepting stories from people impacted by the immigration operations. Its next meeting featuring testimony is Sept. 9.

title: North Dakota expands drought assistance for livestock
description: North Dakota is making more money available to livestock producers hit by drought conditions after an initial pool of funds quickly dried up.  The State Water Commission on Wednesday approved an additional $2 million for the Drought Disaster Livestock Water Supply Project Assistance Program.   The state made $2 million available last week. The Department of[...]
text:
A little water remains in a stock pond near Marion, North Dakota, on Aug. 1, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Torie Piehl/LaMoure County Extension)North Dakota is making more money available to livestock producers hit by drought conditions after an initial pool of funds quickly dried up. 
The State Water Commission on Wednesday approved an additional $2 million for the Drought Disaster Livestock Water Supply Project Assistance Program.  
The state made $2 million available last week. The Department of Water Resources received more than 220 applications in the first week, and funding would have run out Wednesday if the commission had not acted, according to a news release from the Governor’s Office and the State Water Commission. 
Gov. Kelly Armstrong also issued an amended executive order making the program available to livestock producers in all North Dakota counties, rather than only counties and tribal nations that meet a certain threshold.
Armstrong issued his initial executive order last week.
July heat produces ‘flash drought’ with more than half of North Dakota affected

“The intense demand for this water supply program demonstrates just how serious the drought situation is in North Dakota for our livestock producers,” Armstrong said in a news release.
All but 3.2% of the state is affected by drought or abnormally dry conditions, according to the U.S. Drought Monitor’s Aug. 20 update. It showed 38.6% of North Dakota in moderate drought, 26.4% in severe drought, 5.9% in extreme drought and nearly 26% rated abnormally dry. The drought monitor is updated weekly on Thursdays.
The livestock relief program is funded by oil extraction tax revenue, authorized by the State Water Commission and administered by the Department of Water Resources. Each producer is eligible for cost-share on up to three projects and may be reimbursed up to 65%, but no more than $10,000, of the eligible cost of each project. Eligible projects include new wells, rural water system connections, pipeline extensions and pasture taps.  
Program details, eligibility requirements and application information are available at dwr.nd.gov. Producers seeking more information can call 701-328-4959 or email dwrlivestock@nd.gov. 
Additional information on drought resources and current burn ban restrictions and fire danger levels is available at www.ndresponse.gov.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Sheehy pushes federal support for passenger rail plans in Montana
description: HELENA — As airports grow more crowded, U.S. Sen. Tim Sheehy told Montana residents on Wednesday that passenger rail could help fuel more tourism and economic growth in the Big Sky state. Sheehy, a Republican speaking at the Greater Northwest Rail Summit, also gave an update on legislation that would remove federal match requirements by […]
text:
Sen. Tim Sheehy, R-Montana, speaks during the Greater Northwest Rail Summit on Wednesday, August, 26, 2026. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)HELENA — As airports grow more crowded, U.S. Sen. Tim Sheehy told Montana residents on Wednesday that passenger rail could help fuel more tourism and economic growth in the Big Sky state.
Sheehy, a Republican speaking at the Greater Northwest Rail Summit, also gave an update on legislation that would remove federal match requirements by local governments for long-distance passenger rail corridors during the planning and development phases of those projects. Planning phases, and the resulting improvement projects, would be expensive — and the legislation, introduced earlier this year, would shift the responsibility for funding to the federal government.
Sheehy said that legislation likely would be attached to a larger federal bill.
“I think we have a good shot of that passing,” Sheehy said.
That legislation would matter for the Big Sky Passenger Rail Authority, a multi-jurisdictional Montana government group that’s dedicated to bringing back increased passenger rail service from Chicago to Seattle or Portland. The Great Northwest Rail Summit, a three-day event, has brought over a hundred people from multiple states and countries to discuss railroad issues.
That route, called the Big Sky North Coast Corridor, would go through seven states, including all the way across Montana, with much of the proposed service running through rural areas with small tax bases. The route has locally been called the “southern route” as passenger rail does hit much of the Hi-Line through the Empire Builder train.
Sheehy pointed to the potential economic benefits of the service during a conversation with Missoula County Commissioner Dave Strohmaier, who leads the Big Sky Passenger Rail Authority.
Members of the rail authority have pointed to the potential benefits for Montanans, such as moving from city to city for medical appointments, shopping, recreation and even employment. It’s also being looked at by Sheehy as a potential massive boon for tourism, with the senator joking some Montanans may prefer to see the state’s borders closed.
“The reality is, it’s a huge industry,” Sheehy said. “It’s good for the state economy, and then they’re not going to stop coming. I mean, look out the window. Everyone wants to come here, as they should.
Out-of-state visitors to Montana spent roughly $5.6 billion in 2025. About 1-in-11 Montanans have jobs directly supported by tourist dollars.
But Sheehy also pointed to another industry he’s heavily involved in — aviation. Airports are overcrowded, and the demand for air travel is only increasing, he said.
Cars are one solution, Sheehy said, but so is rail — existing easements and railway infrastructure are already in place, which is how the Big Sky Passenger Rail Authority has approached expanding train service.
“We’re not trying to build a new railroad, we’re not trying to blow new tunnels through mountains, we’re not trying to create a new ecosystem,” Sheehy said. “What we’re saying is we already have the route here. The route exists. The authorities are there. Let’s utilize the existing infrastructure we have. Obviously, some investment will be needed, but this could be a model for helping to do it around the country.”

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: $17 billion Meta settlement lands in hotbed of debate over social media regulations in Mass.
description: A landmark agreement both reshapes Instagram and Facebook for teenagers, and adds fuel to legislative debate about permanent reforms.
text:
TEENAGERS ACROSS THE COUNTRY will soon have a significantly different experience on Instagram and Facebook, and lawmakers in Massachusetts just got a nine-figure incentive to wrap up their work on a social media bill.
In the midst of a nationwide reckoning over the addictiveness of social media platforms, and with Bay State legislation regulating the industry in negotiations, a coalition of attorneys general announced a massive settlement with tech giant Meta that could inform Bay State debates over how companies can verify the ages of their users without tripping into intrusive data collection.
Meta — which owns social media platforms Facebook and Instagram — is settling a landmark case targeting its design features, Attorney General Andrea Campbell announced Wednesday morning. It will pay $17.1 billion altogether to 47 states and enact major reforms to how teenagers use Facebook and Instagram under the terms of the deal awaiting court approval.
Massachusetts is set to receive up to $516 million through the settlement, according to Campbell’s office, including approximately $366 million guaranteed to be paid over the next 10 years.
With the exception of the landmark Big Tobacco settlements of the 1990s, Campbell’s office said this is the largest state consumer protection settlement in history.
“The size of the settlement is not what matters most to me or this team,” Campbell said at a press conference Wednesday. “What matters is that this agreement changes what young people will experience when they open their apps. And I want to be clear that today is not the end of this work. It’s just the beginning.”
The deal between Meta and attorneys general across the country landed as Massachusetts lawmakers continue to deliberate about whether to enshrine permanent restrictions on youth social media use in state law.
Under the settlement, users under 13 will be completely banned from using on Instagram or Facebook. For 13- to 18-year-old users, the platforms will need to implement new protections and keep them in place for at least five years.
These teen users will only be able to access Instagram and Facebook for up to two hours per day, and will be completely blocked between the hours of midnight and 6 a.m. Notifications would also be throttled — shut off entirely between 10 p.m. and 7 a.m., and silenced during standard school hours of 8 a.m. to 3 p.m.
Along with mandatory breaks while using the site for teens, Facebook and Instagram will introduce options to disable “autoplay” and algorithmic feed features, which prosecutors have argued contribute to increased time on the platform. The settlement also eliminates some metrics that can create comparison and unhealthy competition between young users, like publicly visible counts of likes and other reactions on teen users’ posts. It would disable filters that mimic cosmetic surgery, in a gesture to the detrimental effects of young people being constantly exposed to idealized faces and bodies.
“These are not simply promises to do better,” Campbell said. “These are changes to the products themselves to start to make things safer for our kids online.”
But the settlement only binds Meta, not other industry giants like Google or TikTok. And the new protections are guaranteed for a limited period of time, unless the parties agree to continue the terms.
Campbell noted that a lawsuit against TikTok is pending. That company is facing similar allegations that it designed its platform to addict young users and exploit their vulnerabilities.
Meta explicitly called for other social media companies to join in its new commitments, rolling out an “open letter” to TikTok and YouTube. (Neither TikTok nor Google, which owns YouTube, responded to CommonWealth Beacon inquiries Wednesday.)
Meta’s chief legal officer, C.J. Mahoney, said the limits on nighttime and school hour alerts “will only work if all our peers join us.”
“Because teens move fluidly across dozens of apps, we need an industry-wide solution. We therefore call on our industry peers, TikTok and YouTube, to implement this new framework, right away,” Mahoney said in a statement.
Wednesday’s settlement resolves a 2023 lawsuit in Massachusetts arguing that Meta violated state consumer protection laws and caused a public nuisance by purposefully designing its Instagram app to addict young users. The tech giant unsuccessfully argued before the state Supreme Judicial Court that it was shielded from suit by a federal law that protects publishers from being liable for things that third-party users might post.
“That groundbreaking ruling allowed our case to move forward, and Massachusetts leadership helped create the leverage needed to pave the way for today’s agreement,” Campbell said.
She made clear that she still wants state lawmakers to put permanent, industry-wide restrictions on the books, using Wednesday’s press conference to urge the Legislature to finish its work on youth social media bills as well as an effort to ban student cellphone use during the school day.
“We view the settlement as a floor, and we now see these protections as a floor for other tech companies to begin to redesign their platforms to protect our kids,” Campbell said. “We also see it as an opportunity for the Legislature not only to adopt these provisions as the floor, but to go beyond them.”
Attorney General Andrea Campbell (right) and Rep. Alice Pesich (left), who is co-leading legislative negotiations over social media limits for minors, field questions from reporters at an August 26, 2026 press conference about a multi-state settlement with Meta. (Chris Lisinski/CommonWealth Beacon)
Both the House and Senate support taking action to limit social media risks for children and teenagers, but so far, Democrats in the two branches have not yet been able to agree on an approach.
Legislative leaders signaled they will continue to pursue action even with the Meta settlement in place. Senate President Karen Spilka on Wednesday pledged to “build on AG Campbell’s victory and keep working to finalize a comprehensive youth social media protections bill so we can expand upon and implement these protections across the board.”
Sen. Brendan Crighton, who’s leading negotiations over the bills alongside Rep. Alice Peisch, an assistant majority leader on House Speaker Ron Mariano’s leadership team, said the new settlement “bolsters the argument” for legislators to act.
“We were company-neutral in looking at the overall issue around social media in our bill,” Crighton told CommonWealth Beacon. “That was done intentionally, to not go after one company or another.”
“So I don’t think [the settlement] changes our approach,” he added. “Our goal was to create regulations across all platforms, and that remains the goal.”
There’s an unusual clause baked into the agreement that could expand what Meta owes Massachusetts. If other major social media platforms that are not covered by the terms of the settlement, like TikTok and YouTube, implement similar protections for young users and pay the Bay State $150 million, Meta would match that additional funding.
The logic may appear somewhat counterintuitive. But if Meta were the only platform to change its policies, officials said, it would be willing to pay less than it would if the entire industry embraced similar reforms, which minimizes any risk of one company being at a disadvantage. As an AG spokesperson put it, the provision“levels the playing field.”
The requirement could be triggered either by TikTok and YouTube’s voluntary participation, or by legislative action to force every company to play by the same rules.
State lawmakers are already weighing bills that would implement major limits on youth social media use. Now, they could win Massachusetts hundreds of millions of dollars more simply by coming to agreement with each other.
In the meantime, Meta has one year to implement systems to identify users under 13 and users between 13 and 18 with a “high level of accuracy.” The settlement mandates that whatever age verification system is implemented cannot require users to submit government identification or other sensitive information to verify their age, but it does not specify a particular mechanism.
That drops the settlement squarely into an international imbroglio over data privacy and youth safety online.
Online privacy and LGBTQ advocates have criticized similar language in House and Senate social media regulation proposals. Advocacy group Fight for the Future has been calling for lawmakers to strike language requiring social media companies to implement an age assurance system when new accounts are created. This, they say, “would create a substantial barrier for adults to speak anonymously online, raising constitutional and free speech concerns.”
In the Bay State, money paid by Meta will go toward “efforts to remediate the harms caused by social media to Massachusetts young people” as well as to the state’s General Fund. The harm-reduction options may include youth crisis intervention and mental health services; after-school, summer, and outdoor programs; advancing digital wellness and literacy; phone-free school initiatives; and training medical providers on interactive media use and body dysmorphia.
The attorney general also touted agreements to create “enhanced parental supervision tools” allowing parents to turn on protective settings and receive notifications on their teens’ usage, content searches, and contact with adults.
These tools, her office said, would be tied to a unique mechanism. Teen accounts by default would have the strict new limitations, but if they were tethered to a parent’s account, they could have more lenient default protections with the tradeoff of more parental oversight.
In a statement, Mahoney said the negotiated framework “will empower parents to easily manage how their children access our platforms.”
The one-company limitation echoes a settlement in 2024 between Campbell’s office and ride-share tech companies Uber and Lyft, which killed a potential ballot measure to treat drivers for multiple apps – not just Uber and Lyft – as independent contractors in exchange for ending a lawsuit charging the companies with violating state labor law.
While the major industry players Uber and Lyft are bound by the settlement setting new wage and benefit standards, other gig-work companies relying on drivers, like DoorDash and Instacart, were left to operate as usual.
For now, the attorney general’s office and the Legislature are traveling on individual tracks toward similar ends. But the coming months of lawmakers weighing data privacy, social media, and cell phone bills offer plenty of opportunities for policy collisions.
