text:
Everton Blair, a former chair of the Gwinnett County Board of Education, speaks at a candidate forum hosted by the Rockdale County Democratic Committee in Conyers, Georgia, on April 16, 2026. Alander Rocha/Georgia RecorderEverton Blair, a former Gwinnett County Board of Education chair, is headed to Washington to finish out the late Congressman David Scott term representing Georgia’s 13th Congressional District after defeating Marcye Scott, the daughter of the late congressman, in a special election.
As of late Tuesday night, Blair led with about 53% of the vote, according to unofficial results from the Georgia Secretary of State’s Office, while Scott had about 47% of the vote. The Associated Press called the race for Blair at around 8:38 p.m. Tuesday.
Blair, a 34-year-old with a doctorate degree in education from Harvard University, is the second Black openly gay man to be elected to Congress and the first representing a Southern state. He ran a progressive campaign by advocating for Medicare for all, speaking out against Israel’s reliance on U.S. tax dollars and its influence in U.S. politics, and pledging to voters that he would be a voice in Washington against President Donald Trump’s policies.
“People are craving for change. We want better in our communities, and it is time for us to shift from a status quo that, frankly, has not been working for hardworking Americans,” Blair said in a phone interview Tuesday night. “And this election is one of many that is a testament to what can change if you pick visionaries who are ready to enact an agenda that actually works and actually makes government work for hardworking Americans.”

title: Voters reject State Question 844 affecting payments to local governments
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Voters struck down a state question that proposed changes to local government entities’ reimbursements for a manufacturing tax incentive. State Question 844 resoundingly failed in a statewide vote Tuesday. It would have given the state Legislature the authority to recalculate how much to reimburse local governments and school districts for pr[...]
text:
A voter marks his ballot at a polling place in the Millwood High School Field House on June 16 in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Courtney Bell/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Voters struck down a state question that proposed changes to local government entities’ reimbursements for a manufacturing tax incentive.
State Question 844 resoundingly failed in a statewide vote Tuesday.
It would have given the state Legislature the authority to recalculate how much to reimburse local governments and school districts for property tax revenue that new manufacturers are exempt from paying.
“Thanks to 844 being on the ballot, voters are immensely more educated on an expensive program in our Constitution that is also very complicated,” said House Speaker Kyle Hilbert, R-Bristow.
House Speaker Kyle Hilbert speaks in the House chamber of the state Capitol on April 16, 2025, in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
The tax incentive program, which voters enshrined in the state Constitution in 1985, exempts new manufacturing facilities from paying property taxes for five years. The state reimburses county governments, schools and other local entities for the lost tax revenue.
For years, a state fund dedicated to paying for these reimbursements has fallen short of their total cost. The Legislature had to add a $64.8 million supplemental appropriation in the 2025 fiscal year to cover repayments to schools alone.
State lawmakers put SQ 844 on Tuesday’s ballot, arguing the price for these reimbursements has gotten too high and disproportionately benefits a few counties.
The state question asked voters to approve a constitutional amendment to give the Legislature the flexibility to pay local entities less than 100% of the exempted property tax income. 
District leaders have said these reimbursements provide transformative funding for their schools. They claimed that reducing the repayments could have negative implications not only for their districts but for public schools statewide.
Opponents of the state question, Hilbert said, urged lawmakers to “look at qualifications on the front end” of the tax incentive program, not reimbursements to counties after companies qualify.
“Certain industries, like future solar farms, should not qualify for this program but that disqualification should not come at the expense of the local school districts,” he said.
Reporter Emma Murphy contributed to this report.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska officials respond to mystery spill near idled Cook Inlet oil platform
description: State and industry officials and the U.S. Coast Guard were responding on Tuesday to an unexplained oil spill roughly 60 miles southwest of Anchorage in Southcentral Alaska’s Cook Inlet. The spill, which produced a long oil sheen on the water near the Trading Bay area on the western side of the inlet, was first spotted […]
text:
Cook Inlet near Clam Gulch is seen on Oct. 23, 2025. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)State and industry officials and the U.S. Coast Guard were responding on Tuesday to an unexplained oil spill roughly 60 miles southwest of Anchorage in Southcentral Alaska’s Cook Inlet.
The spill, which produced a long oil sheen on the water near the Trading Bay area on the western side of the inlet, was first spotted by a pilot on Monday. His report prompted a multiagency response.
The multiagency unified command is composed of the Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation, the U.S. Coast Guard and Hilcorp, the dominant oil and gas operator in Cook Inlet.
The sheen was seen near the idled Spark platform, one of 17 oil and gas platforms in the inlet. Six of those, including Spark, are now inactive. The Spark platform was acquired by Hilcorp as part of its 2012 purchase of Marathon Oil’s Cook Inlet assets. It has been inactive since 1992, said a statement issued by the unified command responding to the spill. The wells associated with the Spark platform were plugged and abandoned by a previous owner in 2009, the statement said.
As of Tuesday afternoon, however, the ongoing investigation has not pinpointed a source of the spill, its size or even the substance, DEC officials said.
An oil-response vessel sent by Hilcorp to the site arrived shortly after 2 a.m. on Tuesday, but its crew was not able to spot the sheen with infrared imaging technology, said the incident command statement. The spill-response vessel, the Endeavor, has been sailing in a grid pattern to search for the spilled material and its possible source, the statement said.

A closeup view of a 2022 Alaska Division of Oil and Gas map shows the pipelines and oil and gas platform locations in Cook Inlet. (Map provided by the Alaska Division of Oil and Gas)

There were no reports of impacts to fish or wildlife as of Tuesday afternoon, said a DEC situation report issued on Tuesday afternoon.
Fish could be potentially at risk, the situation report said. All five species of Pacific salmon swim in the affected waters, and coho and sockeye salmon were migrating through the area at the time the spill was reported, the situation report said.
Representatives of area environmental groups said Tuesday that the event was a warning about risks to the inlet.
Satchel Pondolfino, the clean water lead for Cook Inletkeeper, said she and others are concerned about the apparent association with the idled but still-standing Spark platform.
“It’s just another reason why it’s so important that Alaska use its authority to hold Hilcorp and every other operator accountable for dismantling the infrastructure,” she said.
Activists have called for the removal of such unused infrastructure from the inlet, but the state so far has not ordered any company to do that.
Cooper Freeman, Alaska director of the Center for Biological Diversity, said numerous natural resources continue to be at risk from the incident and others like it.
“It’s gut-wrenching to see the inlet’s beleaguered salmon and belugas take a hit they can’t afford from a miles-long oil spill,” he said in an emailed statement. “We need Cook Inlet’s fish and wildlife to recover, and we can’t keep treating their home like an industrial waste zone. This is yet another wake-up call that our over-reliance on fossil fuels imperils not just our region’s long-term energy stability, but the vitality of our environment for all future Alaskans.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Darline Graham wins GOP nomination for next US Senate term following her brother’s death
description: COLUMBIA — Voters elected Darline Graham to take her late brother’s place on November ballots, as the full backing of President Donald Trump helped overcome criticism of her political inexperience. When The Associated Press called the GOP runoff election at 9 p.m., Graham had 52% of the vote over U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman, with 89% […]
text:
U.S. Sen. Darline Graham speaks to reporters Tuesday, Aug. 11, 2026, in Columbia, South Carolina, after leading the special GOP primary. (Photo by John A. Carlos II/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — Voters elected Darline Graham to take her late brother’s place on November ballots, as the full backing of President Donald Trump helped overcome criticism of her political inexperience.
When The Associated Press called the GOP runoff election at 9 p.m., Graham had 52% of the vote over U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman, with 89% of votes counted.
Graham’s win ensures the first elected female U.S. senator from South Carolina will be sworn into office in January. Sworn in exactly six weeks ago as the appointed senator, Graham faces Democrat Annie Andrews in the general election.
The 62-year-old younger sister of the late U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham led the 10-candidate primary two weeks ago with 33% to Norman’s 25%. But a runoff win was far from guaranteed. Some polls showed Norman ahead hours before polls opened.
“We did everything we could do,” Norman said to a round of applause from supporters at his election watch party in Rock Hill.
Trump, who urged Darline Graham to seek the next six-year term, pitched her candidacy as a tribute to her brother, his best friend: Lindsey Graham died suddenly July 11 in Washington, D.C., of a ruptured aorta, one month after trouncing five GOP opponents on his way to a fifth term.
“She’s the perfect person to carry on the legacy of her brother,” Trump told people who called in to a tele-rally Monday night.
His all-in endorsement included traveling to ruby red Myrtle Beach, where he told thousands of supporters Friday to pretend his name is on the ballot. Voting for Graham, he said, is voting for someone who “fully supports the Trump agenda.”
He recognized he would take the credit or blame. “I asked her to do it. I got her into this whole thing,” he said Monday night. “I have to make sure she gets in because there will be nobody better.”
In a state where Trump won every time he was actually on the ballot, the runoff results were expected to reflect his strength or waning influence. In November 2024, Trump won South Carolina by 18 percentage points. When Trump got behind Graham’s candidacy pre-filing, political commentators outside South Carolina assumed that made her a shoo-in.
But Trump’s surprise pick of a political novice caused many South Carolina voters to rebel. Graham was expected to be the honorary placeholder — an appointment that gave no one the benefit of incumbency in South Carolina’s first open Senate race in 22 years — not the handpicked successor.
Norman attempted to turn that into an advantage. The support and money lining up behind Graham “shows the elite establishment has already picked their candidate. Same ol’ playbook. Same ol’ insiders. I’m not their choice,” he said in an ad.
Following an unsuccessful campaign for governor when he sought the outsider label — repeatedly saying he’s not a career politician — Norman juxtaposed his record over more than two decades in elected office against Graham’s lack of political experience. He’s the proven conservative, he argued: “You know how I’m going to vote.”
Graham embraced her status as unskilled at being a politician.
“They say I’m not a politician. I say guilty as charged,” she repeated Monday night.
Norman, first elected to the state House in 2004, has won two previous special elections, including the 2017 race that sent him to Congress. He opted to seek the governor’s office this year instead of re-election to the U.S. House but placed third in the June GOP primary.
She used that against him.
“He’s run for office 14 times, always chasing the next office. To me, this is just desperation,” Graham told callers Monday. “I am not a career politician.”
She pointed to 30 years of experience in state government, to include the last seven leading the state Commission for the Blind. And she emphasized her humble roots in relating to Americans’ economic struggles, saying that, like her brother, a childhood growing up in the back of her parents’ restaurant and pool hall also instilled a hard work ethic.
“Whatever it was that made Lindsey strong has made her strong,” Gov. Henry McMaster said during a campaign event with her Monday. The perspective she gained in her roles helping people with disabilities is also a strength, he added.
McMaster, who appointed her last month for the term ending in January, endorsed her for the full term on Friday, just before the Trump rally.
He called Graham the better candidate for keeping the Senate seat red.
“Keep this in mind: There is another election after this one,” McMaster said. “We’ve got to win this election in order to win that election in November.”
Norman supporters
For David and Ann Casey of Rock Hill, their votes for Norman came down to time spent in office. They also wanted someone who could push back against Trump.
“Darline’s a great person, but my vote was more for experience,” said Ann Casey, a 63-year-old dental hygienist, after voting at a church off Interstate 77 in Rock Hill.
“I had concern about Darline being a ‘yes’ person to the Trump administration,” added David Casey, a 64-year-old financial advisor. “(Norman’s) capable of hitting the ground running, and he’s not going to be told what to do.”
Graham’s non-response to a question about Taiwan during the only runoff debate sunk her for some voters.
Matthew Gusmer, a farmer in western York County, supported Norman in the governor’s race and in Senate GOP primary two weeks ago but was on the fence about whether to continue supporting him in the runoff — that is, until Graham’s performance in the Aug. 18 debate in Newberry.
“Probably the number one thing that swayed me was in the debate the other night with her comment about foreign policy,” he said.
Asked whether Taiwan is a national security issue for the United States, Graham blanked, eventually acknowledging she’s not informed on the issue.
“I’m just going to be honest up here,” she said. “I’m not a polished politician. National security is not my thing, not my area of expertise.”
“That really just kind of floored me,” Gusmer said. “With everything going on between Russia, Iran, every front, it just really turned me off.”
As a farmer, Gusmer said foreign policy and the impact it can have on things such as prices at the pump, fertilizer, and seed, as well as the cost of land in fast-growing South Carolina, are major issues and he wants a candidate who is well-informed.
Voters for Graham
For Graham’s supporters, her lack of political experience was a plus.
“I like the fact that she’s not a politician,” said Tommy Wood, a 66-year-old engineer from Irmo. “She’s not seeking the job, so she’s willing to serve, where all the opponents are wanting the job.”
Graham kept the same staff as her brother, which brings their institutional knowledge, Wood said. He and his wife, Phyllis Wood, were longtime supporters of Lindsey Graham.
“That’s invaluable,” Tommy Wood said.
When the Woods watched Graham flub an answer on Taiwan during the GOP debate, they felt bad for her, but their opinions never swayed, they said.
They consider themselves politically inclined and don’t think they’d be able to come up with an answer on the fly, so they were sympathetic, they said.
“She was nervous and blindsided, and it didn’t look good,” said Tommy Wood. But, as he heard someone else say, “I don’t care if she knows the difference between Taiwan and Timmonsville,” a tiny town in Florence County.
The couple noted Norman ran for Senate only after losing the nomination for governor. If he wanted to be a senator, he should have made that his primary goal, they said.
“I didn’t like that,” said Phyllis Wood. “Not cool,” Tommy Wood added.
Sandra and John Jackson, of West Columbia, felt her support for South Carolina is more important than her opinions on foreign policy.
“She’s going to keep South Carolina at the forefront of her mission in Washington, D.C.,” said Sandra Jackson, a 69-year-old retired flight attendant.
What Graham lacks in political experience, she makes up for in life experience, the Jacksons said.
“She’s a mother, and she’s run the Commission for the Blind,” Sandra Jackson said. “She has experience.”
“Anybody who runs for office for the first time doesn’t have any experience,” added 78-year-old John Jackson.
Jessica Holdman contributed to this report from Rock Hill, and Skylar Laird contributed from Columbia.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: New testing has Utah worried about zebra mussel spread in the Colorado River
description: Utah wildlife managers say fragments of invasive zebra mussel DNA have been found in a stretch of the Colorado River near Moab.
text:
An employee of the Utah Department of Natural Resources at work to monitor for aquatic invasive species in the Colorado River. (Courtesy of the Utah Division of Wildlife Resources)In an unfortunate first, state wildlife managers say fragments of invasive zebra mussel DNA have been found in a stretch of the Colorado River near Moab. 
The discovery is concerning because the tiny striped mussels pose an outsized threat to rivers and lakes, clogging pipes, covering beaches with razor-sharp shells and damaging ecosystems. The Division of Wildlife Resources wants Utahns and visitors to take extra care not to spread them this year while rafting, boating, paddleboarding or kayaking.
“There is no time like right now to get serious about this threat,” said Trina Hedrick, the division’s sportfish coordinator, in a prepared statement. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The department sees the mussels as an emerging threat after an infestation was recorded near Loma, Colorado last year. And while detection of DNA in the water indicates the presence of an animal somewhere upstream, the division said it does not confirm that living mussels are present in the test area.
Tiny zebra mussels pose an outsized threat to rivers and lakes. (Amy Benson, Wetland and Aquatic Research Center)
As primary users of the Colorado River, rafters and other nonmotorized boaters are the first line of defense in helping reduce the risk, Hedrick said. But she’s still encouraging all boaters to clean, drain, and dry their watercraft when moving from one lake or river to the next.
The Utah Division of Wildlife Resources began sampling for invasive mussels in the Colorado River last year. The agency set up its testing equipment 14 miles downstream of Moab this summer, where it took samples daily for analysis by the U.S. Geological Survey. Four of 22 samples tested positive for zebra mussel DNA in June and July, after earlier specimens from other points along the river did not. 
The mussels, originally from Russia, were brought to North America almost 40 years ago by a transatlantic ship and spread to all five Great Lakes within 10 years, according to the U.S. Geological Survey.
As this summer comes to a close, the state is reminding adventurers planning to launch any watercraft in the river — even a paddle board — that they need to complete Utah’s annual mussel-aware boater course first. 
Those launching motorized boats must also pay an annual fee that funds state measures to keep the aquatic pests from spreading around Utah.

title: Gov. Gianforte, First Lady mourn passing of Dolly Parton
description: Gov. Greg Gianforte and Montana First Lady Susan Gianforte mourned Tuesday the death of entertainer and philanthropist Dolly Parton. Parton died Tuesday at the age of 80, according to the Tennessee Lookout. She had experienced recent health issues, but her nephew, who announced news of her death, said she died peacefully, according to the Los […]
text:
Dolly Parton on stage in Nashville, Tennessee, on March 20, 2025, at the premiere of “Dolly Parton’s Threads: My Songs in Symphony.” Hailing from East Tennessee, Parton’s songwriting, savvy, charm and philanthropy made her a beloved figure globally. (Photo by Jason Kempin/Getty Images)Gov. Greg Gianforte and Montana First Lady Susan Gianforte mourned Tuesday the death of entertainer and philanthropist Dolly Parton.
Parton died Tuesday at the age of 80, according to the Tennessee Lookout.
She had experienced recent health issues, but her nephew, who announced news of her death, said she died peacefully, according to the Los Angeles Times.
“We join the nation and world in remembering Dolly Parton and mourning the loss of a global icon who dedicated her life to inspiring a love of reading in young children, leaving an incredible mark on millions of families across the nation and right here in Montana,” the Gianfortes said in a statement. “Dolly’s warmth, generosity, and passion for learning have brought stories, joy and opportunity into thousands of Montana homes. Her legacy as a champion for children will continue to inspire us all for generations to come.”
Since launching in 1995, Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library has become the “preeminent early childhood book-gifting program in the world,” said the press release from the Governor’s Office.
The flagship program of The Dollywood Foundation has gifted more than 332 million free books in five countries. Every enrolled child receives one high-quality book per month, at no cost to families, no matter their income, according to the Imagination Library.
In June 2023, the first lady joined the Dollywood Foundation in announcing the statewide expansion of Imagination Library in Montana, the news release said. Through the partnership, Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library provides a free book each month to any Montana child, up to age five, who is registered with the organization.
Today, Imagination Library of Montana has 58 partners in all 56 counties serving nearly 30,000 children, about one in two of the state’s eligible children, according to the Governor’s Office. To date, more than 970,000 books have been mailed in Montana since the expansion, the news release said.
Gianforte ordered all flags in the state of Montana to fly at half-staff from Tuesday, Aug. 25, at 6 p.m. until Tuesday, Sept. 1, following President Donald Trump’s order to lower flags in honor of the country music star, the news release said.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Gianforte’s energy task force calls for PSC reform
description: The No. 1 recommendation from Gov. Greg Gianforte’s energy task force is to consider an appointed instead of elected Montana Public Service Commission. Another recommendation is that the Montana Legislature and executive branch ensure the state has coordinated leadership on energy — possibly by bringing state agency leaders together into a formal group. Tues[...]
text:
The No. 1 recommendation from Gov. Greg Gianforte’s energy task force is to consider an appointed instead of elected Montana Public Service Commission.
Another recommendation is that the Montana Legislature and executive branch ensure the state has coordinated leadership on energy — possibly by bringing state agency leaders together into a formal group.
Tuesday, the Governor’s Office released a report from a task force Gianforte commissioned in September 2025 to address how Montana can increase the supply of affordable and reliable energy to meet rising demand and protect consumers.
In the report, the governor notes demand for electricity across the West is projected to increase by more than 20% in the next decade.
The report offers seven recommendations, including ones for the 2027 Montana Legislature to take up, and the governor said the strategies will help guide the state’s energy future.
“You have delivered a thoughtful, serious and practical report that addresses that question and confirms that Montana is well-positioned to lead,” Gianforte said in a statement Tuesday.
The first recommendation, to have Public Service Commissioners be appointed instead of elected, is already being discussed as a draft bill in at least one form, said Sen. Chris Pope, a Bozeman Democrat and member of the task force.
The PSC is made up of five commissioners elected by district and currently all Republican.
Pope said as individuals, members of the PSC are working hard and dedicated to public service, but as a team, the group has fallen “significantly short” and needs “more horsepower” when it comes to clear strategic outcomes for energy.
One hurdle to an appointed commission for Democrats is the governor is currently a Republican, and Democrats won’t want to hand him that power, Pope said. But he said the state needs to depoliticize energy. 
“There needs to be a significant expectation that our Public Service Commissioners are some of the finest, most learned citizens in the state of Montana as it comes to energy policy from the start,” Pope said.
PSC Vice President Jennifer Fielder said she disagreed reform should come in the form of appointed commissioners.
Rather, Fielder said she believes elected officials need a better way to be accountable to professional standards, and the legislature could help by essentially outlining job expectations in statute.
In the past year, the PSC has been dealing with allegations of professional misconduct against Commissioner Brad Molnar. Gianforte suspended Molnar for one year, but Molnar is fighting the suspension.
“Some people (commissioners) believe you’re a free agent with no accountability,” said Fielder, who noted she was expressing her own opinion, not any position of the PSC. “If the legislature were to place accountability standards in statute with provisions for elected officials, I think it would be a win-win.”
Fielder said she has not had time to give the idea her full attention yet but believes it would resolve some of the concerns about the PSC.
The commission is addressing significant cases, including how to handle data centers and the proposed merger of NorthWestern Energy with Black Hills Corp of South Dakota.
The report from the energy task force also recommended energy leadership be appropriately organized in Montana, and Rep. Gary Parry, a Colstrip Republican, said he’s working on that proposal.
Parry, a member of the task force, said few states in the nation don’t have some type of energy authority, a body that will “steer our ship for the future.”
The report said the executive branch, including the PSC, Department of Environmental Quality, Department of Commerce, and other entities should establish an agreement to coordinate energy functions.
Parry said part of the idea is to bring together people who are working at the top levels of industry, environment and energy to set the direction for Montana’s energy future.
“We have an opportunity to either be at the table and be able to chart our own destiny or we’re going to be on the menu,” Parry said.
The report outlined a variety of other recommendations from the Unleashing American-Made Energy Task Force, including the following:

Advance regional markets and transmission development. Have the executive branch provide long-term energy policy leadership, coordinate infrastructure planning and facilitate public-private partnerships.
Drive economic development including by having the executive branch secure support from the U.S. Department of Energy to attract new industry, advanced manufacturing and value added resource development. Clarify how utilities serve large loads such as data centers.
“Right-size” the energy tax framework. Ensure policies encourage investment in electric transmission, natural gas infrastructure and energy generation and storage. Implement energy tax policies that are predictable and preserve Montana’s pro-growth policy.
Build innovative, reliable power supply. Cut geothermal permitting red tape, advance private sector partnerships to support geothermal power development, and develop policy to support nuclear energy development.
Optimize grid utilization and control consumer energy costs. Increase options for households and small businesses to manage energy costs with investments and reduce barriers to private sector investment in energy-saving technologies.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Montana ag groups hammer Trump beef imports
description: President Donald Trump has announced that 300,000 metric tons of product for ground beef to be imported without a tariff quota for the next 90 days and it has been met with criticism both in Montana and beyond. Agricultural advocacy organizations immediately hammered the plan and even some Republican politicians have been critical of the […]
text:
A cow southeast of Dillon, MT, near Sweetwater Basin is pictured in this 2019 photo. (USDA photo / Lance Cheung)President Donald Trump has announced that 300,000 metric tons of product for ground beef to be imported without a tariff quota for the next 90 days and it has been met with criticism both in Montana and beyond.
Agricultural advocacy organizations immediately hammered the plan and even some Republican politicians have been critical of the plan, including Montana’s Sen. Tim Sheehy.
“I’ve advised President Trump against this course of action for a year because American ranchers have been struggling against the packer monopoly for decades, and this will further harm them – most of whom are MAGA Republicans,” Sheehy, a Republican, posted on X.
He said Trump’s “heart is in the right place” for trying to lower food prices, but the “reality is this action will make it more difficult for American ranchers to rebuild our herd and bring prices down for the American people.”
The rest of Montana’s all-Republican federal delegation have been against the move as well.
“Importing foreign beef is only going to hurt our ranchers and increase prices over the long-term,” Sen. Steve Daines said on X.
Montana Cattleman’s Association President Tim Brunner said in a post that, “if you think you can rebuild a national cow herd in 90 days, I’ve got some heifer calves to sell you.”
Ranchers and farmers across the West have been dealing with severe, years-long drought that has made it difficult for cattle producers to rebuild their herds. Both cattle and the things they feed on need water to grow and with a limited supply, there can only be so many cows and so much good rangeland.
In the summer, a cow can drink 20 to 30 gallons of water per day which is fine if the ponds and streams are full on a rancher’s land and the cows can water themselves. It becomes far more difficult when watering cattle begins to involve tanker trucks and hours of work.
“This is a critical time of year for cattle producers, as we approach the season where they are making decisions regarding their herds,” National Cattlemen’s Beef Association Chief Executive Officer Colin Woodall said in a statement. “Cattle farmers and ranchers are responding to strong market signals and historically high demand, and we are already working to rebuild after years of ongoing drought, high input costs and other challenges that have reduced U.S. cattle numbers.”
Montana ranks sixth in the nation in terms of cattle production, with 1.25 million cows, out of an estimated national herd of 27.8 million in 2025. That means Montana represents about 4.5% of the overall beef production, with Texas leading the way at more than 4 million cows.
Walt Schweitzer, president of the Montana Farmers Union and a rancher, said the added beef will represent about 3% of the total beef supply this year in the United States. America is on pace to import about 30% of all beef consumed in-country, he added.
Cattle prices dropped almost immediately, which Schweitzer — who has been highly critical of the four packing companies that control the majority of the American meat market — took to mean that the packing companies might have had some advance knowledge of the deal.
Whatever deal Trump made to import the beef has also not been transparent, Schweitzer added. It’s led to plenty of speculation and little clarity.
“The consumers are going to go to the grocery store and they’re going to buy burger out of the meat counter that is most likely imported, but they’re going to pay the same price,” Schweitzer said Tuesday, “And the only people that are going to make money are the packers, and and it probably is going to be primarily JBS and the Brazilian cartel, because they’re the ones that have that kind of quantity of of scraps available to to fill this market.”
The American Farm Bureau Federation, the nation’s largest agricultural advocacy organization (representing more than 5 million people) came out against the announcement as well. The Farm Bureau represents the interests of many large agricultural and food production businesses. Montana’s chapter expressed its frustration as well.
“Despite high beef prices in grocery stores, prices paid to farmers and ranchers for their cattle have fallen sharply over the past two months, and beef packing plants are shutting down across the U.S. further undercutting a fragile recovery by swamping markets with foreign products and attempting to manipulate prices threatens to wipe out any progress that has been made,” AFBF President Zippy Duvall said in a statement.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Enbridge Line 5 leaks natural gas near Saxon in Iron County
description: A section of the Enbridge Line 5 pipeline leaked natural gas liquid on Tuesday morning near the town of Saxon. Both the Department of Natural Resources (DNR) and Enbridge have confirmed the leak with Wisconsin Examiner, drone video of which is circulating social media showing plumes of smoke or mist-like vapor pouring out and covering […]
text:
(File photo by Laina G. Stebbins/Michigan Advance)A section of the Enbridge Line 5 pipeline leaked natural gas liquid on Tuesday morning near the town of Saxon. Both the Department of Natural Resources (DNR) and Enbridge have confirmed the leak with Wisconsin Examiner, drone video of which is circulating social media showing plumes of smoke or mist-like vapor pouring out and covering an area with parked trucks and construction equipment. 
The leak was caused when a truck — which Enbridge said was unoccupied — rolled over an open excavation site for a Line 5 valve project, over a natural gas transmission line. The leak occurred in rural Iron County. This section of Line 5 was not carrying crude oil. 
Both Enbridge and the DNR said in email statements that no one was injured, though Enbridge stated that nearby rural homes were evacuated as a precaution. The DNR said that the valve project was struck around 10 a.m. on Tuesday, and that Enbridge reported the accident to the federal Environmental Protection Agency’s National Response Center at 11:02 a.m. and the DNR spills hotline at 11:15 a.m.. 
The fire department and Stantec are on site monitoring the air. The line was shut down to prevent further leaks, and the DNR stated work is underway to calculate exactly how much natural gas was released. In a social media post, Iron County Sheriff Paul Samardich said that Sitan Road is closed until further notice, and that a temporary no-fly zone zone has been established in the area. There is also an associated temporary power outage, the sheriff wrote, adding  that local residents should “follow instructions from emergency personnel.”
Enbridge Line 5 has been at the center of controversy for years. Environmental advocates and tribal communities argue that the decades-old Canadian pipeline perpetuates an over-reliance on fossil fuels in a time when communities need to move towards clean and renewable energy sources. A federal judge ruled that Enbridge was trespassing on the sovereign land of the Bad River Band of Lake Superior Chippewa in 2013, prompting a plan to reroute the pipeline around the reservation, which has also been contested. 
The Band and its allies say that the pipeline needs to be shut down as the possibility of oil or gas leaks threaten sensitive ecosystems as well as the Bad River watershed which the tribe and other communities rely on. Supporters of Line 5 and Enbridge say that the company helps maintain American energy supplies and jobs.
Jadine Sonoda, campaign coordinator for Sierra Club of Wisconsin, said that the most recent gas leak is an example of the pipeline’s issues. “This is yet another disaster by Enbridge and their Line 5 pipeline,” Sonoda said Tuesday in an emailed statement. “Just last week, Enbridge argued in court that our concerns about the damage of the construction of the Line 5 reroute, on the wetlands, waters, and nearby communities were unwarranted. They argued that the project is complicated, but they’ve got it under control — yet days later, people are being evacuated from their homes due to poisonous natural gas in the air.” 
Sonoda asked, “How many more disasters will it take for Wisconsin leaders to put a stop to this? How many many people will be harmed before our state regulators finally hold this massive corporate polluter accountable? We want to thank the monitors who alerted people to this right away, and the first responders who are helping people to safety.”

name: Georgia Recorder
title: GOP lawmakers call for more oversight of license plate cameras after string of misuses in Georgia
description: A pair of influential Republican lawmakers are calling for greater oversight into the use of automatic license plate readers that critics say allow law enforcement officers to illegally surveil Georgia residents. Sen. John Albers, a Roswell Republican who chairs the Senate’s public safety committee, said he is working with the Georgia Sheriffs’ Association a[...]
text:
Flock Safety license plate readers are typically mounted on tall poles, with a camera and solar panel on top. The company says its technology is used in more than 6,000 communities across 49 states in partnership with thousands of law enforcement agencies nationwide. (Photo courtesy of Flock Safety)A pair of influential Republican lawmakers are calling for greater oversight into the use of automatic license plate readers that critics say allow law enforcement officers to illegally surveil Georgia residents.
Sen. John Albers, a Roswell Republican who chairs the Senate’s public safety committee, said he is working with the Georgia Sheriffs’ Association and the Georgia Association of Chiefs of Police on a new task force to examine how best to address misuse of the cameras, which are manufactured by companies like the Atlanta-based Flock Safety. 
“We have to be smart, we have to be balanced and we have to be thoughtful as we work together to both have both short and long-term solutions,” he said during a Tuesday press conference at the state Capitol.
In a letter to the state law enforcement groups, Senate President Pro Tempore Larry Walker, a Perry Republican, raised questions in response to “the rise in public concern.” 
Walker wrote that “recent allegations of improper use – resulting in stalking, misidentification, and unjustified arrests – have understandably heightened privacy and accountability concerns for our constituents.” 
Flock Safety tightens safeguards as states, cities question surveillance network

Automatic license plate readers, such as the ones made by Flock, work by capturing license plate data, along with other information like a car’s make and color, and storing that information in a searchable database. Law enforcement agencies that have contracts with Flock can use the database to track down stolen vehicles, locate missing people and solve other crimes.
However, the technology is not without controversy. According to the Georgia Bureau of Investigation, at least 14 people have been arrested and charged this year for misusing a state law that restricts use of the cameras to only official law enforcement purposes. 
Albers cited instances of misuse in an op-ed he wrote calling for greater oversight of the technology. While law enforcement deserves effective tools for fighting crime, he wrote that “backing the blue does not mean ‘writing a blank check’ for government surveillance.”
Sen. John Albers. Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder
He also wrote in the op-ed that he is working with the state law enforcement leaders to identify more ways to tighten up the system and left open the possibility of pursuing a legislative fix next year. 
Flock CEO Garrett Langley recently announced that the company would be bolstering its safety guardrails, including lowering the amount of time that license plate data can be stored in a database from 30 days to seven, automatically suspending users who appear to be misusing the system and requiring police officers to input case number or specify what type of crime they are screening for when searching through the database.
But Christopher Bruce, the ACLU of Georgia’s deputy executive director, said he remains skeptical that the company’s new measures will go far enough to prevent misuse of the system.
Adopting laws that require municipalities with Flock contracts to be more transparent with communities about how their data is used and disclose any instances of misuse, Bruce said, could be one way to ensure that there is public accountability.
“You can have the right to privacy and the right to public safety. It doesn’t have to be compromised,” he said. “We can do this, but there has to be guardrails around surveillance.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Here are the officials of Nebraska’s likely new political parties
description: Nebraska Secretary of State has informed the Supreme Court that he plans to certify the parties on Thursday unless the court orders otherwise
text:
The backroom of the Lancaster County Election Commission office on April 24, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Two new Nebraska political parties have submitted their constitutions and leadership to the Secretary of State’s Office as the next formal step toward becoming official parties in the state. 
The Nebraska Working People Party and America First Party still await a ruling from the state Supreme Court on appeals by the state’s Democratic and Republican parties after a lower-court judge dismissed their objections. Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen has informed the Supreme Court that he plans to certify the parties on Thursday unless the court orders otherwise, according to a letter obtained by the Examiner.
The Nebraska Supreme Court accepted the cases and received briefs earlier this week. It’s unclear which races will have candidates from these two new parties, but the deadline to file names for the Nov. 3 general election is Sept. 1.
The chairperson for the Nebraska Working People Party is Robin Richards, followed by Joe Hunter as the vice chair. Vincent Ruksta is the party’s treasurer; Melissa Harbison is the secretary.  
The America First Party chairperson is John Cartier. Kimberly Bowling-Martin is the vice chair; the secretary is John Knight and Devin Specht is the party’s treasurer. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Both parties have caused an uproar among Republicans and Democrats. Democrats have issues with Richards’ involvement with the Working People Party because State Democratic Party Chair Jane Kleeb has accused U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts of being behind the effort to establish the party, which his top political consultant has denied.
John Cartier of Lincoln, left, and Robin Richards of Ralston respectively led creation of the America First Party and Nebraska Working People Party. (Photos courtesy of John Cartier, Robin Richards and the respective political parties | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Richards, a registered Democrat, endorsed incumbent Republican state Sen. Merv Riepe for the general election after losing as a write-in candidate in Legislative District 12 earlier this year.
Republicans have pointed to Cartier’s connection to Legal Marijuana Now Senate candidate Mike Marvin, who has suspended his campaign and endorsed nonpartisan U.S. Senate candidate Dan Osborn. In its lawsuit, the GOP called Cartier’s effort to establish the America First Party “political sabotage.”
Cartier, in his affidavit for the case, wrote that he is no longer the treasurer for Marvin as of Aug. 14. Cartier also wrote that he was the attorney for Osborn’s 2024 Senate campaign.
Kleeb told the Omaha World-Herald that she believes Richards, Douglas County District Court Clerk Crystal Rhoades and other disaffected Democrats are playing into Ricketts’ hands in his Senate race against Osborn. 
Rhoades has denied any involvement with the Nebraska Working People Party.
At the Nebraska Democratic Central Committee meeting Sunday, Rhoades tried to offer a motion to nominate Kishla Askins to replace Cindy Burbank, who dropped out of the Senate race. Askins had been a candidate in the 2nd Congressional District Democratic primary. 
The Democratic Party committee voted not to fill the vacancy caused by Burbank. William Forbes, who lost to Burbank in the Senate primary, is suing the party to try to force them to name a new candidate. 
The general election is Nov. 3.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: ICE arrests in Minnesota return to pre-surge levels while soaring nationwide
description: Immigration enforcement in Minnesota has returned to pre-Operation Metro Surge levels, according to newly released federal data obtained by the Deportation Data Project. At the same time, federal immigration agents are arresting more immigrants nationwide than before, with the data showing nearly 50,000 arrests in July — higher than any previous month in the[...]
text:
ICE agents search the passenger of a truck as they arrest both him and the driver during a traffic stop Wednesday, Feb. 11, 2026 on Bottineau Blvd. in Robbinsdale. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Immigration enforcement in Minnesota has returned to pre-Operation Metro Surge levels, according to newly released federal data obtained by the Deportation Data Project.
At the same time, federal immigration agents are arresting more immigrants nationwide than before, with the data showing nearly 50,000 arrests in July — higher than any previous month in the Trump administration.
Over half of those July arrests came from just four states: Texas, Florida, California and Georgia.


With new tactics, ICE reaches new high in monthly arrests

Minnesota, which had the fourth-highest number of arrests in January, dropped to 32nd among all states in immigration arrests in July. In January, over 3,000 federal agents were sent to Minnesota and arrested 2,441 immigrants, according to the data. That figure dropped significantly after the surge’s announced end in February; federal agents arrested fewer than 250 immigrants every month from March to July.
The Deportation Data Project obtained arrests data from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement via a Freedom of Information Act request. The data has some limitations — around 5% of arrests do not show where the arrest was made, for example. Still, it is some of the most detailed data on immigration enforcement available.
ICE has previously challenged the accuracy of the Deportation Data Project, even though the figures comes from its own internal data.


The numbers from the most recent Deportation Data Project release are similar but not the same as figures reported directly by the feds: Stateline reported that the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, said it arrested about 51,000 immigrants in July.
The number of arrests in Minnesota matches trends observed by Nick Benson, an activist who tracks ICE flights out of Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport, who recorded fewer people being deported in recent months compared to the surge’s peak in January.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Maryland Supreme Court refuses to hear appeal of D.C. sniper Lee Boyd Malvo
description: The Maryland Supreme Court declined to hear Lee Boyd Malvo's attempt to withdraw his guilty plea to six counts of first-degree murder in the D.C. sniper attacks that terrorized the Washington area for three weeks in 2002.
text:
The Maryland Courts of Appeals Building in Annapolis. (File photo by Bennett Leckrone/Maryland Matters)The Maryland Supreme Court declined to hear Lee Boyd Malvo’s attempt to withdraw his guilty plea to six counts of first-degree murder in the D.C. sniper attacks that terrorized the Washington area for three weeks in 2002.
The court, without comment Friday, let stand lower court rulings that said Malvo is not entitled to have those charges vacated because of an impasse between Maryland and Virginia. That impasse, in which Virginia is refusing to hand over Malvo until he serves four consecutive life sentences for murders there, means Malvo cannot have a resentencing hearing that had been ordered the by Maryland Supreme Court.
“Looks like Malvo has exhausted all of his Maryland sentencing appeal options,” former Maryland Attorney General Doug Gansler said over text. Gansler was the Montgomery County State’s Attorney who originally prosecuted Malvo in the Maryland cases.
“His only recourse for ever being released in Maryland would be a gubernatorial pardon,” he added. “That said, it is unlikely he would ever be released in Virginia so the point is essentially moot.”
Malvo was 17 in 2002 when he and John Allen Muhammad, who was then 41, killed 10 people and injured others over the course of three weeks in a series of random attacks in the D.C. area. Victims were pumping gas, waiting for the bus, cutting grass, going to school and other routine activities when they were shot with a high-powered rifle from the back of a modified car.
Lee Boyd Malvo, then 17, is led into circuit court in Virginia Beach, Virginia, it October 2022. He later pleaded guilty to four murders in Virginia and six in Maryland in the D. C. sniper shootings.  (Photo by Davis Turner-Pool/Getty Images)
In separate trials in Virginia, Malvo and Muhammad were convicted or pleaded guilty to the murders there. Muhammad was sentenced to death and executed in 2009. Malvo received four consecutive life sentences and is serving that time in Virginia.
In 2006, the two were tried in Montgomery County. Malvo pleaded guilty to six counts of first-degree murder and was sentenced to six consecutive life sentences without parole for six murders in the county. Both men were returned to Virginia.
But in 2022, the Maryland Supreme Court granted Malvo a new sentencing hearing after a series of U.S. Supreme Court rulings that limited the ability of courts to sentence minors to life in prison without a chance of parole.
That kicked off a nearly two-year struggle by Maryland officials to get Malvo transferred from Virginia so he could appear in person for  a resentencing hearing. Despite numerous hearings in Montgomery County Circuit Court, and numerous requests by Maryland officials, Virginia refused to transfer Malvo until he has served out his four life sentences in the commonwealth.
Malvo’s attorneys said he would not appear via video conference for a resentencing hearing and argued that, since Maryland could not arrange for Malvo to be physically present for a resentencing, he was essentially being denied a hearing and he was entitled to have his sentences vacated.
Malvo’s attorneys claimed that the state of Maryland failed to uphold their end of the deal by deciding that he “had no right to an in-person sentencing until after he serves four consecutive life sentences in Virginia.”
In September 2024, the Montgomery County Circuit Court denied the motion to vacate his convictions.
That ruling was upheld on May 1, 2026, by a three-judge panel of the Appellate Court in of Maryland.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“The trial court found that the State did not have the power to transport Appellant from Virginia to Maryland, and that sentencing could not occur remotely without Appellant’s consent. In light of those immutable positions, the court concluded that a sentencing hearing could not be scheduled.” Judge Laura S. Ripken wrote for the appeals court. “The court issued a detainer for Appellant to be returned to the Circuit Court for Montgomery County to be sentenced in person when his sentences in Virginia were completed.”
In his appeal to the Maryland Supreme Court, Malvo’s argued that the Appellate Court had deemed Malvo’s case “effectively unreviewable” and “effectively deprived Mr. Malvo of his right to an Eight Amendment compliant sentencing in his lifetime.”
But Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown urged the high court to reject Malvo’s appeal. He agreed with the appellate court that the state had exhausted efforts to get Malvo an in-person trial, and the logistical hurdle caused by Virginia’s unwillingness to temporarily turn over Malvo to Maryland is not a compelling reason to overturn that decision.
“The weakness of Mr. Malvo’s petition – on both the appealability and the merits – is that the issues he presents are unique to the highly unusual procedural posture of this case,” Brown wrote in his filing to the Supreme Court. “He makes no attempt to show that his issues have salience for any other cases or that he is seeking anything more than error correction and the idiosyncratic nature of Mr. Malvo’s case weighs heavily against a conclusion that review would be in the broader public interest.”
Brown’s office declined comment on the case Tuesday. A call to the public defender’s office was not immediately returned.
— Maryland Matters reporter Bryan P. Sears contributed to this report.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Franklin County prison project not canceled, Arkansas corrections secretary says
description: The 3,000-bed Franklin County prison project that’s faced legislative resistance hasn’t been canceled and remains an option, the head of the Arkansas Department of Corrections told lawmakers Tuesday. “Nobody has said that. We haven’t discussed that,” Corrections Secretary Lindsay Wallace said when asked if the project had been canceled. “We very clearly need[...]
text:
Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Sen. Alan Clark listens to testimony from members of the Arkansas Board of Corrections on Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)The 3,000-bed Franklin County prison project that’s faced legislative resistance hasn’t been canceled and remains an option, the head of the Arkansas Department of Corrections told lawmakers Tuesday.
“Nobody has said that. We haven’t discussed that,” Corrections Secretary Lindsay Wallace said when asked if the project had been canceled. “We very clearly need to have more beds. Like I said earlier, given that we did not have funding to move forward with that project … we’re looking at other alternatives while we talk about the larger issue of the bed space, the funding for the Franklin County project or whatever the case may be.”
Arkansas Explained: What is the Franklin County prison project?

Wallace’s comments to the House and Senate Judiciary committees come a week after the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette reported the project had been canceled and that department staff were considering alternatives such as expanding existing prison units. The report cited an email sent in April by a controller for the department that said it had been canceled, as well as an “expansion opportunity plan” from June that did not mention the Franklin County project.  
Following the story, Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders’ office said the Republican governor still believed the Franklin County site was the best option for expanding prison capacity.
“An exchange of ideas by staff doesn’t set state policy and these options have not been approved by the Governor or the legislature,” spokesperson Sam Dubke said last week.
The Franklin County prison has faced fierce resistance from the local community as well as in the Legislature since Sanders announced it in 2024. Proponents for the prison argue it’s necessary, pointing to the increasing number of people sentenced to Arkansas prisons that is projected to continue because of 2025 changes to Arkansas’ sentencing laws. 
As of Aug. 3, the state prison system was operating at around 109% of its listed bed capacity. Some units exceeded that, such as the Benny Magness Unit, which was operating at just over 132% of its listed capacity.
Overcrowded: Protect Arkansas Act to drive continued prison population growth for at least a decade

Wallace spoke at the first of several meetings planned by the joint committees to discuss solutions to the state’s overcrowding, and how to reduce the number of beds the state requires. 
Republican Sen. Alan Clark of Lonsdale told the Advocate the hearings have been in the works since before April’s fiscal session. Clark said if the committees have a strong consensus by December, they will make recommendations for legislators to consider during next year’s regular session, which begins in January.
“We’re going to have a major discussion between now and December,” Clark said. “I think there’s a great deal of agreement that we’ve got to act, and so I think we should see a lot of activity on this subject.”
Legislators heard from members of the Board of Corrections, sheriffs, prosecutors, prison reform advocates and Wallace during the hearing Tuesday, who were tasked with answering a single question.
“I wanted to clear the fog and lay the foundation of, ‘Do we need prison beds?’” Clark said. “The answer to that is yes.”
Now that the question is answered, he said, legislators can begin finding the “complicated and hard” answers to how the state can eventually reduce the number of prison beds it will need.
“Because we do imprison a lot of people in Arkansas,” Clark said. “We should be looking at every solution. A lot of times, you look at every solution just so you know it’s not a solution.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Wildlife groups warn not waive protections to accommodate Louisiana SpaceX site
description: SpaceX’s plans to launch thousands of rockets a year from coastal Southwest Louisiana will put habitat and hurricane protection at risk, according to three wildlife groups that oppose waivers to federal regulations aimed at expediting the development.
text:
The endangered whooping crane is one of the species that makes its home in Pecan Island, the chenier in Vermilion Parish where SpaceX plans to build its largest rocket launch facility. (Photo by Elise Plunk/Louisiana Illuminator)SpaceX’s plans to launch thousands of rockets a year from coastal Southwest Louisiana will put habitat and hurricane protection at risk, according to three wildlife groups that oppose waivers to federal regulations aimed at expediting the development.
The Louisiana Wildlife Federation, National Wildlife Federation and Pontchartrain Conservancy filed comments on proposed rule updates with the Federal Aviation Administration, just ahead of Gov. Jeff Landry announcing the $100 billion project Tuesday in Vermilion Parish. 
The revisions involve 13 wildlife, water and public health laws that the group say would be detrimental well beyond the 200-square-mile footprint for the SpaceX facility near the Freshwater Bayou Canal about 5 miles south of Pecan Island. The groups’ particular concerns center on potential threats to species, some of them endangered, that live in or migrate to the coastal wetlands as well as the loss of their habitat.   
The FAA posted its proposed changes to its commercial space licensing regulations July 30, with the stated intent to “streamline the licensing process and reduce regulatory burden for applicants.
The leaders of the three wildlife groups said in a letter sent Monday to FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford that they do not oppose the space industry and recognized the economic opportunity it could offer Louisiana. 
“Our concern is narrow and specific: The proposed rule would remove, at the licensing stage, the environmental review requirements that ensure launch and spaceport development accounts for its effects on wildlife, habitat, water and coastal resources,” they wrote. 
The federal laws in question include the Endangered Species Act, the Marine Mammal Protection Act, the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, the Clean Water Act and the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act.
Musk plans $100 billion SpaceX launch site in coastal Louisiana

Protected species that make their home along Vermilion’s coast and marshes include the endangered whooping crane. It also provides habitat for piping plover and Kemp’s ridley sea turtle, both near extinction in the wild. The site is also part of the Mississippi Flyway corridor that roughly 40% of all North American waterfowl and millions of migratory birds use, according to the National Wildlife Federation.   
The wildlife organizations want the Federal Aviation Administration to withdraw or “substantially revise” the proposed waivers and to keep federally required environmental reviews in place for the development.
“This is precisely the setting in which project-level environmental review matters most,” the groups’ letter states. “A launch facility of the scale contemplated would involve extensive marsh filling, dredging, road and pad construction, water withdrawals and discharges, high-intensity noise and light.”
At an event in Abbeville, Landry described the SpaceX project as one that would establish Louisiana as a global hub for the aerospace industry. The company expects to provide 3,000 jobs over the next 10 years, with annual salaries averaging $92,600.
The company intends to build five launch complexes, each with two launch pads, on what will be known as Starbase Louisiana. Development plans also call for storage and production facilities for the liquid oxygen and methane mix used to power the SpaceX Starship class rockets. The facility will have its own power plant, a structure for building the vehicles being launched into space and housing for employees and their families. Construction is expected to begin next year with the first launch intended for 2029.

Starbase Louisiana will be SpaceX’s fourth and largest launch facility, joining others in Cape Canaveral, Florida; Lompoc, California; and Boca Chica on the Texas coast near Brownsville.
State officials said SpaceX will work with the Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries, the state’s Coastal Protection and Restoration Authority and other agencies to “proactively address potential impacts to wildlife, fisheries and their supporting habitats.” The company also plans to partner with local groups and experts to avoid and prevent any ecological damage. 
Rebecca Triche, Louisiana Wildlife Federation executive director, said in a statement after the governor’s announcement that she was glad to hear him emphasize the importance of coastal restoration and protection. She also noted that SpaceX acknowledged the value of Louisiana’s coastal habitat and wanted to assist in coastal restoration efforts.
“We’d like to hear more about how this project would strengthen coastal resilience in ways that continue to sustain the abundance of wildlife that Sportsman’s Paradise has traditionally provided,” Triche said. “We did not see details about the reality of the footprint and impacts of launching a reusable and returnable rocket at this site.”
Details in general about the SpaceX project have been sparse leading up to Tuesday’s announcement, as many of the officials involved signed nondisclosure agreements. The use of NDAs has been a hallmark of the Landry administration’s major economic development efforts, with critics complaining they have left impacted communities in the dark and shielded negotiations involving incentives worth many millions of public dollars.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Thompson and Colom urge Black voters to turn out in November amid redistricting fight
description: U.S. Rep. Bennie Thompson speaks at the "Power in the Pews" faith leadership luncheon Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026, at the Hilton Jackson.
text:
U.S. Rep. Bennie Thompson and Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom on Tuesday called for Black Mississippi voters to turn out in November’s midterm elections to fight back against President Donald Trump’s agenda and an expected effort from state leaders to redraw electoral maps in Republicans’ favor.
At a “Power in the Pews” luncheon in Jackson organized by the NAACP, the candidates spoke to a packed room at the Hilton Jackson filled with hundreds of attendees alongside faith leaders, political organizers and Democratic officials.
Churches have long been an engine of political organizing for Black voters in Mississippi and across the Deep South. NAACP workers at the event handed out informational packets on voter engagement and urged attendees to consult their local churches for information on how to get involved. Thompson called such efforts a blueprint for turning out Black voters in Mississippi.
Thompson and Colom warned about what they said were threats to voting rights and Black representation posed by Trump and Republican state officials. Colom, who is gearing up for the final stages of a general election campaign against incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, also took the opportunity to sharpen his closing attacks on Mississippi’s junior senator, whom he labeled “Cindy High Prices.”
“Our junior senator cares more about what her MAGA daddy says than what’s best for Mississippi,” Colom said.
Democratic nominee for the U.S. Senate Scott Colom speaks at the “Power in the Pews” faith leadership luncheon Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026, at the Hilton Jackson. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Colom, who also faces independent Ty Pinkins in the general election, criticized Hyde-Smith for voting for the “Big Beautiful Bill” act and supporting President Trump’s tariffs, which he has said raised prices of consumer goods across the economy. He also accused Hyde-Smith of using political donations for personal travel, such as billing trips to Las Vegas to her campaign account.
“Not only is she allowing the corruption, not only is she remaining silent, she’s partaking in it,” Colom said.
A spokesperson for Hyde-Smith did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Thompson, the only Democrat and only Black member of Mississippi’s congressional delegation, noted the size of the crowd that came out on a Tuesday afternoon. The turnout could be traced to Trump’s unique ability to unite Black voters in opposition, he said.
“Now let me tell you what’s making this happen. It’s that fella in the White House,” Thompson said. “This man has done more to get Black folks together in America than Martin Luther King could have ever done”
If Democrats reclaim a majority in the U.S. House this November, six Black members could become committee chairmen, Thompson told the crowd. 
“There’s nothing like being in the room, in charge,” he added.
Thompson faces Republican Ron Eller and independent Bennie Foster this November. 
Since the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision in the Louisiana Callais redistricting case in May, which weakened the Voting Rights Act, Thompson has been the target of calls from Gov. Tate Reeves and Republican state legislators to redraw Mississippi’s electoral maps.
A legislative joint committee is holding public hearings across the state, and the full Legislature is expected to convene in a special session this fall to redraw at least state legislative maps. That wouldn’t impact this November’s federal election, but Mississippi lawmakers are likely to target Thompson’s seat with redistricting before he’s up for reelection again in 2028.
Colom called the Callais decision “a threat to our democracy” the country hasn’t seen in decades.
“(Gov. Tate Reeves) is going to try to draw lines that prevent the people in this room from being able to pick leaders they want. He wants to pick your leaders for y’all,” Colom said. “He doesn’t want Cindy High Prices to have to compete for votes, because they won’t to have to answer for these terrible policies.”
Charles Taylor, Mississippi’s NAACP executive director, said his organization has been meeting with Black circuit clerks and election commissioners to discuss “election security” and that organizers will “turn out Black folks in droves.”
“The eyes of the country have been on Mississippi this year, and it’s because of the work we’ve been doing day in and day out,” Taylor said. “The election in November is crucially important because it has been a long time since they have tried to roll back our rights like this.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Average Black Hills Energy customer faces potential $45 increase in monthly bill
description: The average Black Hills Energy residential electric customer in South Dakota faces a monthly bill that will be $45 higher if state regulators approve a pending rate increase and surcharge. The company’s latest application this month seeks to add a monthly surcharge of $19.70 for the average residential customer, to recoup costs for the $320 […]
text:
A sign identifies the location of the Lange II natural gas-powered electrical generation plant under construction in northwestern Rapid City, South Dakota, on Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)The average Black Hills Energy residential electric customer in South Dakota faces a monthly bill that will be $45 higher if state regulators approve a pending rate increase and surcharge.
The company’s latest application this month seeks to add a monthly surcharge of $19.70 for the average residential customer, to recoup costs for the $320 million construction of the Lange II natural gas-powered electrical generation plant in northwestern Rapid City. The company has said the plant will meet growing power demands from current customers following the planned retirement of the 1960s-era Ben French plant, and is not in response to any proposals for data center construction. 
“Our most important responsibility is providing safe, reliable energy to our customers and communities,” said Wes Ashton, vice president of South Dakota and Wyoming utilities for Black Hills Energy, in an Aug. 5 news release. “Lange II will replace the Ben French units as a critical system resource to serve customers while enhancing the reliability of our Black Hills Energy electric system.”
Relief from energy bills unlikely as utilities request billions in rate hikes

The company plans to start collecting the surcharge in December, when the new plant is expected to start delivering power. If the state Public Utilities Commission has not made a decision by then, the company could collect the surcharge on an interim basis, subject to refunds for customers later if the commission rejects or reduces the surcharge. The commission would then review the surcharge annually.
The surcharge would come on top of a general rate increase that Black Hills Energy is requesting of about $25 per month for the average residential customer. That proposal would generate $50.6 million in additional annual revenue for the company, which serves roughly 75,000 customers in western South Dakota and also serves customers in seven other states. The company has said the rate increase is justified by infrastructure investments, inflation and the lack of a rate increase since 2014. 
“Our electric base rates have been unchanged for more than a decade, allowing our customers to experience rate stability, which is a priority for us,” said Lynn Kendall, regional public affairs manager for Black Hills Energy. “We are requesting this rate review because it’s necessary for us to update rates to account for the critical investments and improvements we’ve made to our system over the past 12 years, while also accounting for the increased operating costs to serve our customers.”
The company began collecting the higher rate on an interim basis Aug. 18, because the Public Utilities Commission did not make a decision within a 180-day review period. Customers would receive refunds if state regulators ultimately reject the increase or approve a smaller increase. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Rapid City resident John McKee submitted comments to the commission about the proposed rate increase in March, writing that the increase would “directly and materially affect my household’s financial obligations, energy access, and long-term cost stability.” He warned that higher rates could impose “significant financial burdens” on residential customers.
Commission documents show that if both requests are approved at the proposed amounts, the average residential customer’s monthly bill would rise from $98.96 to $143.70 — a 45% increase. 
A group representing some of Black Hills Energy’s largest South Dakota customers, including Monument Health, manufacturers, and mining and materials companies, has filed comments in both commission proceedings. The group wrote that the proposed surcharge would “greatly increase” its members’ cost of doing business.
In addition to its surcharge and rate request to the Public Utilities Commission, Black Hills Energy’s parent company, Black Hills Corp., is pursuing a merger with Sioux Falls-based NorthWestern Energy. Among the states affected by the merger, Montana is the only one in which regulators have not yet approved it.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT funds housing development for Waterbury healthcare workers
description: Connecticut will provide roughly $11.6 million for the project, which is planned at the former Saint Mary’s Grammar School property.
text:
The Connecticut Department of Housing and the city of Waterbury are teaming up on a first-of-its-kind affordable housing development aimed at attracting and retaining healthcare workers.
The complex will include 47 affordable units in four buildings on the site of the former Saint Mary’s Grammar School property in Waterbury that the city acquired in 2023. The buildings have, for the most part, stood vacant for 10 years. 
The site is located across the street from Saint Mary’s Hospital, a couple miles from Waterbury Hospital and within walking distance of downtown, public transportation, restaurants and shopping, said the city’s mayor, Paul Pernerewski.
“If we want to attract and retain healthcare professionals in our community, we need to make sure they have access to quality housing close to where they work, and this is what makes this project particularly significant,” Pernerewski said during a Tuesday afternoon press conference.
The project is estimated to cost between $14 million and $15 million. It will be funded in part through a 2022 measure authorizing the state borrow up to $20 million for the development of housing for healthcare workers. The Waterbury project is the first to tap that funding.
Connecticut will provide roughly $11.6 million in funding for the project, according to Department of Housing Commissioner Seila Mosquera-Bruno. That includes $5.6 million from the healthcare housing initiative, $4.6 million in flexible housing funds and $1.5 million in loans that will need to be repaid. Ives Bank is providing an additional $2.2 million. 
Connecticut officials are also in early-stage discussions with two other hospitals about opportunities for affordable housing development, Mosquera-Bruno said.
Commissioner of Housing for the State of Connecticut Seila Mosquera-Bruno speaks during a press conference about a project that will turn the former St. Mary’s Grammar School property in Waterbury into affordable housing for healthcare workers through partnership between the state, the city, and a private developer on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror
Units in the Waterbury development are intended for middle-income families earning between $40,000 and $80,000 annually, Mosquera-Bruno said. They’ll include studio, one-bedroom and two-bedroom units with rents ranging from $1,000 to $1,500. 
Pernerewski called the project “a major commitment to housing for healthcare workers.”
But groups representing healthcare workers said that while affordable housing is an “important part” of supporting this workforce, the need for it is also a sign that wages are insufficient.
“Essential healthcare workers should not have to rely on affordable housing programs simply to afford to live where they work,” representatives with SEIU 1199NE, a union representing healthcare and service workers across Connecticut, Rhode Island and southeastern Massachusetts, said in a statement Tuesday afternoon. 
A handful of SEIU 1199NE union members were present at Tuesday’s press conference in Waterbury, standing behind the speakers.
Hospital lobbyists in Connecticut have for years been seeking the state’s support in expanding the healthcare workforce. Staffing shortages in the industry were exacerbated during the pandemic, but they continue to pose a challenge years later.
Connecticut needs thousands of new registered nurses a year to make up for retirements — without factoring in nurses who leave the profession for other reasons, like burn out. The annual number of graduates from the state’s nursing programs don’t meet that need. 
Joe Gramando, the developer behind the Waterbury housing development, said it’s currently accepting applications for renters. Construction will start after Labor Day and will take between 12 and 18 months to complete, he said. 
Gramando said he plans to apply for state funds to support the construction of another 50-unit development for healthcare workers in the lot adjacent to the current project site.
