name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Lawmakers discuss regionalization as a possible solution for local ambulance problems
description: PIERRE — State healthcare officials told South Dakota lawmakers this week that coordination among neighboring communities could strengthen local emergency medical services that are struggling with staffing and funding. “This is truly critical to the transformation of EMS in South Dakota,” said Emily Kiel, director of the state Department of Health’s Division[...]
text:
Ambulances are parked in a Spearfish Emergency Ambulance Service facility earlier this year. A task force of South Dakota lawmakers is meeting this summer to discuss ideas for supporting local ambulance service providers. (Photo by Meghan O'Brien/South Dakota Searchlight)
https://southdakotasearchlight.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/regionalization-web.wav
 Listen to an audio version of this story produced by reporter Meghan O’Brien. Broadcasters: See below for a downloadable version with a host intro script.
PIERRE — State healthcare officials told South Dakota lawmakers this week that coordination among neighboring communities could strengthen local emergency medical services that are struggling with staffing and funding.
“This is truly critical to the transformation of EMS in South Dakota,” said Emily Kiel, director of the state Department of Health’s Division of Healthcare Access.
An 11-member task force of state lawmakers that met Monday is using the summer to consider ideas for legislation to support ambulance services across the state. Some services struggle with managing human resources or billing services, said Marty Link, deputy director of the Division of Healthcare Access, and regionalization could lighten the load of administrative tasks.
Regionalization involves sharing resources and functions among ambulance services across a specific geographical area, Link said. It also involves sharing recruitment and retention efforts such as training, continuing education and leadership development.
Kiel told lawmakers that regionalization could eventually lead to a stronger workforce.
Regionalization, telehealth, data-sharing: SD applies for $1 billion from federal rural health fund

“A strong workforce doesn’t simply mean obtaining a magic number of people on a roster,” she said. “A strong workforce understands a patient’s needs and anticipates downstream care priorities.”
Department officials plan to use a portion of South Dakota’s funding over the next five years from the federal government’s Rural Health Transformation Program to support regional emergency medical services hubs. South Dakota has received $189.5 million from the program so far.
Congress included the program in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, in response to concerns that the bill’s Medicaid cuts would hurt rural health providers. Medicaid is a federal-state program that provides health insurance for people with disabilities or low incomes.
The Department of Health consulted with the South Dakota Foundation for Medical Care to design a regional hub system, which could be supported over the coming years with federal funding. But the question lawmakers must answer is how to fund that system long-term, after the rural health program funding is spent.
“We will have to come up with funding,” said Sen. Ernie Otten, R-Tea. “I think the citizens of South Dakota deserve something better than a conversation going on here in the Legislature for over 20 years, and the best that we’ve got is to come up with a model that is self-destructing in front of us.”
Coordinated efforts could lead to faster response times
Link told lawmakers he hopes to achieve a goal of “15 minutes to life” through regionalization.
“It challenges every community and region to consider how they can help ensure that, regardless of where an emergency occurs, a person can receive meaningful care within that 15 minute timeframe or less,” Link said.
An ambulance may not be able to immediately arrive at a rural emergency scene, Link said, and that isn’t the goal.
“The goal here is to really design a system where the closest, appropriately trained resource can begin life-saving action early, connect with that patient, and then enter into that broader healthcare system through EMS,” Link said. “Fifteen minutes to life is really an outcome. Regional infrastructure is what makes it possible.”
In an example of regionalization, Spink County Ambulance Director Eric Schueth told lawmakers about a secondary crew spread across the northern part of the county, called Wildcat Rescue. It’s a mix of EMTs, nurses and one paramedic.
Schueth’s service responds to 911 calls across a 1,800-square-mile area in northeastern South Dakota. Last year, it responded to 565 calls.
‘I have no reason to quit’: South Dakota EMTs still lending a hand in their 80s

Wildcat Rescue can often respond to emergencies in rural areas before the Spink County ambulance crew can arrive on scene. While Wildcat Rescue team members provide primary care, the Spink County ambulance is on its way to provide transport to a hospital if needed.
Spink County also collaborates with Clark, Hand and Faulk counties and with nearby towns such as Huron and Wolsey. After learning about the Department of Health’s vision for regional collaboration, Schueth and leaders of neighboring ambulance crews began meeting in March to learn how each agency could support one another.
“What does everybody need?” Schueth said the service’s leaders are asking. “How can we make each one of our services successful?”
For the coalition in northeastern South Dakota, the answer to that question is sharing resources such as staff, equipment and continuing education instructors. It also means operating under the same policies for patient care, Schueth said, so that “everybody functions as one.”
Some lawmakers on the task force said the success in Spink County could be a sign that regionalization works.
Chief Don Rowland of Watertown Fire Rescue told lawmakers that collaboration is difficult in areas with few volunteer services.
“We do not have another volunteer service in our county, so I provide protection to more than 17 townships in our county,” Rowland said.
Rowland said his department responds to more than 3,000 calls annually and provides service across about 730 square miles.
The task force plans to meet at least two more times over the next two months. Members hope to provide legislative proposals in November, to be considered during the 2027 legislative session that starts in January.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Musk plans $100 billion SpaceX launch site in coastal Louisiana
description: ABBEVILLE — Following months of rumors, SpaceX confirmed Tuesday that it’s building a $100 billion self-sustaining spaceport in Vermilion Parish, marking what state officials say is the largest capital investment in Louisiana history. SpaceX plans to construct what it’s calling Starbase Louisiana near the small rural community of Pecan Island, about 50 miles[...]
text:
Gov. Jeff Landry speaks at a SpaceX event to announce the company's project in Vermillion Parish on Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo: Wes Muller/Louisiana Illuminator)ABBEVILLE — Following months of rumors, SpaceX confirmed Tuesday that it’s building a $100 billion self-sustaining spaceport in Vermilion Parish, marking what state officials say is the largest capital investment in Louisiana history.
SpaceX plans to construct what it’s calling Starbase Louisiana near the small rural community of Pecan Island, about 50 miles south-southwest of Lafayette. 
“We’re here to build something that will open a pathway to the stars for today’s future generations,” SpaceX chief operating officer Gwynne Shotwell said to a room full of politicians, business leaders and reporters who gathered for a highly produced event with live music and catered food to mark the much anticipated announcement.
Starbase Louisiana will feature 10 launchpads, fuel production facilities, a power plant, deep-water shipping port, employee housing and an airport — all to allow the base to be “self-sustaining” and not reliant on outside facilities for many of its critical services.
SpaceX Chief Operating Officer Gwynne Shotwell speaks at an event to announce the company’s Spacebase Louisiana project in Vermillion Parish on Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo: Wes Muller/Louisiana Illuminator)
Shotwell likened the project to a small city with at least 3,000 residents and as many as 10,000 permanent jobs, of which she said local residents will fill 60% of 80%.
SpaceX will pay local taxing authorities a collective $25 million annually instead of remitting property taxes as well as a $20 million upfront payment. The company, owned by the world’s richest person, Elon Musk, is also expected to benefit from other state tax incentives, according to Louisiana Economic Development.
SpaceX has promised to fund coastal and wildlife habitat restoration in the Acadiana region. Shotwell said these efforts would begin immediately but didn’t elaborate on the plans. At a later news conference, Gov. Jeff Landry said SpaceX is going to directly fund some of the projects in Louisiana’s Coastal Master Plan. 
“This is the first time we can marry an economic development project that creates thousands of jobs with coastal restoration and hurricane protection,” Landry said.
The project has been sited on 125,000 acres of coastal marshland nestled between two state wildlife refuges, though the area dedicated to rocket launch facilities is a smaller portion of about 40,000 acres. 
Shotwell said it will not have a significant impact on wildlife.
“Now the birds might fly away during a launch, but I guarantee they come back,” she said. “As soon as the rocket’s gone, they come back.”
Louisiana will be home to the largest Starbase site, joining SpaceX facilities at Cape Canaveral, Florida; Lompoc, California; and near Brownsville, Texas.
Libby Smith Nehrbass of Lafayette attended the SpaceX event with her husband, holding up a small protest sign that read, “Paradise Lost.” She said they own a hunting and fishing camp in Pecan Island and are worried activity at the spaceport will ruin the area with air, light and noise pollution.
“You can’t tell me that birds coexist with rockets,” Nehrbass said. “And why all the secrecy? Why all the laws that take away our rights? It’s just unconscionable. It’s not right.”
Nehrbass was referring to state officials’ widespread use of non-disclosure agreements to engage in negotiations for the SpaceX project and other major economic development undertakings. The aerospace company could also benefit from state legislation approved earlier this year that gives the industry legal immunity from certain lawsuits filed by Louisiana residents.
Libby Smith Nehrbass of Lafayette holds up a sign that reads, “Paradise Lost,” to protest SpaceX’s announcement of Spacebase Louisiana in Vermilion Parish. She and her husband, who own a hunting and fishing lodge on Pecan Island, attended the company’s announcement Aug. 25, 2026, in Abbeville. (Photo by Wes Muller/Louisiana Illuminator)
Others in the community expressed excitement and optimism about the project. 
Abbeville resident Carrie Simon, who runs a nonprofit for abused and neglected children, was at a local Starbucks coffee shop when she heard the SpaceX announcement. She said she’s happy to hear the company has agreed to fund coastal restoration and believes the project will have positive effects across other sectors.
“A lot of businesses aren’t flourishing or aren’t where they need to be,” Simon said. “I know so many people right now looking for work…It can be a ripple effect of growth.”
SpaceX, a once failing startup, is now the world’s most advanced aerospace company, having developed the reusable rockets that now ferry NASA astronauts and deploy satellites into orbit ahead of Musk’s ultimate goal of interplanetary travel. Its sister company, Starlink, has similarly dominated the global satellite and rural broadband market, operating the majority of all maneuverable satellites in earth’s orbit.
SpaceX has promised all Vermilion Parish residents steep discounts on Starlink internet service. 
Simon acknowledged that Musk is a divisive political figure to some but pointed out that he has the means and resources to bring many new opportunities to Vermillion Parish.
“I tell you what if he doesn’t keep his word, it’s not good to make Cajuns angry,” Simon said, jokingly.
Construction on Starbase Louisiana is expected to begin in 2027 with the first rocket launches to take place in 2029.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: ‘So freaking cute’: Supporters pitch Cameron the Capitol Cat statue outside Nebraska State Capitol
description: LINCOLN — The Nebraska State Capitol’s unofficial feline mascot could soon become a permanent fixture outside the historic building he brought warmth and love to for a decade. Until this spring, Cameron the “Capitol Cat” made a home away from home at the Capitol near his downtown Lincoln residence with his owner, Dianna McGinnis. After long […]
text:
Cameron the Capitol Cat, once a mainstay of the Nebraska State Capitol, lounges outside the Capitol building. Aug. 7, 2024. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — The Nebraska State Capitol’s unofficial feline mascot could soon become a permanent fixture outside the historic building he brought warmth and love to for a decade.
Until this spring, Cameron the “Capitol Cat” made a home away from home at the Capitol near his downtown Lincoln residence with his owner, Dianna McGinnis. After long legislative days, staffers and lawmakers alike would greet Cameron, even on nights after heated filibusters or those that stretched toward midnight. Many found relief as he awaited their attention.
Cameron retired in May as the unofficial Capitol greeter when McGinnis moved to assisted living. But his pawprint on lawmakers, staff and community members well beyond Nebraska could soon live on with a statue on the south side of the Capitol off Goodhue Boulevard.
The life-size bronze statue of Cameron would be about 18-20 inches tall and sit atop a pedestal made from Indiana limestone, about 28-32 inches in height. The limestone is proposed to mirror the stone facing and architectural trim of the historic Nebraska State Capitol.
A mockup made with artificial intelligence showing what a statue honoring Cameron, the unofficial “Capitol Cat” mascot for the Nebraska State Capitol, could look like. Supporters of the project hope to hire Idaho sculptor Benjamin Victor to sculpt and design the final sculpture. (Photo rendering using AI courtesy of state Sen. Jana Hughes)
“I mean, let’s be real, it would be so freaking cute and everybody would get their picture by it, and his little head would be petted, and it’d be shiny gold because everybody would rub his little head coming in,” state Sen. Jana Hughes of Seward, who is helping the project, said Friday.
No state or taxpayer funds would go toward the statue. 
Hughes, who joined the Legislature in 2023, and former state Sen. Anna Wishart of Lincoln, who served between 2017 and 2025, will pitch the privately funded project to the Nebraska Capitol Environs Commission on Friday. The meeting is for feedback initially, and the supporters would need final approval before the statue could be affixed near the Capitol.
The commission includes seven voting members — five appointees from the Lincoln mayor and two from the Nebraska governor — who oversee the Capitol Environs District and associated architecture, landscaping, urban planning and real estate.
The purpose of the commission is to maintain and enhance a “dignified setting” for the Capitol, encourage appropriate improvements in the district and protect vistas to the Capitol.
‘Heartwarming story’
Hughes said she first heard of the statue idea around the time lawmakers adjourned in April from one of her constituents, Scott Shafer, who works for the Nebraska Commission on Indian Affairs. Using artificial intelligence, she created a rendering of how the statue could look. However, the final design would fall to the storied sculptor supporters hope to hire.
State Sen. Jana Hughes of Seward, right, smiles while stalking with state Sens. Glen Meyer of Pender, left, and Kathleen Kauth of Omaha. March 26, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Benjamin Victor of Boise, Idaho, the artist behind the Ponca Chief Standing Bear and Dr. Susan La Flesche Picotte statues on Lincoln Mall north of the Nebraska Capitol has agreed to sculpt the bronze Cameron.
“What a warm idea for a sculpture,” Victor said Monday.
Victor sculpted Nebraska’s Chief Standing Bear statue in Statuary Hall in the U.S. Capitol. He has sculpted three other statues in Statuary Hall, the only living sculptor with that honor:

Civil rights leader, journalist and author Daisy Lee Gatson Bates, who fought for school integration and assisted the Little Rock Nine (Arkansas).
Agronomist Norman Borlaug, who developed high-yield, disease-resistant wheat varieties and is often called the “father of the Green Revolution” (Iowa).
Paiute writer, activist and lecturer Sarah Winnemucca, who was one of the first Native American women to testify before Congress (Nevada).

Dianna McGinnis of Lincoln with her cat, Cameron, who became a celebrity around the Nebraska State Capitol and Lincoln and the status of “Capitol Cat” and unofficial greeter. (Photo courtesy of John Shaw)
In his handful of trips to the Nebraska Capitol, Victor said, he met Cameron on multiple occasions. He said it’s awesome to see Cameron’s impact.
“We all know our pets touch our hearts, and they’re part of our lives, and they’re part of our families,” Victor said. “But then to see a cat that just hung around the Capitol all the time and got to know everybody, it’s really kind of an amazing story and a heartwarming story and a wonderful thing as an artist to get to do something like that.”
Supporters had originally thought of adding a bronze Cameron closer to the entrance to the Capitol. However, commission regulations in the Lincoln Municipal Code say the “Capitol Square,” the four blocks where the Capitol sits, is meant to be a “complete and finished design.”
‘As old as the stone’
Wishart said people have been missing Cameron amid his celebrity status in Lincoln, a city of more than 300,000. In Wishart’s daily life, the former lawmaker said, she meets with people who ask about Cameron and tell her they previously drove by just to say “hi” to the Capitol Cat.
“We think that it’s important for his presence to be permanent, because he was such an important little figure there every day at the Capitol,” Wishart said.
Then-state Sen. Anna Wishart of Lincoln greets Cameron, the Nebraska State Capitol’s “Capitol Cat,” on the south steps of the building. (Photo courtesy of Anna Wishart)
With Cameron’s daily presence, Wishart said, it was hard to remember when he first started showing up but believes it was around 2018. She remarked that it almost felt as if Cameron knew when the Capitol would be busy, “and you see him trotting down the street from his home to come and see everybody.”
“It almost feels like he’s as old as the stone of the Capitol,” Wishart said of his presence.
One of the goals, Wishart said, is also to get the statue up “as soon as possible” for McGinnis, who relocated due to serious health decline and chronic pain in recent months. Wishart noted Cameron always had a positive presence and brought out “shared humanity.”
A storied legacy
John Shaw, a local photographer who published a book about Cameron that is sold at a gift shop in the Capitol, among other Cameron merchandise, is also helping the project.
Shaw said Cameron’s family is “very on board” and excited. As of Tuesday afternoon, the fundraising campaign had raised almost $3,500 toward its $37,500 goal just a few days after launching. Shaw has also agreed to donate profits from his photo book about Cameron to the project through October.
Lincoln photographer John Shaw with Cameron the “Capitol Cat” outside the Nebraska State Capitol. (Photo courtesy of John Shaw | Photo by Riley Shaw)
The cost includes Victor’s estimate and ongoing maintenance. Meeting materials indicate minimal upkeep with materials “designed to withstand Nebraska seasonal cycles without degradation.”
While Shaw was not necessarily an animal photographer, he said he always enjoyed photographing Cameron. He has two adopted cats of his own — littermates, which his daughters named Toby, after “The Office” character, and Peanut, for a marking on his nose. 
After publishing his book and writing about Cameron’s retirement, Shaw said, he heard the “deeply emotional stories” people had about Cameron well beyond Nebraska.
Shaw said those stories were about “how they might have had loss in their life, and they came and saw Cameron and how it touched them and reminded them of people they had lost and how comforting he was.”
‘Peaceful constant on the south steps’
Also endorsing the statue is Nebraska’s top legislator, Speaker John Arch of La Vista. 
Arch, who is finishing his eighth and final year, including four as speaker, wrote in a supporting letter that he saw the “intense energy, long hours and rigorous debate” in the Legislature.
“In a setting dedicated to high-stakes public policy, Cameron served a unique and comforting purpose,” Arch wrote. “For over a decade, he was a peaceful constant on the south steps and lawns — offering a quiet moment of warmth to senators, legislative staff, page classes and constituents alike as they entered and exited the building.”
State lawmakers gather around Speaker John Arch of La Vista, center, on the final day of Nebraska’s 2026 legislative session. Arch holds a frame gifted to him signed by all 48 of his colleagues. The picture shows a man herding cats. April 17, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
On one hand, lawmakers work “tirelessly” to represent Nebraskans, Arch said. Yet Cameron “represented the sheer goodwill of our Capitol culture.” Arch said Cameron’s retirement — after a tenure longer than modern lawmakers — marked the “end of a remarkable era.”
Wrote Arch: “Moving his memorial site directly across the street to the south grounds allows us to preserve his story and connection to the Capitol campus while respecting the physical integrity of the building itself.”
The Capitol Environs Commission meeting is 8:30 a.m. Friday in Lincoln.
Cameron the Capitol cat sits inside the vestibule of the south entrance to the Nebraska State Capitol on Nov. 24, 2025. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)Cameron the Capitol cat sits on a reporter's lap at the west entrance to the Nebraska State Capitol on Aug. 7, 2024. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)Cameron, the Nebraska State Capitol's "Capitol Cat," poses on a ledge on the south side of the building. (Photo courtesy of Katie Quintero)Cameron the Capitol Cat, shown in December 2024. (Photo by Erin Bamer/Nebraska Examiner)Cameron, the Nebraska State Capitol's "Capitol Cat," trots down a ledge on the south side of the building. (Photo courtesy of Katie Quintero)Cameron the Capitol Cat was a common sight around legislative sessions. (Photo by Aaron Sanderford/Nebraska Examiner)Cameron the Capitol cat looks up at a reporter's phone on the south steps of the Nebraska State Capitol on the evening of March 18, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen holds Cameron, the Nebraska State Capitol's unofficial mascot, on the south steps of the building in spring 2023. (Photo courtesy of the Office of Governor Jim Pillen)Cameron the Capitol cat outside the south entrance to the Nebraska State Capitol on Feb. 20, 2026. name: Georgia Recorder
title: Dozens of threatened plant and animal species could gain state protection in Georgia
description: Georgia is set to update its list of protected plants and animals for the first time in two decades, and the number of protected species is set to grow by more than 100. On the bright side, 40 species were removed from the list because survey data showed their populations have recovered. On the not-so […]
text:
The eastern diamondback rattlesnake is the longest rattlesnake in the world and its home turf includes southern Georgia. It's one of 145 new species that could be added to a list of protected species in the state. Georgia Department of Natural ResourcesGeorgia is set to update its list of protected plants and animals for the first time in two decades, and the number of protected species is set to grow by more than 100.
On the bright side, 40 species were removed from the list because survey data showed their populations have recovered. On the not-so bright side, 145 new species were added to the list for the opposite reason.
The state Board of Natural Resources reviewed proposed changes to the list Tuesday and are expected to vote on them in October.
It’s a misdemeanor to intentionally harm protected animals or remove plants from state lands without a permit or from private land without the landowner’s permission.
The threatened critters range from the fuzzy to the slimy to the chitinous. The list includes mammals like the hoary bat and eastern spotted skunk, birds such as the red-cockaded woodpecker and whooping crane, and reptiles like the eastern diamondback rattlesnake and Suwannee alligator snapping turtle.
Georgia Wildlife Federation President Mike Worley said revising the list for the first time since 2006 will help Georgia conservationists update their plans for modern times.
“We’re at 11-plus million people in the state of Georgia now,” he said. “We continue to press our suburbs out. We continue to press our urban areas out and absorb more of the rural space and the wild spaces, and we’ve got to figure out ways that we can all coexist.”
Worley added that adding protection at the state level can help species recover before they are placed on the federal endangered species list.
The proposed changes to the list would also carve out a new exemption for sellers of native plants.
It would allow for the sale of 39 protected plant species without a permit from the Department of Natural Resources so long as the plants are harvested from cultivated stock and not collected from the wild.
“We have a growing native plant industry in Georgia, and we’re really glad to see more native plants getting onto the landscape, and right now it’s burdensome,” said Trina Morris, the Department of Natural Resources wildlife conservation section program manager.
“We have to issue permits, and the plants have to have tags to make sure that they were not harvested from the wild and sold for profit. We have a lot of these plants in existing horticultural stock that are regularly sold, and we want that to continue to happen.”
Carolyn Rader with the Georgia Botanical Society said horticulturists once imported non-native plants such as Liriope, also called monkeygrass or lilyturf, which is now considered a nuisance by many.
“I know in my neighborhood, I’m constantly having to dig out Liriope and all that kind of thing,” she said. “The more we can actually encourage the nurseries to stock our native plants, it’s better for our pollinators, it’s better for our ecosystem health, and all of the above.”
A public hearing on the proposed list is scheduled for 7 p.m. on Sept. 8 at the Wildlife Resources Division Headquarters Office in Social Circle, and Georgians can also submit comments by email at wcscomments@dnr.ga.gov using the subject line protected species list.

title: A dying Fish and Wildlife commissioner’s parting letter to WA’s governor
description: Editor’s note: Victor Garcia, who was appointed to the Washington Fish and Wildlife Commission in April 2025, died over the weekend. Before he passed, the hunter, fisherman and retired educator penned a letter to Gov. Bob Ferguson, offering a roadmap for choosing a successor who could help forge stronger ties between commissioners and with the […]
text:
(Photo by Art Wolfe/Getty Images)Editor’s note: Victor Garcia, who was appointed to the Washington Fish and Wildlife Commission in April 2025, died over the weekend. Before he passed, the hunter, fisherman and retired educator penned a letter to Gov. Bob Ferguson, offering a roadmap for choosing a successor who could help forge stronger ties between commissioners and with the diverse interests with whom they interact. Here is an unedited copy of the letter provided by his son.
Dear Honorable Governor Ferguson: 
This letter is in regard to my position on the Washington Fish and Wildlife Commission. I was appointed April 5, 2025, and was to continue until the end of 2030, serving from Skagit County in western Washington. In fact, I had applied twice to serve on the Commission before that time, but my health was considered a potential impediment to fulfilling Commission responsibilities as a citizen representative. I was diagnosed with an aggressive cancer almost 10 years ago and told I had less than a year to live. 
Despite this prognosis, however, I have lived a particularly rich life, with more experiences in that timeframe than most people have the fortune to enjoy over their entire lives. Among these were the birth of my grandson and serving on the Fish and Wildlife Commission. My gratitude to you is boundless for appointing me to the Commission despite the previous administration’s concerns around my health. I hope my service to the Washington public and our magnificent wildlife heritage has met your expectations. 
Regrettably, my cancer has returned with terminal intensity, leaving me no choice but to resign from my seat on the Commission with this letter. These 17 months of service have meant the world to me, having allowed me to hopefully repay some of the debt I feel I owe to nature and to our beautiful region, which have so enriched my life. It has been an honor to support the men and women of the Department of Fish and Wildlife (Department) and the reliable science that they provide to the Commission for critical management decisions.  
It saddens me to leave you with the task of having to fill my seat prematurely. I hope you will indulge me in the opportunity to offer my thoughts on the qualities I believe are important for whoever you may consider to move the Commission and Department forward. I would like to express how deeply impressed I have been by the professionalism and skill of the Department’s leadership and staff, and it is my sincere hope that the Commission will position itself strongly in their support. 
I am also fully supportive of the agency’s mission: “To preserve, protect and perpetuate fish, wildlife and ecosystems while providing sustainable fish and wildlife recreational and commercial opportunities.” I hope you will seek commissioners who are fully committed to that mission as stated, and I would like to suggest certain litmus tests be met to ensure an effective replacement for my position: 

The candidate should support the Department’s mandate in full and as is — not cherry-pick only the parts that they like — and must acknowledge that any change to that mandate must come from the Legislature. It is not the purview of the Commission on its own to modify the mandate.
The candidate must accept the Boldt Decision (the 1974 court ruling affirming certain treaty-protected fishing rights for tribes) as the “law of the land” and embrace co-management of fish and wildlife resources with our Tribal partners.
They must accept the scientific products of our dedicated Department staff as the foundation of the decision-making process.
They must put aside their personal agendas and focus on the total of species and habitats of greatest concern — not only on the more iconic or charismatic species. 
Appointment of a centrist candidate who is willing to work with both sides of an issue and build bridges rather than present roadblocks and lawsuits would alleviate what currently seems to be a state of polarization on the Commission, which is unproductive. 
The candidate should believe in a collaborative approach to conservation, working with Tribes and stakeholders to find middle ground; this will best serve our species and ecosystems.
I firmly believe that Tribes need to retain the authorization and ability to manage wildlife and collect data on their reservations and usual and accustomed hunting grounds in the ways that they see fit (e.g., the Colville Tribe’s wolf management program). 
Candidates should embrace the premise that hunting/fishing and conservation are not mutually exclusive; I would like to suggest that a candidate who has experience in hunting and either sport or commercial fishing brings an understanding of multiple perspectives that can help achieve the best balance. 
I would hope that a new nominee would take up WDFW’s Americans with Disabilities Act Advisory Committee (ADAAC) mantle to ensure equal opportunity for all citizens of our State.

The Commission is struggling from a lack of public trust, as you well know. I believe the root causes of those struggles are Commissioners and interests not fully aligned with the stated mission, but instead aiming to impose elements of their own belief systems or agendas. 
This imposition manifests in unproductive disputes that fail to recognize cultural traditions and sovereign Tribal rights. It also results in the Commission (and Department) putting excessive time and effort into controversial or popularized issues such as black bear and gray wolf management, while leaving little time for larger but less-publicized issues of habitat protection and recovery, which support all species within an ecosystem. 
This misdirection of effort undermines efficient focus on the massive list of critical tasks necessary to address the resource and public challenges called for by the mission, such as those enumerated in the State Wildlife Action Plan. 
I have a hope that animal rights activists and sportsmen can come together to steward the species we all cherish through projects such as wildlife overpasses to promote predator genetic diversity in southwestern Washington. We make the greatest contribution to our natural resources when we collaborate to solve problems rather than engage in copious vanity lawsuits.  
Honorable Governor Ferguson, I am at peace with my situation in large part because I had the opportunity to lead a full and meaningful life of public service, including with the Commission. I thank you again for allowing me one of the very richest opportunities to serve and wish you and those at the Department much success. 
In service, 
Victor Garcia

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska should turn AI time savings into mentor time
description: Alaska has a workforce problem that artificial intelligence could either ease or worsen. The state needs more people who can become skilled, dependable workers. AI can remove routine work and make experienced employees more productive. But if employers simply eliminate the junior tasks that once taught people how the work actually functions, they may save […[...]
text:
A computer screen reflects a window, and shows the default prompt when opening ChatGPT, a popular generative AI application often credited with igniting the AI boom since its release in 2022. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)Alaska has a workforce problem that artificial intelligence could either ease or worsen. The state needs more people who can become skilled, dependable workers. AI can remove routine work and make experienced employees more productive. But if employers simply eliminate the junior tasks that once taught people how the work actually functions, they may save time today while weakening the supply of capable workers tomorrow.
That risk matters in a state already investing heavily in apprenticeship. Alaska’s Registered Apprenticeship program reports thousands of active apprentices and more than 1,000 apprenticeable occupations, while the state’s State Training and Employment Program supports employer-linked training, including on-the-job training and registered apprenticeship.
The lesson from those programs should shape workplace AI adoption far beyond the traditional trades: People develop judgment through real work under experienced supervision.
The latest labor evidence makes the case for designing AI adoption around coached judgment rather than simply removing junior work more urgent. The Stanford Digital Economy Lab’s August 2026 Canaries update found that the employment shortfall for workers ages 22–25 in highly AI-exposed occupations widened from 15% in the July 2025 data vintage to 19% by June 2026.
Employers should respond by automating preparation, not apprenticeship.
Consider the kinds of tasks AI can now handle quickly: drafting a first report, summarizing records, preparing a customer response, assembling research, classifying routine cases or producing a preliminary analysis. Those tasks may look like drudgery, but they also used to give newer workers repeated exposure to the ordinary cases that teach them what normal looks like.
Once that preparation is automated, junior roles should move toward verification and exceptions. A newer employee can check whether an AI-generated summary matches the source record, investigate discrepancies, compare an unusual case with prior examples, test an assumption, explain why a recommendation is uncertain and prepare the question that requires a senior decision.
That is more valuable work than copying information from one system to another. It can also build competence faster, if experienced workers still coach it.
Alaska employers should therefore adopt a simple mentor-time rule: When an AI workflow saves experienced employees time, reserve a defined share of those saved hours for coaching newer workers. Use that time for case reviews, feedback on failed outputs, explanation of difficult judgments and supervised decisions.
The approach fits Alaska particularly well. In a large, geographically dispersed state, employers cannot always solve a talent gap by hiring an experienced replacement from across town. Health care, public administration, natural-resource industries, transportation, professional services and technology all depend on transferring practical knowledge from people who have seen unusual situations to people who have not yet seen them.
Employers should also add one metric to their AI scorecards: time to independent competence. Measure how long it takes a new worker to spot a bad AI output, handle common exceptions, explain a recommendation and complete routine decisions with limited supervision.
That metric changes the economics of automation. A workflow that saves 20 percent of junior hours but makes the remaining employees slower to develop may create a hidden liability. A workflow that removes clerical preparation while giving beginners more exposure to review, exceptions and coached judgment may build stronger employees in less time.
Alaska already understands the logic of apprenticeship. The state should carry that logic into AI-exposed office and professional work.
Use AI to shorten the distance between beginner and expert. Let machines handle more preparation. Give people more responsibility for verification, exceptions, communication and judgment. Then spend part of the time automation saves on the human coaching that keeps Alaska’s workforce growing.

name: Mississippi Today
title: MDOT plans ‘Big Fix’: $400M, 2½-year repair project for I-20 and I-55
description: Mississippi Department of Transportation Executive Director Brad White, left, and Central District Transportation Commissioner Willie Simmons announce a nearly $400 million roads and bridges improvement project called, The Big Fix, Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026, at MDOT headquarters in Jackson.
text:
Leaders at the Mississippi Department of Transportation announced Tuesday that some of Mississippi’s busiest roadways will undergo major renovations over the next two-and-a-half years as part of a $400-million project. 
Called the “Big Fix,” the project will improve roads and bridges on Interstate 20, which runs east-west, and Interstate 55, which runs north-south, in Hinds and Rankin counties. The project, funded with federal and state dollars, will rehabilitate 36 bridges, resurface 32 miles of roadway and deploy new technology to make travel safer. 
Willie Simmons, Central District transportation commissioner, said at a press conference that when the interstate system was constructed in the 1950s and 1960s, it met all engineering and safety standards at the time. But since then, vehicles have grown larger and traffic has increased. 
“Updating this infrastructure today isn’t about correcting the past,” Simmons said. “It’s about keeping pace with today’s demands and tomorrow’s needs.” 
The project along I-20 will span from Wiggins Road in Jackson to just east of the Pearson Road interchange in Pearl. The project will also run along I-55 from McDowell Road to north of the High Street interchange in Jackson. 
Construction will start next month and is scheduled to conclude toward the end of 2028. Most road closures are expected to occur at night and on weekends to minimize traffic disruption. 
Two full interstate closures on I-20 in each direction will occur: one in 2027 and another in 2028. The westbound lane will be shut down for 45 days during the summer of 2027, and the eastbound lane will be shut down for 45 days in the summer of 2028. 
Explanation of the Mississippi Department of Transportation’s $400-million renovation of I-55 and I-20 is presented on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026, at MDOT headquarters in Jackson. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Agency leaders said about 110,000 vehicles travel in this area each day, so the agency has worked with local elected officials, emergency services and industry leaders for years to plan safe alternate routes. 
Detour routes have not yet been announced but will be posted on the agency’s website as the road closures approach. 
Brad White, executive director of MDOT, said the agency decided to renovate the longer stretch of road at one time instead of targeting portions of road piecemeal to save taxpayers money in the long term and reduce the disruption to drivers. 
“By doing the project this way, you’re turning a project that otherwise would have taken decades to be built into one that could be done within a two-and-a-half-year time,” White said. 
The public can visit GoMDOT.com/TheBigFix for more information and updates about the project.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Class-action lawsuit claims UnityPoint Health shortchanged hourly workers
description: A potential class-action lawsuit filed on behalf of employees of UnityPoint Health alleges the hospital chain has violated wage-and-hour laws by rounding down workers’ actual hours. Plaintiffs Jennifer Randolph and Maggie McMahon, on behalf of themselves and other UnityPoint hourly workers, are suing Iowa Health System, which does business as UnityPoint Heal[...]
text:
(Stock photo by Greenleaf123/Getty Images)A potential class-action lawsuit filed on behalf of employees of UnityPoint Health alleges the hospital chain has violated wage-and-hour laws by rounding down workers’ actual hours.
Plaintiffs Jennifer Randolph and Maggie McMahon, on behalf of themselves and other UnityPoint hourly workers, are suing Iowa Health System, which does business as UnityPoint Health, under the Fair Labor Standards Act.
UnityPoint Health operates 18 regional medical centers and 17 community-network hospitals in Iowa, Illinois and Wisconsin. The company says it employs roughly 29,000 people and generates annual revenue of more than $4.7 billion.
The lawsuit, while focused on Illinois workers and violations of both federal and Illinois state labor laws, was filed this week in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa, where UnityPoint Health is based.
Court records indicate Randolph is a registered nurse who worked for UnityPoint for roughly 16 years at locations in Bettendorf, Rock Island, Ill., and Moline, Ill. McMahon worked for UnityPoint’s Rock Island location from June 2006 through March 2024.
The lawsuit alleges that during the past 10 years, UnityPoint has used a company named Kronos, later renamed UKG, for timekeeping services related to hourly employees.
That timekeeping service, the lawsuit claims, was configured in a manner that rounds off the actual time employees clock in and clock out.  For example, the lawsuit asserts, if a worker is scheduled to begin work at 9 a.m., and clocks in between 8:53 a.m. and 9 a.m., the individual is not credited for the additional minutes of work time. The same is allegedly true of employees who work up to seven minutes past the end of their shift.
UnityPoint, the lawsuit alleges, “systematically rounds time off both ends of its hourly employees’ work shift to the advantage of (the company) and to the financial harm and underpayment of its hourly employees.”
The aggregate sum of unpaid wages for all of the affected employees “is substantial on a daily, weekly, and annual basis,” the lawsuit claims, particularly because UnityPoint employs thousands of hourly employees.
The lawsuit seeks court approval of class-action status, as well as a judgment in the amount of all back wages due UnityPoint workers, plus statutory damages and attorneys’ fees. The lead attorney for the plaintiffs in the case is Nate Boulton of the Des Moines law firm of Hedberg & Boulton, a former Iowa state senator.
While UnityPoint has not yet filed an answer to the pending lawsuit, it did file and answer to the same set of allegations made by the same plaintiffs in April 2026 when the case was first initiated in Illinois Central District Court.
In that case, which was dropped once the Iowa case was filed, UnityPoint specifically denied rounding off workers’ actual hours and also denied paying its hourly employees based on rounded time rather than actual hours worked.

title: US Rep. Vasquez backs 2 federal data center bills as developments come under scrutiny in New Mexico
description: U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.) on Tuesday announced he had co-sponsored two federal bills aimed at data center transparency.
text:
U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.) on Aug. 25, 2026, announced he signed on as a co-sponsor to two federal bills aimed at placing guardrails around data center developments nationwide. (Courtesy photo)U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.) on Tuesday announced he had co-sponsored two federal bills aimed at data center transparency.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Vasquez signed on as a co-sponsor to the FAIR Data Act, sponsored by Rep. Josh Riley (D-N.Y.), and the Data Center Water and Energy Transparency Act of 2026, sponsored by Rep. Lauren Underwood (D-IL).
The FAIR Data Act would shield residential electric customers and small businesses from shouldering increased energy costs related to large data centers. The Data Center Water and Energy Transparency Act of 2026 would require developers to provide state and local governments that have data centers, or are considering them, with information pertaining to energy and water consumption. Companies that don’t comply would face fines of up to $20,000 per day.
“New Mexico’s water, air and resources belong to us, not to billionaires from coastal states who see an opportunity to extract profit from our land,” Vasquez said in a statement. “I’ve been appalled at the backroom deals, silencing of dissenting voices, shady NDAs and shell companies, and the overall lack of transparency from those who seek to do business in our state.”
Vasquez’s announcement came one day after his cCongressional colleague U.S. Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.) sent a letter to several state agencies demanding detailed information about water usage for Project Jupiter, the Oracle and OpenAI data center under construction in southern New Mexico, which lies in the 2nd Congressional District Vasquez represents.
The only direct mention of Project Jupiter in Vasquez’s announcement was a reference to his July condemnation of a security guard’s use of physical force at a Doña Ana County meeting where residents protested against the development.
Earlier this year, Vasquez called on elected officials in a small New Mexico county to adopt a data center moratorium as a Canadian tech CEO sought to build a massive data center and solar array in their community.
Source NM reported that neither Green Data nor its CEO, Jason Bak, had ever successfully built a data center. Yet Bak’s company sought to build on 10,000 acres in partnership with New Mexico Tech, the local university.
County commissioners ultimately adopted the moratorium and New Mexico Tech nixed the deal, in large part because it didn’t have enough contiguous land to host the development.
“New Mexico should absolutely compete for the jobs and technology of the future, but we are not going to sell out our water, our clean air or our way of life to do it,” Vasquez said in his Tuesday statement. “If you want to do business here, you need to be transparent, listen to local residents, and most importantly, prove to New Mexicans that projects will serve, not steal from, our communities.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Brinks says Senate won’t vote on Money Out of Politics measure, leaving voters to decide
description: The Michiganders for Money Out of Politics ballot proposal seeking to bar political contributions from major utility companies and government contractors is headed for the November ballot, after Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids) said the chamber will not take up a version of the proposal in the Legislature.  Under Michigan law, after a […[...]
text:
Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks, D-Grand Rapids, speaks to reporters at the Michigan Capitol in Lansing, Mich., after Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer's eighth and final State of the State address on Feb. 25, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)The Michiganders for Money Out of Politics ballot proposal seeking to bar political contributions from major utility companies and government contractors is headed for the November ballot, after Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids) said the chamber will not take up a version of the proposal in the Legislature. 
Under Michigan law, after a referendum is approved for the ballot by the Board of State Canvassers, the Legislature has 40 days to take up and pass the measure or the proposal goes to the voters in the general election. 
“MMOP has successfully gathered more than half a million signatures and the message from Michiganders is clear: They want this on the ballot in November. Senate Democrats already agree that there is too much dark money in politics, and we are eager to hear what voters have to say on this issue,” Brinks told the Detroit Free Press on Tuesday. “In that spirit, we will not be subverting the will of the voters, taking it up legislatively.”
Brinks, who was recently named the running mate of Democratic gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson, made her statement shortly after a version of the proposal passed through the Republican-controlled Michigan House of Representatives with bipartisan support in the chamber. Votes in favor from the Democratic side included House Minority Leader Ranjeev Puri (D-Canton), while the only Republican to vote against the proposal was Rep. Jim DeSana (R-Carleton). 
House Speaker Matt Hall (R-Richland Township) celebrated his chamber’s passage of the legislation, saying that they were trying to stop large corporations from “screwing the people” in campaign finance contributions. 
Hall said in a press conference Tuesday afternoon that the proposal for which the group gathered signatures was intended to put it before the Legislature.
“I’ve heard the argument that there’s an attempt to put this on the ballot. I would just say this: if that was the purpose, they could go and do a constitutional amendment,” Hall said. “And a constitutional amendment would go on the ballot. That’s not what we have here. What we have here is one of the processes that the purpose of this is to put it before the Legislature.” 
He was critical of Brinks’ intention not to vote on the legislation throughout the press conference, calling it a “mistake” not to bring the Senate into session to vote on the proposal. 
“I think we took a big step today, so my hope is that Winnie Brinks now will bring the Senate back and do their job and take a vote,” he said. “We can make it a guarantee, we can do it right now. This thing might not pass.”
House Speaker Matt Hall (R-Richland Twp.) presents on proposed cuts within Michigan’s FY27 budget at a press conference. April 16, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
However, throughout the process of gathering signatures, organizers for the proposal have focused their efforts on getting the proposal on the ballot for general election voters as opposed to passing it through the legislature. 
Michiganders for Money Out of Politics leaders celebrated Brinks’ decision not to take up the proposal, saying that Hall “should be ashamed of himself.”
“Leader Brinks gets it. Michiganders are fed up with out-of-control corporate political spending and are ready to change our political system this November. We thank her for respecting the will of over half of million voters who made it clear they want to vote on this measure in November, said Maura Cowley, campaign manager for Michiganders for Money Out of Politics. “Don’t be fooled – what we saw from Hall today was nothing more than political gamesmanship. He never had any intention of getting money out of politics. If he did, he wouldn’t have let common-sense, bipartisan policies to root out corruption in politics sit in committee time and time again.”  
Attempts by Republican lawmakers to adopt the legislation to keep it off the November ballot could have made it easier to amend or overturn later, Michigan Reps. Carrie Rheingans (D-Ann Arbor) and Betsy Coffia (D-Traverse City) told Planet Detroit prior to the vote in the House.
“The thousands of Michiganders who organized, collected signatures, and successfully qualified this initiative for the ballot deserve the opportunity to vote on it this November,” Rep. Emily Dievendorf (D-Lansing) posted on Facebook to explain why they voted against the proposal in the House. “The question before us today was not whether every legislator agrees with every provision. It was whether we trust Michigan voters to have their say.”
A vote in the Legislature was one of two final hurdles that the proposal faced before going to the voters in November, along with a lawsuit filed by Protect MI Free Speech, a group in opposition to the proposal. As of Aug. 20, no oral arguments had been scheduled on that lawsuit, according to Planet Detroit.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Mass. gives schools a playbook for ICE at the door
authors: Colin A. Young I State House News Service
description: The governor's office shared new guidance for how Massachusetts schools and child care centers should handle federal immigration enforcement.
text:
AS SCHOOLS ACROSS MASSACHUSETTS prepare to welcome students back and adjust to new responsibilities under the state’s recent immigrant protection law, the governor’s office Tuesday shared new guidance for handling situations that involve immigration enforcement at schools and child care centers.
The state guidelines provide “clear steps to follow if ICE agents arrive on site or request access to a student, child or their information,” the administration said, and touches on considerations like designating staff points of contact, reviewing and responding to requests, involving legal counsel when appropriate, documenting interactions, notifying families and protecting confidential information.
The immigrant protection law that Gov. Maura Healey signed August 5 expanded protections against warrantless civil immigration arrests to courthouses, public schools, child care centers and health care facilities. It also required schools and state-funded or licensed child care programs to adopt policies governing interactions with civil law enforcement – and have them in effect by September 1 or the first day of the 2026–2027 school year, whichever is earlier. 
“As families prepare for the new school year, every child should feel safe walking into their classroom and every parent should feel confident dropping them off,” Healey said in a statement. “The PROTECT Act makes clear that schools and child care programs are places for children to learn and grow, not places for ICE to target families. These resources give educators and providers the clear guidance they need to put those protections into practice.”
The Department of Elementary and Secondary Education released model policies and procedures for school districts, charter schools and educational collaboratives on Tuesday. The administration’s suggestions “also provide procedures for alerting school communities when civil law enforcement agents are confirmed on school grounds while protecting individual privacy” and for updating student emergency contacts.
Policies and guidance for licensed and state-funded child care centers, family child care homes, school-aged child care programs and group care facilities came from the Department of Early Education and Care. EEC also partnered with the Massachusetts Office for Refugees and Immigrants to provide “Know Your Rights” training for the early education and care sector, including information about immigrant and refugee rights, available legal resources and interactions with immigration and law enforcement officers.
When Healey signed the law in Chelsea, the city’s manager said it offered relief to many in the community who have been afraid to go to work, school and other locations over fears of running into ICE agents. Chelsea has among the highest foreign-born populations in Massachusetts, with US Census numbers showing about 46 percent of the city’s residents are immigrants.
“We in the city have seen the cost of that fear: empty classroom seats, neighbors who have left the state, businesses that have shuttered, and trust broken between residents and our institutions that are meant to protect them,” Fidel Maltez, Chelsea’s city manager, said.
House Speaker Ron Mariano, a former teacher, said “dangerous and illegal actions taken by federal immigration agents have immigrants in Massachusetts living in fear as they go about their daily lives, including when they bring their children to school.” He said the new law and the guidance for schools “are about ensuring that the Commonwealth is doing everything it can to preserve schools as safe spaces for learning, rather than allowing them to become opportunities for warrantless harassment and detainment.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Absentee ballot requests begin in Iowa for Nov. 3 election
description: Iowans were able to begin requesting absentee ballots for the 2026 general election on Tuesday, even as the Trump administration continues to fight in court for changes in the process of voting by mail. Tuesday was officially 70 days before the Nov. 3 election, which means Iowans can begin submitting Absentee Ballot Request Forms to […]
text:
The Dallas County absentee and special precinct board met in Adel Tuesday, Nov. 12 to count absentee and provisional ballots submitted in the 2024 general election. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Iowans were able to begin requesting absentee ballots for the 2026 general election on Tuesday, even as the Trump administration continues to fight in court for changes in the process of voting by mail.
Tuesday was officially 70 days before the Nov. 3 election, which means Iowans can begin submitting Absentee Ballot Request Forms to their local county auditor’s office in order to receive a mailed absentee ballot for the election. The deadline for submitting an absentee ballot request form is 5 p.m. Oct. 19 — 15 days before the election.
The written application doesn’t need to be notarized or witnessed, but must include information that verifies the voter’s identity, such as a person’s Iowa driver’s license or non-operator ID number, or the PIN number on an Iowa Voter ID Card.
Iowa county auditors can begin mailing out absentee ballots Oct. 14. The ballots must be received by the county auditor by 8 p.m. on Nov. 3, Election Day, in order to be counted. If a person is not able to return their absentee ballot to their county auditor’s office on Election Day, there are still options to vote — voters can surrender their voted absentee ballot at a polling location and cast a regular ballot, or vote using a provisional ballot if they cannot surrender the absentee ballot.
The process of beginning absentee ballot requests comes in 2026 one day after the U.S. Supreme Court issued an unsigned emergency docket opinion finding 23 Democratic-led states do not have standing to stop his executive order related to mail-in ballot processing by the U.S. Postal Service.
Trump executive order still in court
Trump signed an executive order in March that directed the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and the Social Security Administration to compile a list of voting-age American citizens in each state and share it with state election officials. It also required the U.S. Postal Service to only send and receive ballots that include tracking barcodes.
Despite the Monday ruling, another U.S. District Court decision blocking the USPS from carrying out parts of the executive order in a case filed by the League of Women Voters of Massachusetts and several other voting rights groups, remains in place.
A spokesperson for Iowa Secretary of State’s office said in an email the state office overseeing elections expects “no direct impacts on Iowans as a result of this ruling.” Iowa Secretary of State Paul Pate, a Republican, told reporters at the Iowa State Fair earlier in August he was opposed to the federal government’s recent approach to regulating mail-in ballots.
“Iowans really lean into being able to vote in the mail,” Pate said. “We have a very high percentage of that. We’ve done it right in the state. And I caution the White House and anybody who wants to listen to us in D.C. (to) come out and look at us in Iowa. I feel pretty good about how we do it here. So take a couple of pages from our playbook, and you’ll be maybe feel more comfortable. I understand where some of their frustration might come from, where some of their passion. But let’s not lose sight that — my humble opinion — the Constitution says elections are run by the states. And with all due respect to the president, I hope he’ll trust Iowans to run our elections.”

description: Debbie Churchill has been selected as the next executive director for the Montana Republican Party. She replaces former party executive director Andrew Pierce, who held the position for about a year. Churchill is a fifth-generation Montanan from a ranching family south of Chinook. A graduate of the University of Montana school of law, Churchill is […]
text:
Montana GOP Headquarters in Helena, MT. Credit: Keith SchubertDebbie Churchill has been selected as the next executive director for the Montana Republican Party.
She replaces former party executive director Andrew Pierce, who held the position for about a year. Churchill is a fifth-generation Montanan from a ranching family south of Chinook. A graduate of the University of Montana school of law, Churchill is a retired real estate planning attorney.
She’s volunteered since 2019 for the state Republican Party and was the state party’s first Grassroots Director, a press release from the Montana Republicans said.
“This party isn’t built in Helena. It’s built in county central committee meetings and at kitchen tables from Chinook to Miles City,” Churchill said. “My job is to make sure every one of those Republican volunteers has what they need to win.”
She currently is also involved with the Jefferson County Republican Central Committee.
“Debbie has spent years building the MTGOP from the grassroots up, and she knows this party county by county,” Montana Republican Party Chairman Art Wittich said. “Her leadership, organizational experience, and commitment to Montana Republicans make her the right person to lead our staff into the general election.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Higher education in Louisiana, short $800M, appears headed for a funding overhaul
description: A legislative task force is staring at a growing problem with higher education in Louisiana: How to fund a system with more demands than ever before while state and federal dollars are on the decline.  Louisiana uses a outcomes-based formula to fund its colleges and universities. The bulk of the money provided, 70%, is considered […]
text:
Graduates stand at the end of University of Louisiana at Lafayette commencement exercises May 16, 2025, at the Cajun Dome. (Greg LaRose/Louisiana Illuminator)A legislative task force is staring at a growing problem with higher education in Louisiana: How to fund a system with more demands than ever before while state and federal dollars are on the decline. 
Louisiana uses a outcomes-based formula to fund its colleges and universities. The bulk of the money provided, 70%, is considered base funding to cover their operational expenses. The remaining 30% rewards schools for reaching benchmarks, such as student retention, and meeting state priorities like workforce needs. 
Questions about the formula were first raised earlier this year when some conservative lawmakers became aware of an old metric that incentivized universities to graduate already-enrolled minority students. Though it had already been removed from the formula, this metric became the topic of a U.S. Department of Education investigation. 
The task force, which held its first meeting Tuesday, comes together at a time when higher education financing in Louisiana faces myriad challenges. They include schools being asked to do more to promote workforce development as Louisiana launches a series of major industrial projects. 
Louisiana’s higher education funding problems are not new ones, although they have become more acute. During Gov. Bobby Jindal’s tenure from 2008-16, the state was in a self-inflicted fiscal crisis, with the governor choosing to use single-year budget surpluses to fund ongoing state government expenses. Higher education was on the chopping block annually to balance the budget, leading colleges and universities to switch from being primarily state-funded to student tuition-supported. 
Since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, inflation has created additional constraints across state government. Gov. Jeff Landry has kept higher education spending at a standstill since he took office in 2024. 
Elizabeth Bentley-Smith, the Landry administration’s deputy commissioner of higher education for finance and administration, told the task force that Louisiana’s public colleges and universities are underfunded by more than $800 million. 
Increased costs for college athletics have been amplified over the past few years with the advent of revenue sharing and name, image and likeness payments. Schools are now diverting money from other items previously covered through philanthropy, such as facility upkeep, to keep their team rosters intact, university officials said. 
Louisiana’s college sports programs are losing money. Can sales taxes save them?

As a result, nearly every athletic department at Louisiana’s Division I schools operates at a deficit, adding additional budget pressure to their universities.
These factors, plus declining enrollment at several institutions, have created budget crises at schools, including the University of New Orleans (now LSU New Orleans) and the University of Louisiana at Lafayette. 
UNO faced a $30 million budget shortfall and implemented a spending freeze, layoffs and staff furloughs in an attempt to make ends meet. Due to the budget crunch, the school was transferred from the University of Louisiana System to the LSU System, with legislators approving more than $20 million to pay for the move.
UL Lafayette faced an approximately $50 million shortfall and implemented similar austerity measures. 
The problem is likely to compound moving forward, with college enrollment anticipated to fall and the federal policy landscape uncertain. 
Louisiana’s population is shrinking and its birth rate is declining. The state is projected to see a 7.5% to 15% decrease in students who attend college by 2029, the Public Affairs Research Council detailed three years ago in a report on falling enrollment in Louisiana. 
That’s a problem because Louisiana’s colleges and universities have become increasingly dependent on student tuition dollars. 
“This is a potential harbinger of things to come,” PAR President Steven Procopio told the task force. 
On top of the state-level problems, federal policy could also lead to challenges for higher education, two analysts from the State Higher Education Executive Officers Association told the panel. 
The Pell Grant program, which provides funding for low-income students to attend college, is already operating at a shortfall, which is projected to continually increase. Tom Harnisch, SHEEO’s vice president for government relations, said Congress either needs to provide more Pell funds, restrict who’s eligible or reduce award amounts. 
The latter two options would be a problem for Louisiana, where 42% of college students get the award compared with 32% nationwide. 
In addition, changes in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act reduced federal loan opportunities for graduate school students and could eliminate financial aid opportunities entirely for some programs if they fail the “do no harm” standard. It means graduates from those programs earn no more compared with those without that level of education. 
Higher Education Commissioner Kim Hunter Reed said the Board of Regents is examining these changes to estimate their impact to Louisiana’s college and university budgets. 
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act will also reduce Medicaid funding over the next 10 years, which will cut hard in Louisiana, one of four states facing the largest decreases. Historically, higher education has absorbed the brunt of major budget cuts in Louisiana. 
As these costs pile up, Kristine Strickland, chancellor of Fletcher Technical Community College in Terrebonne Parish, said so do the expectations. 
The governor has announced a series of major economic development projects throughout the state, each with their own specialized workforce needs. Many of these companies have made donations to the community colleges and universities that will train the students they intend to hire, but the brunt of funding these new programs falls on the schools themselves. 
“We’re being called upon more and more to be responsive in an immediate time frame,” Strickland said at the task force meeting. “We do know that standing up new programs is a more expensive venture than maintaining current programs, and then taking those to scale is even more expensive.” 
Sen. Mike Reese, R-Leesville, who chairs the task force, said it will meet at least three more times and hear budget presentations from campus leaders as well as state economic development and labor officials. 
Reese, who became McNeese State University president on July 1, said he wasn’t sure if the committee’s report, which must be submitted to the Legislature by February, would overhaul the state’s higher education formula or just recommend tweaks.

name: VTDigger
title: UVM president says school’s budget deficit is closed despite declining enrollment
description:
Just before the fall semester begins at the University of Vermont, President Marlene Tromp delivered a “State of the University” address. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  UVM president says school’s budget deficit is closed despite declining enrollment.
text:
University of Vermont President Marlene Tromp delivers her State of the University address in Burlington on Tuesday, August 25, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
BURLINGTON — The University of Vermont has closed its $12 million projected budget deficit, President Marlene Tromp reported just days before first-year students are set to arrive on campus. 
Tromp delivered the first “State of the University” address to trustees and hundreds of staff Tuesday with one resounding message: “We will not be daunted in the face of the challenges before us.” 
Her declaration of the university’s resiliency comes after the school warned in March that it projected a 15% decline in freshman undergraduate students this fall compared with last year and a 7% decrease across all undergraduate enrollment. 
In Tromp’s presentation, she reported that about 10,800 students are currently enrolled at the university this fall. And, as expected, freshman enrollment is down. 
Still, the university has been able to fully close its projected budget deficit by eliminating vacant staff positions and “operational inefficiencies,” Tromp said in an interview Tuesday. 

READ MORE

Along with declining enrollment, the university is facing a combination of “serious challenges,” including cuts to federal funding for research and a difficulty recruiting students from Vermont, Tromp said during her address. 
Colleges and universities across the country have long anticipated that enrollment would decline as they face a phenomenon dubbed the “demographic cliff.” Fewer people are projected to attend college in part because Americans started having fewer babies around the start of the Great Recession in late 2007. 
Universities, especially those in New England, have been hit the hardest, Tromp said, as they’re forced to compete for students. 
“We are building a three-year planning process so we can think ahead, and instead of being reactive, we can be proactive in the face of the changes that are before us,” Tromp said. 
About 2,600 first-year students are enrolled this fall, according to Adam White, a spokesperson for the university. UVM usually aims to enroll about 3,000, he said. 
Vermont has its own demographic struggles. With fewer young people in the state and a small overall population, there are limited ways that residents can support the university, which increases UVM’s tuition compared with other public universities, Tromp said. 
Amid sweeping cuts to federal grant funding for scientific research, Tromp said that UVM received $222.6 million in research funding for the 2026 fiscal year — an “extraordinary outcome” given the headwinds in the federal funding landscape. 
“Some universities were really struck hard by those cuts, and we were very fortunate that we didn’t face as many as a lot of other universities did,” Tromp said in the interview. 
In some cases, the university was able to provide short-term funds to keep research projects afloat while grants were paused, she said.
In her speech, Tromp highlighted one professor who lost grant funding for a project that sent graduate counseling and social work students to work in rural schools. After losing her national grant funding, the professor crowdsourced money to keep the project going.  
The university is also set to launch an aggressive fundraising campaign through the UVM Foundation, Tromp said, which raises money for the university’s endowment. 
“I’m really excited about it because that will help us weather a lot of storms,” she said.
